n.3: Increased control is unnecessary and counterproductive at high maturity.
n.0: Minimal communication risks misalignment despite strong performance.
n.1: Over-governance slows decision-making without clear benefit.

Leadership.q: A project team is meeting deadlines but quality is declining because members are rushing work to avoid criticism from a demanding sponsor. Which leadership action would MOST improve sustainable performance?
o: Ask the sponsor to communicate directly with team members to increase urgency
Increase pressure on the team to maintain delivery pace and avoid stakeholder concern
Move quality checks to the end of each stage so progress is not disrupted
Rebalance expectations by reinforcing quality standards and creating space for honest escalation
Reward individuals who deliver fastest to reinforce the required pace
Leadership.w: Leadership influences performance by shaping conditions for motivation, quality and honest communication. The project manager should reduce fear-driven behaviour while maintaining standards.

n.1: More pressure may protect pace briefly but is likely to worsen quality and motivation.
n.2: Delaying quality checks does not address the motivational problem causing poor work.
n.0: Direct sponsor pressure may increase anxiety and reduce team ownership.
n.4: Rewarding speed can reinforce the behaviour that is damaging quality.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor encourages an experienced project manager to spend time mentoring several junior members of staff over the coming year. From the organisation's perspective, what is the primary intended benefit of establishing this mentoring arrangement?
Leadership.w: Mentoring builds skills and confidence in junior staff.

n.1: The purpose is development, not reducing workload.
n.2: Mentoring isn't focused on task speed.
n.0: Documentation is still needed.
n.3: The goal is growth, not sponsor visibility.

Leadership.q: A project manager has taken on a newly formed team whose members are unfamiliar with the work and unclear about task priorities. Considering when firmer guidance is warranted, which TWO scenarios MOST justify a shift towards a more directive leadership style?
o: A high-performing team consistently delivers without supervision
A team lacks experience and shows confusion over task priorities
A mature team demonstrates strong ownership and accountability
A new team is unfamiliar with processes and requires structured guidance
An experienced team requests greater autonomy over decisions
Leadership.w: Low competence and uncertainty require directive leadership to provide clarity and structure.

n.0: High-performing teams do not require increased direction.
n.4: Requests for autonomy suggest readiness for less directive styles.
n.2: Mature teams benefit from delegation rather than direction.

Leadership.q: A project manager is preparing to give a team member some difficult performance feedback. What role does emotional intelligence play in how the manager handles this feedback conversation?
o: It replaces the need for regular communication
It helps leaders deliver feedback constructively and sensitively
It allows leaders to ignore team responses
It removes the need to provide feedback
It guarantees that all feedback is positive
Leadership.w: EI helps leaders consider emotions when delivering and responding to feedback.

n.3: Feedback remains important.
n.2: Ignoring responses is not a feature of EI.
n.0: EI enhances, not replaces, communication.
n.4: Not all feedback will be positive, but EI helps manage this.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to introduce something that will genuinely raise team members' job satisfaction rather than merely stop them becoming dissatisfied. Within Herzberg's theory, which of the following is a motivator that directly enhances job satisfaction?
Leadership.w: Recognition is a motivator that fosters satisfaction; the others are hygiene factors.

n.4: Policy is a hygiene factor.
n.3: Working conditions are hygiene factors.
n.1: Salary is a hygiene factor.
n.2: Supervision quality is treated as hygiene in Herzberg’s model.

Leadership.q: A manufacturing manager finds routines well-established and team highly skilled, so he delegates almost all decisions. Which of the following factors was NOT relevant in prompting this change?
Leadership.w: Market volatility was not a factor in deciding to delegate authority to a skilled team working on routine tasks.

n.0: High competence justified the decision to delegate.
n.3: Clear procedures supported a delegating style.
n.2: High commitment allowed the manager to trust the team.
n.1: Time constraints can lead leaders to delegate to trusted team members.

Leadership.q: A project manager is comparing McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y to decide how much direction and oversight a particular team requires. Which of the following statements contrasting Theory X and Theory Y is FALSE?
o: Theory Y sees work as a natural activity
Theory X views employees as lazy
Theory Y trusts employees to self-direct
Theory X assumes workers seek responsibility
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes employees avoid responsibility, not that they seek it.

n.1: Theory X indeed views people as lazy.
n.0: Theory Y regards work as inherently satisfying.
n.3: Theory Y trusts self-direction and autonomy.
n.2: Theory X managers use close control and supervision.

Leadership.q: When selecting people for a new project team, a project manager plans to use Belbin team roles to inform how the team is built and managed. Regarding the appropriate use of this model, which statement is MOST appropriate?
o: Belbin roles are mainly used to rank team members by leadership potential
Belbin roles determine formal authority within the project organisation structure
Belbin roles should be used to permanently label individuals and restrict their tasks
Belbin roles replace the need for defined project roles and responsibilities
Belbin roles help identify behavioural contributions and possible team balance gaps
Leadership.w: Belbin roles describe behavioural contributions and can help a project manager understand team balance and gaps.

n.2: Belbin should not be used to rigidly label or limit individuals.
n.3: Belbin does not replace formal project roles and responsibilities.
n.0: Belbin is not a ranking system for leadership potential.
n.1: Belbin roles are behavioural, not formal authority positions.

Leadership.q: A technically strong project team is generating many ideas but repeatedly fails to convert them into practical actions. Which Belbin team role would MOST directly address this gap?
o: Resource Investigator, by identifying external contacts and opportunities
Implementer, by turning concepts into structured and workable plans
Plant, by introducing more original ideas and alternative solutions
Monitor Evaluator, by assessing ideas for logic and strategic fit
Specialist, by providing deeper knowledge in a narrow technical area
Leadership.w: An Implementer is useful where ideas need to be converted into practical plans and organised action.

n.2: A Plant would add more ideas, but the team already has enough ideas and lacks practical conversion.
n.3: A Monitor Evaluator assesses options but does not primarily turn ideas into action.
n.0: A Resource Investigator looks outward for opportunities and contacts, not implementation discipline.
n.4: A Specialist provides expertise, but the issue is execution rather than technical depth.

Leadership.q: A project manager is choosing the most appropriate leadership style for a piece of work being handed to a particular group. Which pair of situational factors is most important to weigh up when making that choice?
Leadership.w: Follower readiness and task complexity determine which leadership approach will be effective.

n.3: Hierarchy and office location are not primary situational leadership factors.
n.0: Budget and market share are business metrics, not leadership style determinants.
n.4: Group size and branding do not drive situational style selection.
n.2: Training schedules and reporting structure are unrelated to style choice.

Leadership.q: A project manager publicly blames individuals for defects during team meetings. Defects are then hidden until late in delivery. What is the BEST explanation of the performance issue?
o: The quality process is too detailed and should be simplified immediately
The team is likely in a performing stage and needs less intervention
The project manager should increase individual performance tracking
The team lacks technical competence and needs additional formal training
The leadership climate is discouraging openness and weakening problem reporting
Leadership.w: Blame-based leadership damages psychological safety, causing people to hide issues rather than raise them early.

n.3: The issue described is concealment caused by fear, not necessarily lack of competence.
n.0: Simplifying the process does not address the leadership behaviour causing hiding.
n.2: More tracking may increase fear and further reduce openness.
n.1: A performing team would normally surface and resolve issues proactively.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants a single set of actions that will both reduce dissatisfaction and actively motivate the team, addressing hygiene factors and motivators together as Herzberg describes. Which of the following approaches would most likely satisfy both needs simultaneously?
o: Raising salaries WITHOUT enriching the job content
Improving workplace facilities AND offering credit for high performance
Improving job security AND increasing supervision levels
Providing free snacks AND refreshments only
Enforcing stricter policies AND closely monitoring attendance
Leadership.w: Better facilities address hygiene; performance credits address motivators like recognition and achievement.

n.2: Reviews alone may not address motivators sufficiently.
n.0: Salary is hygiene; without motivators, satisfaction is limited.
n.4: Stricter policies only tackle hygiene factors.
n.3: Free snacks are only a minor hygiene improvement.

Leadership.q: During an urgent crisis, a leader shifts to an autocratic style to make rapid decisions. Which of the following was NOT a reason for this change?
o: To accelerate decision-making under time pressure
Because the situation had high stakes
Leadership.w: Gathering broad input is not consistent with an autocratic approach in a crisis.

n.2: Time pressure in a crisis justifies faster decision-making.
n.3: High stakes support an autocratic approach when speed is vital.
n.4: Uncertainty often leads leaders to take a more directive stance.
n.1: Critical need for quick action justifies autocratic control.

Leadership.q: A team has resolved earlier conflicts and now collaborates effectively, with clear roles and shared understanding of objectives. Which stage BEST describes this behaviour?
o: Forming, where roles and expectations are still unclear
Norming, where cohesion and mutual understanding develop
Adjourning, where focus is on project completion and disengagement
Performing, where the team is fully autonomous and optimised
Leadership.w: Norming is characterised by collaboration, clarity, and reduced conflict following the storming phase.

n.0: Forming lacks the clarity and cohesion described.
n.2: Storming would involve ongoing conflict, not resolution.
n.4: Performing reflects higher autonomy and productivity beyond norming.
n.3: Adjourning relates to closure, not team cohesion.

Leadership.q: A capable project team has become passive because the project manager makes all meaningful decisions. What is the MOST likely leadership impact on performance?
o: The team may lose ownership and reduce discretionary effort
The team may become more efficient because decision-making is centralised
The team may require fewer communications because accountability is removed
The team will usually become more innovative due to clearer control
The team will avoid conflict and therefore perform more consistently
Leadership.w: Excessive control can reduce ownership, motivation and initiative, especially where the team is capable of contributing to decisions.

n.1: Centralised decisions can sometimes be faster but often reduce engagement and initiative.
n.3: Innovation usually falls when team members are denied meaningful influence.
n.4: Avoiding conflict does not necessarily improve performance or commitment.
n.2: Removing accountability is more likely to weaken performance than improve communication.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that despite high technical capability, the team struggles to agree on approaches and decisions, leading to delays. Which stage BEST explains this behaviour?
o: Norming, where consensus is easily reached and roles are clear
Performing, where decisions are made efficiently without conflict
Forming, where capability is still developing and roles are unclear
Storming, where disagreements and competing views affect progress
Adjourning, where focus is on closing activities rather than decisions
Leadership.w: Storming is characterised by conflict and difficulty in decision-making despite capability.

n.2: Forming would involve uncertainty rather than strong disagreement.
n.0: Norming implies smoother decision-making and alignment.
n.1: Performing teams resolve decisions efficiently.
n.4: Adjourning is not relevant to decision-making challenges.

Leadership.q: A project manager is checking their understanding of Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which separates the factors that prevent dissatisfaction from those that actively create satisfaction. Which of the following dual-fact statements about Herzberg's theory is correct?
o: Safety needs are motivators AND they include company policy
Self-actualization is a hygiene factor AND includes salary
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction AND they create high motivation
Physiological needs motivate performance AND include teamwork
Motivators drive satisfaction AND include factors like recognition
Leadership.w: Herzberg’s motivators (e.g., recognition) truly drive job satisfaction and motivation.

n.2: Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction but don’t create motivation.
n.0: Safety needs are Maslow’s, not Herzberg’s motivators.
n.3: Physiological needs and teamwork belong to different models.
n.1: Self-actualization is Maslow’s top level, not a hygiene factor, and salary is hygiene.

Leadership.q: A project manager oversees a newly assembled team that is enthusiastic and eager to contribute, but whose members produce work of uneven quality and still lack full competence in some tasks. Which leadership approach BEST reflects effective adaptation to this situation?
o: Applying strict control to eliminate performance variation
Delegating fully to leverage motivation and encourage independence
Reducing interaction to avoid interfering with motivation
Coaching through guidance while encouraging involvement in decisions
Escalating performance issues without direct intervention
Leadership.w: Coaching balances guidance with engagement when motivation is high but capability is uneven.

n.1: Delegation assumes consistent competence which is not present.
n.0: Strict control may reduce motivation despite capability gaps.
n.2: Reduced interaction fails to support capability development.
n.4: Escalation does not replace leadership responsibility.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to develop the capability of team members while still guiding delivery, and chooses to adopt a coaching leadership style during the project. Which TWO leadership behaviours are MOST aligned with that style?
o: Escalating performance issues without direct team engagement
Maintaining strict control over task execution and decision-making
Providing clear direction while encouraging team input on decisions
Supporting problem-solving while developing individual capability
Allowing full autonomy with minimal oversight or guidance
Leadership.w: Coaching combines direction with support, helping develop competence while involving the team.

n.4: Full autonomy reflects delegation, not coaching.
n.1: Strict control aligns with directive style.
n.0: Escalation avoids leadership engagement.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to help capable team members grow and take ownership rather than simply telling them what to do. Why is adopting a coaching style particularly valuable for the development of the team?
o: It encourages individuals to develop their own solutions
It removes the need for team meetings
It ensures tasks are always completed faster
It is required by law in all organisations
It focuses solely on task allocation
Leadership.w: Coaching helps team members grow by guiding them to find their own answers and build confidence.

n.2: Speed is not the main reason for using a coaching style.
n.1: Team meetings remain valuable in any style.
n.4: Task allocation is directive, not coaching.
n.3: Coaching is not a legal requirement.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that one item from Herzberg's list of motivators also corresponds to the higher levels of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Which of the following motivators does Herzberg include that Maslow places near the top of his hierarchy?
Leadership.w: Recognition (a motivator) aligns with Maslow’s self-esteem or self-actualization levels.

n.1: Salary is a hygiene factor.
n.2: Company policy is hygiene.
n.0: Working conditions are hygiene.
n.3: Supervision is treated as hygiene.

Leadership.q: A project manager is setting realistic expectations for a mentoring arrangement they are establishing with a junior colleague. Which of the following is NOT a benefit that mentoring typically delivers in a project environment?
o: Ongoing professional development of the mentee
Leadership.w: Mentoring focuses on development, not instant task completion.

n.0: Mentoring transfers experience and insights.
n.2: Mentoring develops professionals.
n.4: Mentoring builds confidence.
n.3: Mentoring supports career goals.

Leadership.q: A project manager reflecting on what ultimately drives high-performing individuals turns to the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs. Which of the following statements best describes Maslow's concept of self-actualisation?
Leadership.w: Self-actualization is the highest level in Maslow’s hierarchy, where one realizes full personal potential.

n.0: Physiological needs are the most basic level.
n.1: Job security relates to safety needs.
n.3: Social bonds are love/belonging needs.
n.2: Safety needs concern personal security and health.

Leadership.q: An organisation is introducing a significant change and staff are anxious about what it means for them. Why might a project manager with high emotional intelligence be better placed to support such a change initiative?
o: They avoid all discussions about change
They focus only on the technical details
They can recognise and address emotional responses to change
They use a single leadership style for every situation
Leadership.w: EI helps leaders support people through the uncertainty and stress of change.

n.0: Avoiding discussion increases resistance to change.
n.4: Ignoring feedback harms change adoption.
n.1: Change success depends on emotional and technical aspects.
n.3: Flexibility is vital in leadership.

Leadership.q: A project manager is drawing out the practical leadership lessons of Maslow's hierarchy of needs when managing a diverse team. Which of the following is NOT a sound implication of the model for how a leader should act?
Leadership.w: Not every employee aspires immediately to self-actualization; leaders must meet lower-order needs first.

n.1: True: basic needs form the foundation.
n.3: True: security is a safety need.
n.0: True: belonging is key.
n.2: True: esteem needs involve recognition.

Leadership.q: After a project manager began publicly praising individuals for their specific contributions during team meetings, overall productivity noticeably improved. Which motivational theory does this outcome best illustrate?
Leadership.w: Public praise is a motivator (recognition) in Herzberg’s framework, boosting satisfaction and performance.

n.2: Safety needs are unrelated to recognition.
n.3: Hygiene factors don’t motivate performance.
n.4: Theory X would not emphasize praise.
n.0: McClelland’s model is different, focusing on acquired needs.

Leadership.q: After onboarding a skilled development team, a manager observes they are both capable and highly motivated. Which of the following pairs of factors did the manager assess when selecting his leadership style?
Leadership.w: He evaluated team competence and motivation to choose the appropriate style.

n.1: Task complexity and culture were not mentioned as decision drivers.
n.4: Budget and team size did not inform his leadership choice here.
n.0: Reporting and policies are not core situational leadership factors.
n.3: Risk and stakeholder count do not directly determine style in this model.

Leadership.q: A project is losing momentum because the team discusses issues extensively but avoids difficult decisions. Which Belbin role is MOST likely missing?
o: Shaper, because the team needs challenge, drive, and pressure to act
Completer Finisher, because the team needs final checking of completed outputs
Plant, because the team needs more ideas before deciding on direction
Specialist, because the team lacks detailed knowledge of technical constraints
Teamworker, because the team needs more emphasis on harmony and inclusion
Leadership.w: A Shaper challenges inertia, drives progress, and pushes the team through obstacles and indecision.

n.4: More harmony may worsen avoidance if the issue is lack of challenge.
n.3: The issue is not lack of knowledge but reluctance to make decisions.
n.2: More ideas may increase discussion rather than action.
n.1: A Completer Finisher is more relevant when outputs need final accuracy checks.

Leadership.q: A leader encourages a team member to reflect on their performance and set new goals. This is an example of:
Leadership.w: Coaching focuses on personal reflection and growth.

n.3: Micromanagement does not promote reflection.
n.1: Directive style gives instructions, not promotes reflection.
n.0: Autocratic leadership does not encourage team input.
n.4: Laissez-faire is hands-off and does not foster goal setting.

Leadership.q: A project team that was previously cohesive begins to experience renewed conflict after a significant change in scope and the introduction of new members. What is the MOST appropriate interpretation?
o: The team is progressing towards performing as project complexity gradually increases
The team is norming as it adapts to the new challenges
The team is adjourning due to reduced focus on delivery
The team has returned to storming due to changes in structure and context
The team has failed to maintain performance and should be replaced
Leadership.w: Teams can revert to earlier stages such as storming when changes disrupt established dynamics.

n.4: Regression does not imply failure requiring replacement.
n.0: Performing would not involve renewed conflict.
n.1: Norming reflects stability, not renewed disruption.
n.2: Adjourning is unrelated to mid-project changes.

Leadership.q: After taking over a cross-functional team with tight deadlines and varying skill levels, a new manager must decide how much direction and support to provide. Which of the following pairs of factors should he assess before choosing his leadership approach?
Leadership.w: Task urgency and team competence directly influence whether to use a more directive or supportive style.

n.2: Office space and dress code do not impact leadership style choice.
n.1: Popularity and reviews are not primary situational factors.
n.4: Meeting frequency and memo format are unrelated to style adaptation.
n.3: Budget and market trends inform strategy, not moment-to-moment leadership style.

Leadership.q: A project manager wants to use recognition and reward to lift the performance of the delivery team over the course of the project. Which approach is MOST likely to be effective?
o: Use recognition mainly to compensate for unclear objectives
Recognise only senior team members because their work has greater project impact
Recognise visible effort only at the end of the project to avoid distraction
Link recognition to specific behaviours and outcomes that support project objectives
Give identical praise to all team members regardless of contribution
Leadership.w: Recognition is most useful when it is specific, timely and connected to behaviours that improve project performance.

n.2: Delayed recognition loses impact and may not reinforce desired behaviours.
n.4: Generic praise can feel meaningless and may not influence performance.
n.0: Recognition cannot compensate for lack of clear objectives.
n.1: Recognition should reflect contribution, not seniority alone.

Leadership.q: A project manager leads a technically strong team whose members have become passive and reluctant to take initiative on their work. To rebuild commitment, which TWO actions would BEST help the project manager increase ownership in this capable but disengaged team?
o: Focus solely on individual underperformance rather than team conditions
Increase approval layers so decisions feel controlled
Delegate appropriate authority while keeping outcomes clear
Remove all accountability until morale has improved
Involve the team in decisions that affect how work is delivered
Leadership.w: Involvement and appropriate delegation increase ownership while still maintaining clarity over outcomes.

n.3: Removing accountability weakens ownership rather than building it.
n.1: More approval layers usually reduce autonomy and engagement.
n.0: Focusing only on individuals may ignore leadership and team environment causes.

Leadership.q: A project manager under schedule pressure begins driving the team mainly through deadlines, criticism and fear of consequences. Considering the effect of this style, which TWO risks are MOST associated with relying mainly on pressure and fear to drive project performance?
o: Quality normally improves because people feel safer challenging issues
Short-term compliance may replace genuine commitment
Learning and improvement may reduce because people avoid exposing problems
Trust is likely to increase because expectations are strict
Team members may become more willing to report mistakes early
Leadership.w: Fear-based leadership can produce compliance but reduces openness, learning, commitment and long-term performance.

n.4: Fear usually reduces early reporting of mistakes.
n.3: Strictness without safety often reduces trust.
n.0: People are less likely to challenge quality issues when they fear blame.

Leadership.q: A newly appointed manager tends to supervise closely and control the team tightly, believing this reflects human nature at work. Which of the following is a core assumption of McGregor's Theory X that would underpin this behaviour?
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes that people inherently avoid work and need external control to perform.

n.2: That aligns with Theory Y.
n.1: Theory X assumes the opposite.
n.4: Self-direction is a Theory Y belief.
n.0: Intrinsic motivation is a Theory Y concept.

Leadership.q: A leader working with a remote team notices morale is low due to isolation. To improve motivation, she adopts a more ______ style, offering support and encouragement through regular check-ins.
Leadership.w: A supportive style addresses team morale by offering encouragement and assistance.

n.1: Directive style focuses on instructions, not morale support.
n.0: Delegating involves less leader involvement, unsuitable for low morale.
n.3: Autocratic emphasizes control, not supportive engagement.
n.4: Hands-off is similar to delegating and does not provide needed support.

Leadership.q: A project manager introduces performance bonuses hoping to lift a demotivated team, yet after several weeks morale and engagement remain stubbornly low. Which motivational theory best explains why the financial incentive failed to improve satisfaction?
Leadership.w: Herzberg’s model suggests that while bonuses (a hygiene factor) prevent dissatisfaction, they don’t create true motivation or job satisfaction.

n.2: Maslow’s model doesn’t distinguish hygiene versus motivators.
n.0: Theory Y assumes employees are self-motivated, not about hygiene factors.
n.4: Self-actualization is the highest need, unrelated to simple bonuses.
n.1: Motivation factors (e.g., recognition) do drive satisfaction, but bonuses are hygiene factors.

Leadership.q: A project manager applying a situational leadership approach is deciding how much direction and support to offer different members of the delivery team, whose experience and attitudes vary. Which TWO factors MOST directly influence the appropriate leadership style?
o: Team member motivation and willingness to perform
Team member competence in relation to the task
Project budget constraints and cost pressures
Leadership.w: Situational leadership is primarily based on competence and commitment (motivation) of team members.

n.1: Reporting expectations influence communication, not leadership style selection.
n.3: Budget pressures affect decisions but not directly leadership style choice.
n.4: Governance context may influence constraints but is not the primary driver.

Leadership.q: A seasoned sales team has high expertise and confidence. The leader delegates tasks and decision-making to them. Why did the leader adopt a delegating style?
o: The team demonstrated high competence and commitment
The leader lacked time to support
Leadership.w: Delegating is appropriate when team members are both capable and motivated to work independently.

n.4: The schedule was not mentioned as influencing his decision.
n.2: Increased oversight would require a directive style, not delegation.
n.3: Delegation was based on team capability, not the leader’s time constraints.
n.1: The scenario described high morale, not low morale.

Leadership.q: A project manager introduces a small amount of constructive challenge, clearer goals and regular feedback. Team performance improves without additional resources. What does this MOST clearly demonstrate?
o: Leadership behaviour can influence performance conditions
Motivation is mainly controlled by financial incentives
Resource availability is usually irrelevant to project results
Performance issues are normally solved by tighter governance
Team development models replace the need for planning
Leadership.w: Leadership affects performance by influencing clarity, challenge, feedback, confidence and motivation, even without changing resources.

n.1: The scenario shows non-financial leadership factors improving motivation.
n.2: Resources still matter, but they are not the only performance driver.
n.4: Leadership and team development support planning; they do not replace it.
n.3: Governance alone does not explain improved motivation and performance.

Leadership.q: A team's morale steadily declines because leadership concentrates solely on enforcing process compliance and never acknowledges good work or achievement. Which motivational model best explains this dip in morale?
Leadership.w: Ignoring recognition (a motivator) while focusing on hygiene factors leads to dissatisfaction per Herzberg.

n.2: Maslow doesn’t separate hygiene vs. motivators.
n.4: Theory Y is about self-motivation, not hygiene neglect.
n.0: McClelland’s model is a different needs theory.
n.1: Theory Z relates to Japanese management styles.

Leadership.q: A project team has recently formed and members are unclear about roles, hesitant to contribute, and rely heavily on the project manager for direction. Which stage of team development is MOST evident?
o: Norming, where shared understanding and cohesion are already established
Adjourning, where focus shifts to closure and disbanding activities
Storming, where conflict dominates and individuals challenge authority openly
Performing, where the team operates autonomously with minimal oversight
Forming, where individuals seek clarity and depend on leadership for structure
Leadership.w: Forming is characterised by uncertainty, dependency on the leader, and lack of clarity about roles and expectations.

n.2: Storming involves visible conflict and challenges, not initial uncertainty and reliance.
n.0: Norming reflects established cohesion, which is not yet present.
n.3: Performing requires maturity and autonomy not evident here.
n.1: Adjourning relates to project closure, not early-stage team behaviour.

Leadership.q: Two team members are in open disagreement and tensions are rising within the project team. Why is emotional intelligence so important for a project manager who wants to resolve this conflict effectively?
o: It removes the need for feedback
It ensures the leader always gets their way
It helps leaders understand different perspectives and manage reactions
It enables leaders to ignore problems until they disappear
Leadership.w: Leaders with emotional intelligence can empathise and manage team tensions effectively.

n.4: Ignoring issues leads to unresolved conflict.
n.0: Feedback is still needed, even with EI.
n.3: Formal processes may still be needed.
n.1: Effective conflict management is not about 'winning'.

Leadership.q: A project manager is deciding how much autonomy to give a capable team. Drawing on McGregor's work, which statement best describes the Theory Y set of assumptions the manager would hold about their employees?
o: They dislike work and must be coerced
They seek responsibility and are self-motivated
Leadership.w: Theory Y posits that employees are inherently motivated and seek responsibility when given the chance.

n.0: That describes Theory X.
n.2: Theory Y assumes less need for close supervision.
n.3: Theory Y associates employees with adaptability.
n.4: Theory Y acknowledges non-monetary motivators like achievement.

Leadership.q: A project manager reviewing how to keep the team engaged draws on Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory to distinguish elements that merely prevent dissatisfaction from those that genuinely motivate. According to that theory, which of the following is considered a hygiene factor?
Leadership.w: In Herzberg’s model, hygiene factors (e.g., salary, company policy) prevent dissatisfaction but don’t drive satisfaction.

n.2: Achievement is a motivator, not a hygiene factor.
n.1: Recognition is a motivator that increases satisfaction.
n.3: Opportunities for growth are motivators.
n.4: Responsibility falls under motivators in Herzberg’s theory.

Leadership.q: During the early stages of a project, the team avoids conflict and appears polite but lacks honest discussion about issues. Which stage is MOST likely?
o: Adjourning, where engagement is reduced as the project ends
Performing, where problems are addressed proactively
Storming, where conflict is openly expressed and challenged
Forming, where individuals avoid conflict and seek acceptance
Norming, where trust allows open discussion of issues
Leadership.w: Forming is characterised by politeness and avoidance of conflict as individuals seek acceptance.

n.2: Storming involves open conflict, not avoidance.
n.4: Norming allows for more honest communication.
n.1: Performing teams address issues directly and effectively.
n.0: Adjourning is unrelated to early-stage behaviour.

Leadership.q: A project manager is applying Maslow's hierarchy of needs to the workplace and wants to illustrate each level with a fitting example. Which of the following pairings correctly matches a Maslow need with an example?
Leadership.w: Love/belonging needs include social connections and supportive relationships within the team.

n.3: Mentorship addresses esteem or self-actualization, not basic physiological needs.
n.2: Team events are social (belonging), not safety needs.
n.1: A comfortable workspace relates to safety, not esteem.
n.0: Salary is tied to physiological or safety needs, not self-actualization.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor asks a senior colleague to mentor a promising team member. Which of the following is a key feature that distinguishes a mentoring leadership style from other approaches?
o: Offering long-term guidance based on experience
Leadership.w: Mentors support others with advice and guidance based on their experience, usually over a longer period.

n.1: Daily task assignment is a directive style, not mentoring.
n.4: Mentoring supports development, not just deadlines.
n.2: Personal growth is key to mentoring.
n.3: Mentoring often involves giving feedback.

Leadership.q: A project leader deliberately gives team members greater autonomy and encourages their personal growth and development in their roles. In Maslow's hierarchy, which need level is this leader primarily addressing?
Leadership.w: Autonomy and growth support self-actualization, Maslow’s highest need level.

n.0: Basic survival needs are not about autonomy.
n.3: Esteem covers respect and recognition, not autonomy.
n.1: Safety is about security and stability.
n.2: Belonging is about social connections.

Leadership.q: A project manager notices that different team members respond inconsistently to the same leadership approach. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?
o: Inconsistency indicates poor team discipline rather than leadership issues
Variation in response suggests the team lacks technical competence
The team should align to the leader’s preferred style rather than the reverse
A single leadership style should be applied consistently to ensure fairness
Leadership style should be adapted to individual needs and levels of development
Leadership.w: Situational leadership requires adapting style to individual capability and motivation rather than applying a uniform approach.

n.3: Consistency in style does not address differing development levels.
n.0: The issue relates to leadership adaptation, not necessarily discipline.
n.2: Effective leadership aligns to team needs, not personal preference.
n.1: Response variation is not solely linked to technical competence.

Leadership.q: A project manager applying situational leadership theory recognises that the appropriate style is not fixed but should shift according to particular characteristics. According to the theory, a leader should adapt their style based on the characteristics of the _____.
Leadership.w: Situational leadership matches the style to follower characteristics such as ability and willingness.

n.4: Industry context influences business strategy but not immediate style choice.
n.2: Physical environment is not a core situational leadership factor.
n.0: Market trends affect business planning, not direct style adaptation.
n.3: Corporate strategy guides goals, not follower-focused style changes.

Leadership.q: A high-performing team consistently delivers outputs, adapts to challenges without escalation, and requires minimal direction from the project manager. Which stage is MOST applicable?
o: Storming, where team members challenge each other frequently
Performing, where the team operates efficiently and independently
Norming, where collaboration exists but autonomy is limited
Forming, where leadership direction is critical to progress
Adjourning, where focus shifts away from delivery activities
Leadership.w: Performing reflects high autonomy, efficiency, and adaptability with minimal supervision.

n.3: Forming requires strong leadership and lacks autonomy.
n.0: Storming is characterised by conflict, not efficiency.
n.2: Norming involves collaboration but not full autonomy.
n.4: Adjourning occurs at the end of the project lifecycle.

Leadership.q: During a company merger, a leader seeks input from both legacy teams to foster collaboration. He uses a ______ approach to involve employees in decisions.
Leadership.w: A participative approach invites team members to share ideas and influence decisions.

n.2: Delegating grants autonomy but does not actively involve employees in decision-making.
n.3: Autocratic excludes employee input.
n.1: Directive focuses on giving instructions, not collaboration.
n.4: Transactional centers on exchanges, not joint decision-making.

Leadership.q: A manager who subscribes to McGregor's Theory X believes staff will not perform unless closely directed and monitored. According to Theory X, management must apply ______ to get results from employees.
Leadership.w: Theory X assumes employees must be controlled or coerced to achieve objectives.

n.3: Empowerment aligns with Theory Y, not X.
n.0: Theory X distrusts employees, preferring control.
n.2: Autonomy is a Theory Y principle.
n.1: Self-direction contradicts the Theory X view.

Leadership.q: During delivery, a previously high-performing team begins missing milestones due to uncertainty introduced by frequent scope changes. Which leadership adaptation is MOST effective?
o: Avoid intervention to observe how the team adapts to changing conditions
Delegate responsibility fully to allow the team to manage scope independently
Increase directive control to enforce compliance with the original plan
Shift to a coaching style that clarifies priorities while supporting problem-solving
Escalate the issue to governance without adjusting leadership approach
Leadership.w: A coaching style addresses reduced confidence while leveraging existing capability, helping the team adapt to uncertainty.

n.2: Purely directive control ignores the underlying uncertainty and reduces adaptability.
n.1: Full delegation assumes confidence that is currently diminished.
n.0: Non-intervention fails to address declining performance.
n.4: Escalation does not replace the need for leadership adjustment.

Leadership.q: Under a project manager who has grown increasingly controlling, the team's behaviour has shifted over recent weeks. Reflecting on how people now respond to the leadership style, which TWO signs suggest leadership is negatively affecting team performance?
o: Capable individuals stop offering suggestions or challenge
Team members hide problems until formal reviews
The team uses lessons learned to improve its approach
Team members understand priorities and escalate early risks
The team asks for clarification when requirements are ambiguous
Leadership.w: Concealing issues and withholding contribution indicate a leadership climate that may be reducing trust, motivation and ownership.

n.3: Early escalation and clear priorities indicate healthy performance behaviours.
n.4: Seeking clarification is usually constructive rather than negative.
n.2: Using lessons learned shows positive improvement behaviour.

Leadership.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager whether a delivery team has fully matured, having observed how it now operates day to day. Which TWO scenarios would indicate that the team has reached the performing stage of development?
o: The team relies on structured guidance for all decisions
The team avoids taking ownership of decisions
The team consistently delivers outputs with minimal supervision
The team experiences frequent unresolved conflict
The team adapts to changes without requiring direction from the project manager
Leadership.w: Performing teams demonstrate autonomy, adaptability, and consistent delivery.

n.0: Reliance on guidance reflects earlier stages.
n.1: Avoiding ownership indicates lack of maturity.
n.3: Frequent conflict suggests storming.

Leadership.q: Partway through the project, a newly formed team has begun openly disagreeing over roles and priorities, with tension rising between individuals as they compete for influence. At this stage of team development, which leadership response is MOST appropriate?
o: Apply strict control to suppress disagreement and enforce compliance
Provide facilitation to manage conflict and clarify roles and expectations
Delegate all decisions to the team to encourage independence
Escalate interpersonal issues immediately to senior stakeholders
Avoid intervening to allow conflicts to resolve without influence
Leadership.w: During storming, leaders should facilitate resolution of conflict and provide clarity to guide the team forward.

n.4: Non-intervention can allow conflict to escalate.
n.2: Full delegation may worsen unresolved conflict.
n.0: Suppressing disagreement can damage trust and cohesion.
n.3: Escalation avoids addressing team dynamics directly.

Leadership.q: An experienced leader agrees to act as a mentor to a newly appointed project manager over the coming months. What is the main benefit of taking this mentoring approach for the new manager?
o: It reduces the mentoring leader's own workload
It guarantees the project will be successful
It helps the new manager gain skills and confidence
It speeds up the completion of all tasks
It removes all conflict from within the team
Leadership.w: Mentoring provides guidance, support and builds confidence in less experienced colleagues.

n.0: Responsibility for leadership remains with the leader.
n.1: Project success can't be guaranteed by mentoring alone.
n.3: Mentoring focuses on development, not task speed.
n.4: Conflicts can still arise even with mentoring.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project identifies a risk that could either increase costs or reduce them depending on supplier performance. How should this risk be treated?
o: As both a threat and an opportunity
As a fixed constraint on the budget
As an opportunity for the budget only
As a threat to the budget only
Risk & Issue Management.w: Some risks have dual outcomes depending on how they unfold.

n.4: There is also potential benefit.
n.3: There is also potential loss.
n.2: This is not fixed.
n.0: It has not occurred.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager reviews the risk register and considers marking certain entries as closed. In a well-run project, when is it appropriate to close a risk?
o: As soon as the project has been formally initiated and started
Routinely at the end of every project team meeting
Each time another new risk is identified on the project
As soon as any issue arises during the project
Once the risk has been fully addressed or is no longer relevant
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are closed when they are resolved, transferred, or are no longer a threat.

n.0: Closure should only occur after resolution.
n.2: New risks are analysed, not closed immediately.
n.3: Issues and risks are managed separately.
n.1: Routine meetings review, not close, risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Why do iterative life cycles often require more frequent risk and issue reviews?
o: Escalation is only possible in linear cycles
Risk registers are not used in iterative cycles
Project scope and priorities change regularly
Issue management is ignored in iterative cycles
Risk management is unnecessary in iterative life cycles
Risk & Issue Management.w: Frequent reviews allow the team to respond quickly to changes in scope or direction.

n.4: Risk management is always needed.
n.0: Escalation occurs in both approaches.
n.3: Issue management is essential in all cycles.
n.1: Risk registers are used in all projects.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue is logged during a project retrospective in an agile environment. What makes the management of this issue unique?
o: It requires no documentation at all in agile environments
It will be held over unaddressed until the project closes
It will be reviewed and actioned more rapidly due to shorter cycles
It must always be escalated to the board whatever its severity
Only senior managers are permitted to review and resolve it
Risk & Issue Management.w: Agile/iterative environments address issues promptly within short cycles.

n.1: Issues should not be ignored.
n.4: Team-level action is common in agile.
n.0: Documentation is always required.
n.3: Escalation is based on severity, not routine.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is choosing between two positive-risk responses for an opportunity and wants to be clear on how they differ before deciding. What distinguishes the exploit response from the enhance response when dealing with opportunities?
o: Exploit accepts the opportunity; enhance rejects any associated cost
Exploit guarantees benefit; enhance increases the chance or impact
Exploit increases the chance; enhance guarantees the benefit is realised
Exploit shares the opportunity; enhance removes it from the register
Exploit applies to threats; enhance applies only to opportunities
Risk & Issue Management.w: Exploit seeks to ensure the opportunity is realised; enhance boosts the chance or impact.

n.2: Both apply to positive risks (opportunities).
n.3: Exploit is for high-value opportunities.
n.4: Enhance does not eliminate, only increases benefit.
n.0: Transfer is for threats and opportunities, but not exploit.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk response has been agreed that requires a specific mitigation plan to be put into effect. As roles are allocated, the project manager needs to be clear who will actually carry out the mitigation activities. Who is most responsible for carrying out this action?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The risk action owner is responsible for executing the agreed response actions.

n.0: Risk owner oversees but does not necessarily execute.
n.1: The PM coordinates but does not always execute.
n.3: Stakeholders are not directly responsible.
n.4: Board provides governance.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Whether a project is delivered through a linear or an iterative life cycle, its manager applies structured risk and issue management throughout. Regardless of the life cycle chosen, what is the ultimate goal of these risk and issue management processes?
o: To satisfy audit requirements without affecting the eventual project outcome
To support successful project delivery by controlling uncertainty and resolving problems
To generate a comprehensive risk record for the organisation's insurers
To transfer accountability for outcomes from the manager to the sponsor
To remove all uncertainty so that no risks can ever materialise
Risk & Issue Management.w: Managing risks and issues increases the chance of delivering projects on time, on budget, and to scope.

n.4: Stakeholder engagement remains important.
n.3: Documentation supports control, not bureaucracy.
n.2: Project managers are still essential.
n.0: Good management supports timely completion.

Risk & Issue Management.q: As issues are resolved, a project manager formally marks each one as closed in the issue log rather than simply leaving it open. What is a key reason for closing resolved issues in this way?
o: It signals that the remaining issue budget can be reallocated elsewhere
It automatically updates the risk register with a new mitigation plan
It demonstrates effective management and provides a record for audit and learning
It confirms the associated risk can now be removed from the project
It transfers ownership of the issue to the operational support team
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure ensures proper records and supports organisational learning.

n.4: Records should be retained, not deleted.
n.1: Unresolved issues must be addressed.
n.3: Closing issues doesn't affect unrelated risks.
n.0: Projects are not restarted due to issue closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When building the budget for a project with significant uncertainty, the project manager deliberately sets aside a sum of money to be drawn on only if identified risks actually occur. What is this budget called?
Risk & Issue Management.w: A contingency fund is used to cover unexpected risks that arise during a project.

n.0: Quality reserves are related to quality assurance, not risk.
n.2: Profit margin is not a risk management tool.
n.4: Stage gates control progress, not contingency.
n.1: Stakeholder funds are not standard in risk management.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager structures the risk analysis so that the team examines only the negative uncertainties facing the project. Considering how this narrows the process, what is the main risk of focusing only on threats during risk analysis?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Ignoring opportunities limits potential value creation.

n.2: Not the main risk.
n.0: Irrelevant.
n.4: Not the core issue.
n.3: Performance may suffer.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk owner accepts responsibility for several risks but never nominates anyone to carry out the agreed response activities. As delivery continues, what is the most likely outcome of this omission?
o: Increased stakeholder confidence in risk handling
Improved accountability across the whole risk process
Faster resolution of the identified risks
A reduced need for ongoing risk monitoring
Lack of clear responsibility for implementing responses
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without action owners, responses may not be executed effectively.

n.1: Accountability decreases.
n.2: Resolution may be delayed.
n.3: Monitoring is still required.
n.0: Confidence may drop.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team knows a risk is unlikely but chooses to do nothing until it happens. What response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance is choosing to tolerate a risk, taking no action until it materialises.

n.2: Avoidance seeks to remove the risk proactively.
n.1: Transfer moves risk to another party.
n.4: Exploit is for opportunities.
n.0: Share is for opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A newly identified risk carries a proposed response whose cost exceeds the financial limits delegated to the project manager, so a higher authority must sign it off. What ensures the correct approval and escalation process is followed?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The governance framework defines who can approve what and the escalation path.

n.2: Stakeholder analysis is important, but governance sets approval limits.
n.3: Brainstorming does not define authority.
n.1: Communication plans support, but do not define, authority.
n.4: Procurement strategy relates to suppliers, not escalation.

Risk & Issue Management.q: While reviewing the issue log for a long-running project, a project manager notices several very similar issues have been raised and resolved individually over recent weeks. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this pattern?
o: The recurring issues are routine and can be ignored
Each issue should simply be closed as quickly as possible
The issues are coincidental and should be handled individually
There may be an underlying root cause not being addressed
The project is performing efficiently despite the recurrences
Risk & Issue Management.w: Recurring issues indicate systemic problems requiring root cause analysis.

n.2: Patterns suggest linkage.
n.4: Performance is likely poor.
n.0: Ignoring worsens the problem.
n.1: Closure without resolution is ineffective.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project sponsor questions why the project manager is investing effort in identifying and managing uncertainty on a new product launch. What is a primary benefit of effective risk management in projects?
o: It reduces the need for stakeholder engagement
It increases the likelihood of project success
It shortens the project duration automatically
It guarantees zero issues will occur
Risk & Issue Management.w: Effective risk management makes project success more likely by anticipating and managing uncertainties.

n.4: Issues may still arise, even with good risk management.
n.1: Risks can be reduced or managed, not eliminated entirely.
n.0: Stakeholder engagement is always important, regardless of risk management.
n.3: Risk management does not directly shorten duration.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager records a new risk but fails to analyse its potential impact. What is the main problem with this?
o: The team cannot prioritise or respond effectively
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without analysis, the risk cannot be properly managed or prioritised.

n.0: Not all risks need escalation.
n.1: Risks are only closed after resolution.
n.4: Only realised risks become issues.
n.3: The project plan may still be valid.

Risk & Issue Management.q: On a troubled project, no one is clear who approves risk responses, escalation paths are undefined, and the risk register is rarely reviewed by any oversight body. What is the likely result of such poor governance in risk and issue management?
o: Unclear decision-making and increased project risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without clear governance, risks and issues may be missed or mismanaged, increasing uncertainty.

n.1: Poor governance often leads to delays, not speed.
n.0: It increases, not guarantees, project failure risk.
n.3: Issues will still occur and may be ignored.
n.4: Poor governance can reduce morale due to confusion.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During risk analysis, a project manager assesses a particular risk as unlikely to occur but judges that its impact would be severe if it did materialise. Given this combination of low likelihood and high impact, what is the best approach to managing it?
o: Monitor closely and have a contingency plan ready
Close the risk now because it is judged unlikely
Postpone any analysis of the risk until project end
Transfer the risk onto a different project altogether
Take no action given its low likelihood of occurring
Risk & Issue Management.w: High-impact risks need to be monitored and contingency planned, regardless of likelihood.

n.4: Ignoring risks can lead to project failure.
n.1: Risks should only be closed when no longer relevant.
n.3: Risks should be managed in the current project.
n.2: Delays can increase exposure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager delivering a linear, phased project conducts a formal review of the risk register at every stage gate before authorising the next phase. Why is carrying out risk reviews at these points particularly important in a linear life cycle?
o: Linear projects rarely need any form of risk escalation
Formal risk reviews add value only at the point of closure
Iterative projects review their risks only at the final cycle
Stage gates provide natural points for formal risk review and control
Linear projects encounter far fewer risks than iterative ones do
Risk & Issue Management.w: Stage gates in linear projects are ideal for structured risk reviews and decisions.

n.4: Risks can change at any time in any project.
n.2: Iterative cycles also require risk reviews, but at different intervals.
n.1: Risk reviews should occur throughout the project.
n.0: Escalation may be required in any life cycle.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team identifies a chance to adopt an innovative method that could deliver benefits, but decides not to pursue it because of the uncertainty involved. In choosing to forgo the opportunity, what is the key trade-off being made?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Choosing not to pursue an opportunity sacrifices potential benefits to reduce risk.

n.0: Not relevant.
n.3: Not the main trade-off.
n.4: Irrelevant.
n.1: Not applicable.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During early planning, a project manager schedules risk workshops and puts mitigating actions in place well before any threats can occur, rather than waiting for problems to arise. In risk management, what is the main objective of taking such proactive responses?
o: To document every risk thoroughly for the project closure report
To prevent risks from materialising or reduce their impact in advance
To respond quickly once a risk has already become an issue
To escalate all risks to the sponsor before assessing them
To transfer each identified risk to a third-party insurer
Risk & Issue Management.w: Proactive responses aim to control risks before they occur.

n.2: Proactive means acting early, not delaying.
n.0: Risk management aims to prevent issues, not create them.
n.4: Communication is always vital.
n.3: Escalation is only for risks beyond team authority.

Risk & Issue Management.q: To keep a software development project away from a period when key staff would be unavailable, the project manager reschedules the build so it no longer overlaps with the peak holiday season. Which risk response does this rescheduling represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoiding a risk removes it from the project by changing the schedule or plan.

n.2: Reduction lessens the probability or impact, but doesn't remove the risk.
n.4: Sharing is for opportunities.
n.1: Acceptance means tolerating the risk.
n.0: Exploiting is for opportunities.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A sponsor wants the project's outcomes to be as predictable as possible so that reliable commitments can be made to the business. Which of the following is most likely to improve project predictability?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Proactive management of risks and issues makes outcomes more predictable.

n.4: Minor risks can escalate if ignored.
n.2: Good communication supports risk management.
n.3: Each project faces unique risks.
n.1: Regular reviews are important for control.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During start up of a project exposed to volatile external conditions, the project manager develops plans for how the team will act if certain identified risks occur. What is the main purpose of contingency planning in projects?
o: To build additional profit margin into the project budget
To limit the need for stakeholder risk communication
To serve as a substitute for detailed project planning
To ensure the project can respond effectively to unforeseen events
To remove every identified threat before the project begins
Risk & Issue Management.w: Contingency planning prepares the team for unexpected events, improving resilience.

n.4: Elimination of all risk is impossible.
n.0: Contingency is for control, not for increasing costs.
n.2: Project planning and contingency planning work together.
n.1: Stakeholder communication is always needed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager chooses to delay addressing a known issue to avoid stakeholder concern. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Faster resolution once more information becomes available
Improved team performance through fewer delivery interruptions
A temporary reduction in overall project risk exposure
Improved stakeholder confidence through reduced early disruption
Increased impact and reduced control over the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Delaying action increases the likelihood and severity of negative outcomes.

n.3: Trust may decrease.
n.2: Risk increases.
n.0: Resolution is delayed.
n.1: Performance may decline.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk response has been implemented but is not being monitored. What stage of the risk process is being neglected?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Monitoring ensures responses remain effective and risks are tracked.

n.0: The risk is already identified.
n.3: Analysis has been completed.
n.4: Response has already been planned.
n.1: Closure occurs later.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An organisation follows a defined issue management process on its projects, beginning with the capture and examination of each issue as it arises. In this process, what is the purpose of the logging and analysis stage?
o: To prepare the project's financial status and cost reports
To define and assign the project team's roles
To confirm final sign-off of the project deliverables
To forecast and plan for future project risks proactively
To record issues and understand their cause and impact
Risk & Issue Management.w: Logging and analysis ensures every issue is documented and fully understood for effective management.

n.2: Deliverables are managed separately from issue logs.
n.3: Planning for risks is a separate process.
n.1: Role assignment is not the purpose of issue analysis.
n.0: Finance reporting is separate.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Working through the issue management process, a project manager assigns responsibility for each newly analysed issue to an owner without delay. In terms of managing the project, what is the benefit of assigning these actions promptly?
o: It eliminates the need for escalation
It accelerates resolution and limits project impact
Risk & Issue Management.w: Prompt action assignment ensures issues are dealt with quickly, limiting negative consequences.

n.3: Excess documentation is not the primary benefit.
n.0: Swift action can speed closure, not delay it.
n.2: Team responsibility is increased, not reduced.
n.1: Escalation is still available if needed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: To manage the risk that newly installed equipment might fail, a project manager purchases a warranty under which the manufacturer would bear the cost of any failure. Which risk response does taking out this warranty represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: A warranty shifts some or all risk of equipment failure to another party.

n.4: Reduction lowers risk probability/impact, not responsibility.
n.2: Avoidance eliminates the risk entirely.
n.0: Acceptance is passive, not proactive.
n.3: Enhance is for opportunities, not threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager keeps a thorough written record of every decision and action taken while managing project risks. Beyond simply meeting procedure, what is the main advantage of documenting all risk management actions in this way?
o: It guarantees a successful outcome for the project
It removes all project risk from the project completely
It provides an audit trail and supports learning
It lowers the overall cost of the project
It removes any future need to escalate risks
Risk & Issue Management.w: Documentation enables tracking, accountability, and organisational learning.

n.0: Success is improved, but not guaranteed.
n.3: Cost may still be incurred in managing risks.
n.4: Escalation may still be necessary.
n.1: Risks can be managed, not eliminated.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Having assessed a significant threat to a project's schedule, the project manager wants to put a suitable contingency action in place should the risk occur. Which of the following is a contingency action for an identified project risk?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Contingency actions often include time or budget set aside for unexpected problems.

n.0: Communication is critical, not a contingency action.
n.1: Updates should not be delayed.
n.3: Workshops are important for risk identification.
n.4: Meetings should be maintained for coordination.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is dealing with an issue whose resolution would require decisions and funding that sit well beyond their delegated authority. Recognising this limit, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Escalate the issue to the appropriate governance level
Delay action until more information is available
Assign it to another team member
Convert it into a risk for future tracking
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation ensures issues beyond authority are addressed at the correct level.

n.1: Delaying worsens impact.
n.2: Closure requires resolution.
n.3: Authority is still required.
n.4: Issues are not future risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager identifies a risk, analyses it and keeps it under review, but at no point refers it upward to senior management or the board. What does the fact that the risk has been handled entirely without escalation indicate?
o: A required escalation step was overlooked in error here
The risk no longer needs any form of active management
The risk is certain to develop into an issue
The project team can manage the risk within their authority
No further risks remain to be managed on the project
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are only escalated if beyond the team’s control; otherwise, they are managed at team level.

n.1: All risks require some form of management.
n.0: Escalation is not always required.
