n.1: Transparency is improved by clear records.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk action owner reports that all the mitigation activities assigned to them for a particular risk have now been completed. Following good risk management practice, what should happen next?
o: The risk owner should review and confirm whether the risk can be closed
The risk should be closed immediately with no further review needed
The risk should be reassigned directly to a different action owner
The risk should be escalated straight to the project sponsor for action
The completed outcome should be recorded but otherwise left unactioned
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure requires confirmation that the risk is no longer relevant.

n.1: Closure requires validation.
n.3: Escalation may not be needed.
n.2: Reassignment is unnecessary.
n.4: Outcome must be reviewed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During response planning, a project manager decides to change the project plan so that a particular threat can no longer arise at all. Which risk response strategy is being used to completely remove the threat from the project in this way?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Avoiding a risk removes the threat by changing plans or processes.

n.4: Accepting means tolerating the risk, not removing it.
n.3: Sharing is for opportunities, not threats.
n.0: Enhancing relates to opportunities, not threats.
n.2: Rejecting is not a formal risk response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At a regular meeting, the project board is presented with a summary of escalated issues together with the decisions it is being asked to make. Which aspect of risk and issue management does providing the board with this summary support?
o: Appraisal of individual team member performance levels
Detailed technical analysis of the project deliverables
Governance and oversight in risk and issue management
Management of project procurement and supplier contracts
Quality control checks carried out on project deliverables
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation summaries enable senior decision-makers to oversee project risks and issues.

n.1: Technical analysis is separate from board review.
n.0: Appraisals are HR, not risk processes.
n.4: Quality control reviews deliverables, not issues.
n.3: Procurement is not the focus here.

Risk & Issue Management.q: On an infrastructure project, the risk manager finds that a significant threat cannot be avoided, its likelihood cannot be reduced, and transferring it through insurance proves prohibitively expensive. With the other options exhausted, which threat response should the project manager adopt as the last resort?
Risk & Issue Management.w: If risk cannot be avoided, reduced, or transferred, acceptance may be the only option.

n.4: Exploit is for positive risks.
n.0: Enhance is for opportunities.
n.3: Sharing is for positive risks.
n.2: Rejection is for opportunities, not threats.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A newly appointed project manager is being coached on how project management distinguishes between the terms 'risk' and 'issue' when managing uncertainty. What is the difference between a risk and an issue?
o: Risks affect only cost, whereas issues affect only the schedule
The two terms describe exactly the same thing in practice
An issue is a future opportunity; a risk is an active problem
Issues are future threats; risks are current problems being managed
A risk is a potential event; an issue has already occurred
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are potential events, while issues are current problems that must be managed.

n.2: Opportunities are a type of risk, not issue.
n.0: Risks can be schedule or quality related as well.
n.3: Issues are current, risks are potential.
n.1: There is a clear distinction between risks and issues.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is coaching a new team member on risk terminology and explains that risk covers more than just possible problems. To clarify the concept, which statement best distinguishes a threat from an opportunity in risk management?
o: A threat arises earlier in delivery than an opportunity
A threat creates uncertainty, whereas an opportunity removes it
A threat is internal, whereas an opportunity is external
A threat always carries greater impact than an opportunity
A threat negatively impacts objectives, whereas an opportunity positively impacts them
Risk & Issue Management.w: Threats have negative effects, while opportunities have positive effects on objectives.

n.1: Both introduce uncertainty.
n.0: Timing does not define type.
n.2: Both can be internal or external.
n.3: Impact varies.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager identifies a new threat at a formal review and needs to keep it under regular review until it is either resolved or closed. Which process ensures that the risk is tracked in this way throughout the remainder of the project?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk monitoring tracks identified risks throughout the project until they are resolved or closed.

n.4: Escalation is only required for issues or risks beyond authority.
n.3: Budget control focuses on finances, not risks.
n.2: Quality assurance relates to deliverables, not risks.
n.0: Resource planning allocates resources, not risk tracking.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is explaining the different responsibilities within the risk process to the team, using practical examples. Which situation best illustrates the role of a risk action owner?
o: Implementing a mitigation plan for a specific risk
Reporting overall project progress to stakeholders
Approving governance decisions across the whole project
Monitoring the overall risk status over time
Documenting and maintaining the full risk register
Risk & Issue Management.w: Action owners are responsible for executing specific response actions.

n.3: Monitoring is the risk owner’s responsibility.
n.2: Governance is not their role.
n.4: Documentation is broader.
n.1: Reporting is not specific to action owners.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Summarising a training session, a tutor asks the group to explain, in overall terms, the fundamental reason that governance underpins effective handling of threats and issues across an organisation's projects. In summary, why is governance crucial to risk and issue management?
o: It shifts full responsibility for every risk decision onto individual project team members
It ensures risks and issues are managed transparently, consistently, and in line with organisational policy
It lets each project define its own risk policy independently of the organisation
It removes the need for any formal risk management process within projects
It guarantees that identified risks will never affect the project's agreed schedule
Risk & Issue Management.w: Governance is essential for structured, effective, and accountable management of risk and issues.

n.0: Governance reduces uncertainty.
n.3: Escalated risks require attention.
n.4: Governance supports timely action.
n.2: Risk can be controlled, not prevented entirely.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager is briefing the team on what disciplined risk and issue management can realistically deliver, and wants to correct a common misconception. Which of the following is NOT a direct benefit of risk and issue management?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk and issue management does not guarantee profit, though it does improve control and predictability.

n.4: Planning improves as risks are identified and managed.
n.0: Stakeholders trust well-managed projects.
n.2: Issues are addressed faster.
n.3: Project outcomes become less variable.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Towards the end of a project phase, the manager formally closes a risk that has been fully resolved and updates the risk register accordingly. How does closing the risk in this way benefit the project?
o: It increases the risk register size
It eliminates all future project threats
It removes the need for stakeholder communication
It confirms risks are resolved and frees up resources
It allows issues to be ignored
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk closure marks risks as resolved and lets the team focus elsewhere.

n.0: Resolved risks are removed from the register.
n.1: Some threats may always remain.
n.2: Communication is still necessary.
n.4: Issues must always be managed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager realises that multiple risks have been identified but not analysed. What is the primary consequence of this gap?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Without analysis, risks cannot be prioritised or managed effectively.

n.4: Communication is not the main issue.
n.3: Engagement is secondary.
n.2: Flexibility is not improved.
n.1: Documentation is not the core concern.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager identifies a positive risk that could bring significant benefit to the project and wants to take deliberate action to make certain that it actually happens. Which response is best suited to an opportunity the manager wants to ensure is realised?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Exploiting means ensuring an opportunity occurs and maximising the benefit.

n.3: Avoid is used for threats.
n.1: Transfer is used for threats.
n.2: Reduce is a threat response.
n.4: Reject is not a standard response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager identifies an opportunity in the risk register but decides to make no change to the plan and to take no active steps to bring it about, simply leaving it to occur or not. Which response to the opportunity does this represent?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Accepting an opportunity means no active steps are taken to make it more likely.

n.4: Exploiting is to ensure the opportunity occurs.
n.3: Sharing means partnering for the benefit.
n.0: Enhancing increases likelihood or impact.
n.1: Reject is to actively decline.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager decides not to pursue a new opportunity as it doesn't align with the project objectives. What response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Rejecting is a valid response for opportunities that do not add value or fit the strategy.

n.4: Sharing means collaborating to realise an opportunity.
n.3: Exploiting seeks to maximise the benefit.
n.1: Enhancing increases probability or impact.
n.2: Acceptance means tolerating without action.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A PMO reviews how project teams allocate and re-allocate the actions arising from risks and issues across its linear, stage-gated projects and its iterative, agile projects. How does the assignment of actions typically differ between linear and iterative life cycles?
o: Linear cycles reassign actions continuously; iterative cycles fix them at project start
Iterative cycles assign actions once; linear cycles reassign them within each stage
Iterative cycles delegate actions to suppliers; linear cycles retain them internally
Both cycles assign actions only when the project board formally convenes
Iterative cycles reassign actions frequently; linear cycles review actions at stage boundaries
Risk & Issue Management.w: Frequent reviews in iterative cycles lead to more dynamic action management.

n.1: Actions are assigned in both life cycles.
n.0: Action tracking is important in all projects.
n.3: Actions are managed throughout, not just at closure.
n.2: Life cycles affect action management practices.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Partway through a project, a key sole-source supplier unexpectedly goes out of business, threatening delivery of essential components. Which contingency plan might help the project manager respond effectively?
o: Ignore the event and hope for the best
Inform only the team, not stakeholders
Wait for the issue to resolve itself
Risk & Issue Management.w: Alternative suppliers should be identified in advance as part of risk and contingency planning.

n.1: Risks require proactive response.
n.0: Scope changes are not an immediate solution.
n.3: Action is needed, not inaction.
n.2: Stakeholders must be kept informed of major risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Late in the delivery phase of a project, a team member identifies a new threat that had not previously been recorded in the risk register. As project manager, what is the best response?
o: Assess the risk and update contingency plans
Ignore it because the project is nearly finished
Blame the team for late identification
Risk & Issue Management.w: Every risk must be assessed and contingency plans updated, even late in the project.

n.1: All risks must be managed, regardless of timing.
n.3: Risk responses are always required.
n.2: Delays in action can increase project threats.
n.4: Risk management should be constructive, not punitive.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A software team delivers a product through short, repeated iterations, and finds that fresh risks tend to surface with each new cycle of work. To manage this pattern of continually emerging threats, what process must the team follow?
o: Hold all risk responses back to the final iteration
Revisit risk identification and analysis at the start of each iteration
Escalate every newly emerging risk straight to the project board
Defer identifying any new risks until the project completes
Produce a separate business case for each new risk
Risk & Issue Management.w: Iterative projects require regular review of risks as scope and priorities shift.

n.3: Risks must be managed as soon as they emerge.
n.0: Timely action is crucial in iterative projects.
n.2: Only critical risks should be escalated.
n.4: A new business case is not required for each risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team has identified and analysed a significant risk to delivery and now needs to decide how it will be handled, for example by avoiding, reducing or transferring it. Which stage of the risk management process determines the appropriate response strategy?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Response planning defines how risks will be managed.

n.0: Identification only lists risks.
n.2: Analysis informs but does not decide responses.
n.3: Monitoring tracks risks.
n.1: Closure ends the process.

Risk & Issue Management.q: An issue is raised in the log during delivery, but competing priorities mean no owner is assigned and no action is taken for several weeks. As the project manager reviews the log, what is the most likely consequence of this inaction?
o: The issue will reduce stakeholder expectations
The issue will automatically convert into a risk
The issue will resolve itself without intervention
The issue may escalate and increase impact on the project
The issue will be closed during reporting cycles
Risk & Issue Management.w: Delays in addressing issues typically increase their severity and impact.

n.2: Issues rarely resolve without action.
n.1: Issues do not convert into risks.
n.4: Closure requires resolution.
n.0: Expectations may worsen.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The team decides to add resources to increase the chance of delivering an early benefit. What risk response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Enhance means taking action to make an opportunity more likely or impactful.

n.1: Exploit ensures the opportunity will definitely occur.
n.2: Avoid is for negative risks.
n.4: Acceptance involves no proactive steps.
n.0: Transfer is for negative risks.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager captures an emerging issue in the issue log and completes an assessment of its likely impact on the project's objectives. Having logged the issue and analysed it, what comes next in the issue management process?
o: Close the issue immediately without any further action
Draw down the full contingency budget to cover it
Move the issue back onto the risk register
Postpone any action until the project reaches closure
Escalate or assign actions to resolve the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Once analysed, issues should be assigned for resolution or escalated as needed.

n.0: Premature closure leaves issues unresolved.
n.2: Issues are already occurring, not just potential risks.
n.3: Delaying may worsen the impact.
n.1: Budget changes are not the first response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: The project sponsor chooses not to act on a minor risk due to its low impact. What risk response is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Acceptance is appropriate when the risk is low and the cost to act outweighs the benefit.

n.2: Enhance is for positive risks (opportunities).
n.4: Transfer is for shifting risk to another party.
n.0: Avoidance removes the risk.
n.3: Reject is for opportunities not pursued.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project manager increases testing and reviews to lower the chance of a software defect. What is this approach called?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Reduction means taking action to decrease the probability or impact of a risk.

n.2: Acceptance involves no action.
n.4: Transfer would shift risk to another party.
n.1: Sharing is not relevant to threats.
n.0: Reject is not a formal risk response.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk that once threatened a project's schedule has been mitigated successfully and no longer poses any credible threat to the objectives. As the project manager updates the risk register, what is the correct next step for this risk?
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks should be formally closed when no longer relevant.

n.4: Reanalysis is unnecessary.
n.1: Escalation is not needed.
n.3: Transfer is not applicable.
n.0: Formal closure is required.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A team logs an issue, analyses it, and assigns actions. What final step is needed to complete the issue management process?

Transfer the issue to the risk register

n.1: Records should be retained for audit and learning.

n.0: Timely closure is best practice.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When setting up the risk register and issue log, a project manager names a specific individual as owner for each entry rather than leaving them unassigned. Why is it important to assign ownership for each risk and issue in this way?
o: It guarantees the risk or issue will not occur

n.0: Ownership supports management, not prevention.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team identifies a potential supplier delay but takes no further action. At which stage of the risk process has the team stopped?

n.3: No response has been defined.

Risk & Issue Management.q: As a project closes, the project manager considers how insights gained from managing threats and issues throughout delivery should be handled under the organisation's governance arrangements. Risk & Issue Management.q: An examiner asks candidates to identify a genuine example of governance operating within risk and issue management on a project. Which of the following best illustrates governance in risk and issue management?

The team records risks but takes no formal mitigating action
The team escalates every minor risk directly to the sponsor

n.1: Documentation is critical for governance.
n.3: Escalation should be proportionate.
n.2: Stakeholder involvement is encouraged.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A programme manager oversees delivery using both a stage-gated linear approach and an iteration-based agile approach, and wants to understand how the two handle referring risks upward. What distinguishes risk escalation in an iterative life cycle from that in a linear life cycle?

Iterative cycles omit formal risk reviews and reassessment altogether
Only linear projects ever escalate their risks to the board

n.3: Boards can be involved in both life cycles.
n.2: Formal reviews remain important.
n.4: Escalation is for management, not ending the project.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project team runs consistent processes for both risks and issues, moving each entry through a defined series of stages from identification through to resolution. For both of these management processes, what is the final step once an entry has been dealt with?

n.3: Creating risks/issues is not the goal.
n.4: Business cases are not produced at this stage.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A project board wants assurance that every issue raised during delivery can be traced from the point it is escalated through to how it was resolved. What aspect of governance is essential for tracking how issues are resolved in this way?

Risk & Issue Management.w: Documented processes ensure consistency, traceability, and learning.

n.0: Roles are defined by governance, not randomly.

Team Management.q: A project manager is reviewing the behaviours displayed by her team and wants to identify anything that undermines effective teamwork. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of effective teamwork?

Team Management.q: Early in a remote project, the team leader recognises that members who cannot see each other day to day need a firm foundation of confidence in their leader and one another. n.3: Transparency requires openness.
n.4: Check-ins are important for remote teams.

Team Management.q: A project manager is leading a hybrid team in which some members work in the office while others join remotely from home. What is a key leadership challenge that is unique to managing this kind of hybrid team?

Scheduling every team meeting as an in-person session only
Ensuring equal participation and inclusion for both remote and in-person members

Team Management.q: A project team using Belbin's team roles is at risk of settling for a mediocre outcome and needs someone to push it harder and drive progress past the obstacles it faces. Team Management.q: A project team is evaluating several proposed options and wants a member who can objectively analyse the ideas and weigh up their merits to help the team avoid costly mistakes. Using Belbin's model, which team role is best suited to this?

Team Management.q: A project manager observes that, several weeks in, the team is still struggling to reach the performing stage of its development and remains stuck in earlier stages. Which of the following is most likely to be causing this delay in the team reaching peak performance?

Team Management.q: A project manager is reviewing what distinguishes a genuinely effective team from a group of individuals who simply happen to work in the same area. Which of the following is a key characteristic of an effective team?

Team Management.q: A project manager has just convened a brand-new team, and members are still getting to know one another and are unsure of what is expected of them. Which of the following is a likely challenge the team will face during this forming stage?

Team Management.q: A project manager is allocating Belbin team roles and needs someone who will turn the agreed plans into practical actions and keep the work organised so that deadlines are met. Which Belbin team role is primarily responsible for this?

Team Management.q: Within an effective project team, members routinely give one another honest, constructive feedback on their work. What is the impact of this kind of feedback on the team?

n.3: Good feedback encourages engagement.
n.1: It should not create a negative environment.
n.0: Feedback helps creativity, not limits it.
n.4: Effective feedback boosts motivation.

Team Management.q: A project manager applies Belbin's model to assign roles across the team, matching individuals to the roles that suit their natural tendencies. What outcome is most likely to result from taking this approach to team composition?
o: Team members compete to perform the same dominant role
Team members play to their strengths and cover each other's weaknesses
Team members focus only on their own individual objectives
Team members rotate at random through every possible role
Team members are assigned tasks strictly by their job title
Team Management.w: Belbin’s model enables complementary teamwork and better overall results.

n.4: Role overlap is avoided in Belbin’s approach.
n.0: Different roles contribute to all types of work.
n.2: Communication is always important.
n.3: Deadlines remain important.

Team Management.q: A project manager is using Tuckman's model to explain to a sponsor how a newly assembled team will develop over time before it becomes fully effective. What is the correct order of the stages in Tuckman's model of team development?
Team Management.w: Tuckman's model describes team development as Forming, Storming, Norming, then Performing.

n.4: This order is incorrect according to Tuckman's model.
n.2: This sequence does not follow the model's stages.
n.3: Storming is not the initial stage in Tuckman's model.
n.1: This mixes up the stages and their correct order.

Team Management.q: An experienced manager used to leading from the office is frustrated that the informal, face-to-face style that worked well before is falling flat with a newly remote team. A colleague explains why the old approach struggles online. Why might traditional face-to-face leadership styles not work for virtual teams?
o: Virtual teams have no need for leadership
Remote teams lack in-person cues and spontaneous interaction
Feedback is unnecessary in remote settings
All virtual teams operate the same way
Digital tools replace all management needs
Team Management.w: Virtual teams require new methods due to lack of informal, face-to-face communication.

n.0: Leadership remains essential.
n.4: Tools help but don’t replace leadership.
n.3: Each virtual team is unique.
n.2: Feedback is still critical.

Team Management.q: A project team has been working together productively for some time, and the project manager wants to keep it effective through the maintenance stage of its life. Which factor is most important for sustaining ongoing team effectiveness at this stage?
o: Repeatedly assigning members the same tasks
Speed of the initial team formation
A focus only on short-term goals
Team Management.w: Ongoing communication and feedback sustain team effectiveness.

n.3: Formation is only the first step.
n.0: Ignoring conflict can harm team functioning.
n.4: Both short- and long-term goals matter.
n.2: Task variety can help maintain motivation.

Team Management.q: A project manager notices that her team is hesitant to voice concerns. What is the most likely stage of development?
Team Management.w: In the forming stage, members are still getting comfortable and may avoid raising issues.

n.4: Performing teams communicate openly.
n.0: Storming involves open conflict, not hesitancy.
n.3: Norming teams have established communication.
n.2: Adjourning is when the team is closing down.

Team Management.q: A project manager deliberately builds a team drawing on members from a range of backgrounds, cultures, and disciplines. Which of the following is a benefit of having such a diverse team?
o: Wider range of perspectives and ideas
Greater reliance on a single viewpoint
Team Management.w: Diversity brings creativity and different viewpoints to problem-solving.

n.1: Disagreements can happen, but the main benefit is diversity of thought.
n.4: Decisions may take longer but are better informed.
n.3: Diverse teams are often more adaptable.
n.0: Creativity increases with diversity.

Team Management.q: A project manager takes over a newly formed team whose members work remotely across several sites and rarely meet in person. Keen to keep engagement high throughout delivery, the manager reviews options for leading the group. Which of these is an effective leadership strategy for supporting virtual teams?
o: Delegating all tasks and removing oversight
Regularly scheduled video calls to foster connection
Setting a single meeting time for all global members
Team Management.w: Video calls help virtual teams build relationships and maintain engagement.

n.4: Email alone may cause misunderstandings and disconnect.
n.1: Some oversight and interaction are still needed.
n.0: Informal chat helps build trust.
n.3: Time zones must be considered for global teams.

Team Management.q: A project manager has brought together a group of specialists who have never worked together before, and they are meeting as a team for the very first time. As the team begins the forming stage of its development, what should be the main focus at this point?
o: Resolving deep-rooted conflicts between established members
Establishing agreed norms and shared ways of working
Getting to know each other and understanding the project goals
Formally closing the team and recognising achievements
Delivering peak output against agreed team objectives
Team Management.w: Forming is all about introductions and clarifying the team's objectives.

n.0: Deep conflicts arise in later stages like storming.
n.4: Individual evaluation is not the focus at this early stage.
n.1: Disbanding occurs during adjourning.
n.3: The final deliverable comes much later.

Team Management.q: A project team has successfully delivered its outputs and is now being brought together for a final session before members return to their functional roles. In terms of team development, which statement best describes the purpose of this adjourning stage?
o: Bringing the team to a formal close and recognising achievements
Clarifying roles and getting to know one another
Working through conflict over control and direction
Reaching peak collaboration towards the team's goals
Establishing agreed norms and shared ways of working
Team Management.w: Adjourning is about closing the project and celebrating accomplishments.

n.1: Roles are winding down, not being assigned.
n.2: Initial conflicts are resolved much earlier.
n.4: Objectives are set at the start.
n.3: Relationship building happens at forming.

Team Management.q: A project manager is assembling a team and deliberately selects members with a variety of Myers-Briggs personality types rather than similar profiles. When considering the benefits of this approach to team composition, what is a major advantage of having such a diverse team?
o: A wider range of ideas and approaches
Team Management.w: Diversity brings broader perspectives and creative solutions.

n.2: Diversity can actually make decisions slower at times.
n.3: Meeting needs are not directly reduced by diversity.
n.0: Leadership is still important for guiding the team.
n.1: Misunderstandings can still happen.

Team Management.q: A project manager is using the Margerison-McCann Team Management Wheel to understand the preferences of team members. One member consistently seeks out new opportunities and enthusiastically champions fresh ideas across the team. What does the 'Explorer-Promoter' role focus on?
o: Exploring opportunities and promoting new ideas
Team Management.w: Explorer-Promoters are enthusiastic about new possibilities and spreading ideas.

n.1: Quality control is the Controller-Inspector role.
n.0: Admin tasks are not the main focus.
n.3: Explorer-Promoters embrace, not resist, change.
n.2: Specialists provide technical expertise.

Team Management.q: A project manager is reflecting on why the organisation places such emphasis on people working together well rather than in isolation. When teamwork is effective on a project, what is a primary benefit that typically results?
Team Management.w: Teams that work well together solve problems more creatively and efficiently.

n.2: Effective teams usually complete projects more efficiently.
n.1: Effective teams share information openly.
n.3: Effective teamwork boosts morale.
n.0: Misunderstandings are reduced in effective teams.

Team Management.q: A team is working together smoothly, solving problems with little oversight and achieving goals. What team stage does this describe?
Team Management.w: The performing stage is when a team works independently and effectively.

n.0: Forming is about coming together, not peak performance.
n.3: Storming is marked by conflict.
n.2: Norming focuses on resolving differences.
n.1: Adjourning is the disbandment stage.

Team Management.q: A project involves a highly technical element that requires deep, in-depth knowledge in a narrow subject area that no other team member possesses. Using Belbin's model, which team role is best suited to provide this expert knowledge?
Team Management.w: The Specialist role provides in-depth knowledge and technical skills.

n.3: Coordinators clarify goals and delegate.
n.1: Shapers drive progress.
n.0: Plants generate ideas.
n.2: Implementers organise and deliver tasks.

Team Management.q: A programme relies on a virtual team drawn from offices in Europe, Asia and North America, with members from a range of cultural backgrounds. The team leader wants to get the best from everyone across these differences. Which leadership approach is most effective for managing global virtual teams?
Team Management.w: Time zones and cultural differences require flexible, sensitive leadership for global teams.

n.0: Fixed times can exclude some members.
n.2: Feedback remains vital.
n.1: Written memos are often insufficient.
n.4: In-person meetings are impractical for global teams.

Team Management.q: When an unexpected change is introduced part-way through the project, the team adjusts its approach and adapts to the new requirements quickly and without difficulty. What characteristic of an effective team does this behaviour demonstrate?
Team Management.w: Effective teams are flexible and able to adjust to new challenges.

n.2: Good teams embrace learning and change.
n.3: Purpose is shared in effective teams.
n.0: Roles can be fluid to meet needs.
n.4: Collaboration is high in effective teams.

Team Management.q: A project manager wants to ensure the team includes someone who can generate original ideas and imaginative solutions to difficult problems. In Belbin's model of team roles, which role is characterised by this creative, idea-generating contribution?
Team Management.w: The Plant is the creative innovator in Belbin’s team roles.

n.1: Implementers focus on turning ideas into action.
n.2: Coordinators focus on clarifying goals.
n.3: Shapers challenge the team to improve.
n.4: Completer Finishers focus on accuracy and detail.

Team Management.q: A project manager is assigning roles and wants someone who will scrutinise the work closely for errors and make sure deliverables are completed to a high standard. Which of the following best describes the 'Completer Finisher' role in Belbin's team model?
o: Drives the team forward and challenges any inertia
Clarifies the team's objectives and delegates the work
Pays attention to detail and ensures work is finished accurately
Brings new contacts and fresh ideas into the team
Provides scarce specialist knowledge and key technical skills
Team Management.w: Completer Finishers are detail-oriented and ensure tasks are finished thoroughly.

n.0: Shapers drive teams forward.
n.3: Resource Investigators bring in ideas and contacts.
n.1: Coordinators clarify objectives.
n.4: Specialists provide deep expertise.

Team Management.q: A project manager has worked hard to build a high level of mutual trust among team members. Which of the following is a direct result of this trust within an effective team?
o: Greater willingness to share information and ideas
Team Management.w: Trust encourages openness, information sharing, and collaboration.

n.3: Effective teams cooperate, not compete.
n.2: Trust does not undermine leadership.
n.0: Secrecy is reduced, not increased.
n.1: Morale and retention are better in trusting teams.

Team Management.q: A project manager observes that the team has quickly moved past its earlier disagreements, agreed on shared goals, and established productive working relationships and ways of working together. Using Tuckman's model, which stage of development is the team in?
Team Management.w: Norming is when teams establish norms, resolve differences, and agree on goals.

n.0: Storming is about conflict and disagreement.
n.3: Forming is the initial introduction stage.
n.1: Performing comes after norms are established.
n.4: Adjourning is the closure stage.

Team Management.q: A project team has completed its final deliverables, and members are preparing to move on and return to their business-as-usual roles as the team prepares to disband. According to Tuckman's model, which stage of development is the team in?
Team Management.w: Adjourning is the final stage where teams disband and celebrate achievements.

n.4: Forming is the initial stage.
n.2: Performing is about effective work, not closure.
n.0: Storming is about conflict.
n.1: Norming is about establishing ways of working.

Team Management.q: A project manager wants to use a team model built around eight distinct work functions, including roles such as Creator-Innovator and Controller-Inspector, arranged around a wheel. Which team model includes these eight work functions?
Team Management.w: Margerison McCann's Team Management Wheel features eight distinct work functions.

n.3: Katzenbach and Smith focus on high performance teams.
n.4: Hackman studies team effectiveness factors.
n.2: Belbin identifies nine team roles.
n.1: Tuckman focuses on team stages.

Team Management.q: A project team includes members who occasionally clash, and the project manager values having someone who supports colleagues and helps smooth over disagreements to keep the group harmonious. Which Belbin team role is most likely to fulfil this function?
Team Management.w: The Teamworker role focuses on supporting colleagues and smoothing over differences.

n.1: Shapers drive performance, not harmony.
n.4: Resource Investigators bring in ideas.
n.3: Completer Finishers focus on details, not relationships.
n.2: Monitor Evaluators analyse and critique.

Team Management.q: A project manager is drawing on Hackman's work to understand what makes a project team effective within the wider organisation. According to Hackman, which of the following is an essential element for team effectiveness?

Team Management.w: Organisational support gives teams resources and recognition needed for effectiveness.

n.3: Teams share accountability.
n.1: Feedback is critical for improvement.
n.2: Skill variety is important.
n.4: Stakeholders are part of most projects.

Team Management.q: A project manager uses a mix of instant messaging, video calls, and shared documents for their hybrid team. This is an example of:
o: Adapting leadership style to meet diverse communication needs
Depending on formal email as the sole channel
Prioritising in-person meetings over all technology
Restricting team input to reduce distractions
Delegating every decision to the wider team

n.2: Hybrid teams rely on technology.
n.4: Leaders should stay involved.
n.1: Email alone can be limiting.
n.3: Input should be encouraged.

Team Management.q: A project manager is bringing together a new team at the very start of a project, where individuals are still unclear about their responsibilities and the project's purpose. In Tuckman's team development model, what is the main focus of this 'forming' stage?
Team Management.w: Forming is about clarifying roles and project purpose.

n.0: Disputes happen more in storming.
n.4: Peak productivity comes later.
n.1: Adjourning is about disbanding.
n.2: Reviews are not the central activity at forming.

Team Management.q: A project team is caught in the storming stage, with members clashing over roles and struggling to move forward productively. What should the leader focus on to help the team move past this stage?
o: Encouraging honest communication and setting clear expectations
Team Management.w: Open communication and clear roles resolve storming-stage conflicts.

n.3: Feedback is key, not a hindrance.
n.0: Routine tasks don't address core issues.
n.4: Meetings support clarity and trust.
n.2: Face-to-face communication is more effective at this stage.

Team Management.q: A project has been delivered and the team is about to disband and move on to other assignments, reaching the adjourning stage of its development. During this stage, what should the project manager's main focus be?

n.3: Roles are usually winding down, not being assigned.
n.2: Conflicts are typically resolved earlier.
n.1: Trust building is a focus of the early stages.
n.0: Objectives are set at the beginning, not at adjourning.

Team Management.q: A project manager wants a newly formed team to progress quickly from the forming stage to the norming stage so that it settles down and begins working well together. Which factor is most likely to influence how quickly this transition happens?
o: The size of the physical workspace
The choice of project management software
The level of trust built among team members
Team Management.w: Trust helps team members resolve conflicts and progress more quickly through the stages.

n.2: Funding impacts resources, not team dynamics.
n.1: Software helps with tools, not relationships.
n.0: Workspace size is less important than team cohesion.
n.3: Meeting frequency alone does not drive development.

Team Management.q: An organisation has moved to a hybrid model, with some project team members in the office and others working from home. o: Problems are consistently solved more quickly
Remote members may feel excluded or less visible

Remote work makes it easier for misunderstandings to occur
Online teams can safely rely on assumptions
Virtual teams have no real need for defined roles
Clear expectations tend to reduce team accountability

n.0: Clear expectations are always important.
n.2: Assumptions lead to problems.

Team Management.q: A project manager observes that one team member is especially good at clarifying the team's objectives and delegating work appropriately to the right people. According to Belbin, which team role does this member most likely fulfil?

n.1: Monitor Evaluators provide critical analysis.
n.2: Resource Investigators explore opportunities.

n.4: Specialists offer in-depth expertise.

To reduce day-to-day interaction between members
To avoid misunderstandings and ensure information is shared consistently
To keep project updates accessible only to leaders

Team Management.q: A newly formed project team has moved beyond its initial development phase and is now delivering work steadily. o: Rotating all members out of the team
Providing regular feedback and encouraging open dialogue

n.2: Reduced communication undermines effectiveness.
n.0: Excessive rotation disrupts team development.
n.3: Teamwork is more than individual effort.

Team Management.q: A team is described as having complementary skills, shared accountability, and a commitment to common goals. Which model highlights these features?

Team Management.q: A project team is working efficiently, has a high level of autonomy, and regularly meets its goals. Which stage best describes this?
Team Management.w: Teams in the performing stage operate independently and deliver strong results.

n.3: Storming is about conflict, not peak performance.
n.4: Forming is the initial stage.
n.0: Norming focuses on agreement and cohesion.
n.1: Adjourning is when the team disbands.

Team Management.q: A project manager notices that members of her team demonstrate strong mutual respect and a high level of trust in one another. What is a likely benefit of this within the team?

Team Management.q: After deliberately adapting the way they lead a mix of office-based and home-working staff, a project manager reviews the outcomes at the end of a phase. Cutting back the team's use of collaborative software
Ensuring equal access to information for all team members

Team Management.q: A project team that previously experienced tension has now settled down, with members cooperating well and agreeing on how they will work together. In Tuckman's model, what characterises a team in this norming stage of development?

Team Management.q: A project manager observes that the team is operating with high morale, strong mutual trust, and the flexibility to adapt quickly to changing circumstances. Using Tuckman's model, which stage of team development is most associated with these qualities?

Team Management.q: A project manager is using Margerison-McCann's Team Management Wheel to understand each member's preferred work activity. Which activity is most closely associated with the 'Controller-Inspector' on the wheel?

Team Management.q: A project manager fails to define who is responsible for what, leaving the team without clear roles and responsibilities. What outcome is the most likely result of this situation?

Team Management.q: A project manager introduces the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator to the team so that members can better understand their own and each other's preferences and working styles. What is a likely benefit of using this approach with the team?

Team Management.q: A project team has been working together for several months and, having resolved its earlier tensions and agreed ways of working, has now reached the performing stage of Tuckman's model. What behaviour is most likely to be observed from the team at this stage?

Team Management.q: A senior stakeholder asks a project manager what the organisation can expect to gain when the project team works well together. Which of the following is most likely to improve as a result of effective teamwork?

Team Management.q: A project manager is tracking a team through Tuckman's model and is watching for the point at which members begin to resolve their differences and agree how they will work together. According to Tuckman, at which stage does this happen?

n.0: Forming is the initial coming together.

Team Management.q: A project manager wants to model the kind of communication that characterises high-performing project teams. Which of the following best describes the communication found in effective teams?

Let remote members work independently with minimal support
Foster team building and frequent, inclusive communication

Prizes individual success above collective results
Works in isolation with minimal shared purpose

Team Management.q: A project manager who has always led co-located teams is asked to run an entirely remote team for the first time. Team Management.w: Clear, regular communication is vital for remote team cohesion and effectiveness.

Team Management.q: During a project, the team leader notices members openly clashing over direction, competing for influence, and challenging one another's authority. Using Tuckman's model of team development, which stage is most likely to demand strong conflict management skills from the leader?

Team Management.q: A project manager is reflecting on what sets a genuinely high-performing team apart from an ordinary working group. According to Katzenbach and Smith, high-performing teams are distinguished by which of the following?
o: A focus on individual goals rather than shared ones
Minimal communication between the individual team members
Mutual accountability and a strong commitment to a common purpose
Rigidly fixed role definitions for every member
A large team size and a strict reporting hierarchy
Team Management.w: Katzenbach and Smith highlight mutual accountability and commitment as critical to team performance.

n.4: High-performing teams may be small and flexible.
n.0: Common purpose, not just individual goals, drives performance.
n.1: Effective teams communicate frequently.
n.3: Roles may be flexible in high-performing teams.

Team Management.q: During a long delivery phase, a leader notices that several remote members of the project team have begun to feel isolated and disconnected from colleagues based at head office. Wanting to strengthen morale and belonging, the leader considers what to do. Which approach can help address this?
o: Setting only one-on-one calls with co-located staff
Team Management.w: Informal virtual social activities can boost morale and inclusion for remote members.

n.3: Less communication increases isolation.
n.4: Ignoring feedback worsens engagement.
n.2: All team members should feel included.
n.1: Video helps create connection.

Team Management.q: A project manager decides to use a personality-preference model such as Myers-Briggs to help team members understand one another better. What is a key benefit of applying such a model in team management?
o: Guaranteed project completion ahead of schedule
Team Management.w: Personality models help tailor communication and manage differences effectively.

n.4: Personality models do not guarantee faster projects.
n.1: Ongoing training is still beneficial.
n.2: Feedback remains essential.
n.3: Disagreements can still occur.

Team Management.q: An organisation is deciding whether to invest in developing leaders who can adapt their style for hybrid and virtual working. The sponsor asks the project manager to set out the business case for doing so. Which is an advantage of adapting leadership for hybrid and virtual teams?
Team Management.w: Adapted leadership attracts and retains diverse talent and enables flexible work.

n.2: Accountability should remain strong.
n.4: Politics can be reduced with transparency.
n.1: Technology use should increase.
n.3: Innovation usually increases with good leadership.

Team Management.q: A project team faces conflicts as members adjust to roles and responsibilities. Which stage of team development does this best describe?
Team Management.w: Storming is the stage where conflicts and disagreements are most common.

n.2: Forming is when the team comes together.
n.3: Performing is characterised by effective, harmonious work.
n.1: Adjourning is when the team disbands.
n.4: Norming follows storming and is about resolving conflict.

Sustainability.q: As a construction project reaches closure, the sponsor asks for the final environmental performance figures to be captured in the closure report for lessons learned. Which TWO sustainability measures should be reported at this stage?
o: Seating plan changes and desk allocations
Team birthday count and office decorations used
Number of parties held and social events attended
Final waste diversion rate and energy savings achieved
Holiday leave balances and payroll totals
Sustainability.w: Waste diversion and energy savings quantify environmental performance at project end.

n.1: Party counts have no bearing on sustainability outcomes.
n.2: Social events are unrelated to environmental measures.
n.0: Facility arrangements do not reflect sustainability performance.
n.4: HR metrics are separate from environmental reporting.

Sustainability.q: A project manager planning the procurement and consumption of materials for a large infrastructure scheme is asked to weigh long-term consequences alongside cost and time. Why must the team prioritise sustainability principles when planning resource use?
o: To reduce the level of team collaboration
To shorten the overall project delivery timeline
To balance environmental, social and economic impacts
To maximise short-term financial profits only
To eliminate all project risk entirely
Sustainability.w: Sustainability principles guide resource planning to achieve balanced environmental, social and economic outcomes.

n.3: Short-term profits may conflict with long-term sustainability goals.
n.0: Sustainability aims to improve collaboration, not reduce it.
n.4: Risk cannot be entirely eliminated, only managed.
n.1: Timelines are separate from sustainable resource priorities.

Sustainability.q: When appraising options for a new manufacturing facility, the sponsor asks the team to weigh each choice against its environmental, social and economic consequences together rather than cost alone. Which term describes this combined evaluation approach?
Sustainability.w: The triple bottom line framework assesses projects on people, planet and profit dimensions.

n.3: Scope creep is uncontrolled scope changes.
n.0: Critical path identifies the longest sequence of tasks.
n.1: Earned value measures project performance against cost and schedule.
n.4: A RACI matrix defines roles and responsibilities.

Sustainability.q: A team is documenting the sustainability responsibilities it will carry throughout the planning phase of a public-sector project. Reviewing the draft entries, which of the following is NOT a genuine sustainability responsibility in project planning?
Sustainability.w: Overlooking regulations contradicts the responsibility to comply with environmental standards.

n.3: Assessing social impacts is a key sustainability responsibility.
n.4: Resource management ensures efficient consumption.
n.2: Long-term planning is core to sustainable outcomes.
n.1: Supplier monitoring ensures ethical and sustainable sourcing.

Sustainability.q: A sponsor sets specific environmental, social and economic targets for a construction project and asks the project manager to establish ongoing sustainability monitoring. What is the primary purpose of this monitoring?
o: To track performance against environmental, social and economic targets
To boost team morale and stakeholder confidence levels
To reduce the volume of project reporting documentation
To justify increasing the overall project scope and budget
To provide grounds for extending the project deadlines
Sustainability.w: Monitoring ensures projects meet predefined sustainability targets across multiple dimensions.

n.3: Expanding scope is unrelated to monitoring sustainability.
n.1: Morale may benefit, but it is not the monitoring objective.
n.4: Deadlines are schedule concerns, not monitoring goals.
n.2: Documentation reduction conflicts with accurate monitoring.

Sustainability.q: A solar farm project issues a report monthly to show power output and emission reductions. Frequent reporting improves ____ with stakeholders.
Sustainability.w: Regular updates keep stakeholders informed, fostering transparency and trust.

n.3: Reporting frequency does not inherently increase complexity.
n.2: Timely reporting helps prevent overruns, not cause them.
n.1: Communication reduces disputes, not create them.
n.0: Clear reports minimize errors, not increase them.

Sustainability.q: A project manager wants to capture stakeholders' perceptions and priorities regarding the project's sustainability performance so the results can feed into future planning. This feedback is most commonly collected through ____ surveys.
Sustainability.w: Surveys targeting stakeholders gather perceptions and priorities related to sustainability performance.

n.0: Risk surveys focus on potential threats, not stakeholder perceptions.
n.4: Quality surveys address product standards, not stakeholder views on sustainability.
n.2: Budget surveys relate to financial allocations, not sustainability feedback.
n.3: Marketing surveys gauge market reactions, not sustainability opinions.

Sustainability.q: In a water treatment project, weekly summaries include turbidity levels and energy use. Which metric would NOT be relevant for sustainability reporting?
Sustainability.w: Engagement rates measure marketing success, not environmental performance.

n.3: Turbidity indicates water quality, key to environmental impact.
n.2: Energy consumption is central to sustainability metrics.
n.4: Sludge volume reflects waste management performance.
n.0: Chemical dosing rates affect environmental and safety measures.

Sustainability.q: A project manager preparing the budget for an office refurbishment is asked to show how the sustainability choices being made will affect overall project cost. Which TWO factors most directly influence the impact of sustainability priorities on that cost?
o: Brand logo design and marketing tagline
Choice of materials and waste management processes
Team party frequency and catering quality
Sustainability.w: Material selection and waste handling methods directly affect both sustainability impact and project cost.

n.3: Office décor does not significantly influence sustainability costs.
n.2: Social events are separate from core project expenses.
n.4: HR policies are unrelated to sustainability costs.
n.0: Marketing design choices don’t drive sustainability expenditure.

Sustainability.q: A project manager is mapping the sequence of activities involved in producing a credible sustainability report for external review. Considering the steps proposed, which of the following is NOT a key step in sustainability reporting?
Sustainability.w: Transparency, not concealment, is essential to credible sustainability reporting.

n.4: Collecting data is the foundation of any report.
n.3: Verification ensures accuracy of reported information.
n.0: Publishing allows stakeholders to review performance.
n.2: Reviewing targets assesses whether objectives were met.

Sustainability.q: A project manager is briefing a delivery team on the principles that should shape sustainable decision-making on a long-running programme. Reviewing a list of proposed principles, which of the following is NOT a genuine principle of sustainable project management?
o: Prioritising short-term gains over long-term benefits
Sustainability.w: Focusing on short-term gains undermines the long-term orientation of sustainability principles.

n.3: Stakeholder engagement supports effective sustainability decisions.
n.4: Energy efficiency is central to environmental sustainability.
n.1: Equity is part of the social dimension of sustainability.
n.2: Minimising harm is a primary environmental goal.

Sustainability.q: A community housing project installs a rainwater harvesting system to cut its reliance on the municipal water supply, and the project manager is asked to report the resulting benefits. Which TWO impacts align with this decision?
o: Lower water bills and reduced resource depletion
Expanded spectator seating and event planning
Higher catering costs and more office parties
Increased meeting frequency and longer holidays
Sustainability.w: Harvesting rainwater decreases utility expenses and conserves natural resources, supporting sustainability priorities.

n.4: Meeting schedules and holidays are unrelated to water use.
n.3: Catering and parties do not impact sustainability of water resources.
n.1: Branding changes do not affect environmental sustainability.
n.2: Event seating plans are separate from resource conservation.

Sustainability.q: A project manager preparing to distribute the completed sustainability report must decide which audiences have a legitimate need for the environmental and performance data. Which TWO stakeholder groups typically receive sustainability reports?
Sustainability.w: Regulators require compliance data and investors evaluate long-term risks and value creation.

n.4: Catering and décor are not primary recipients of sustainability data.
n.3: Maintenance teams use operational data, not stakeholder reports.
n.2: Event planners focus on logistics, not reporting needs.
n.1: Social clubs manage culture, not compliance or investment decisions.

Sustainability.q: During a land-rehabilitation project on a former industrial site, the team replants native vegetation and regularly tests the soil quality to confirm the ground is recovering. Which sustainability responsibilities are being fulfilled by this work?
o: Office seating reconfiguration and décor selection
Team morale building and party planning
Sustainability.w: Restoring vegetation and monitoring soil fulfill the environmental responsibilities of sustainable projects.

n.1: Budget and branding are separate management activities.
n.3: Morale and parties are cultural considerations.
n.2: Décor and seating relate to facility management.
n.0: HR tasks do not represent sustainability responsibilities.

Sustainability.q: During a high-rise project in an urban area, the team tracks carbon emissions to guide material choices. Which principle is being applied?
Sustainability.w: Measuring and reducing carbon emissions reflects the principle of minimising environmental impact.

n.0: Speed is a schedule concern, not sustainability.
n.1: Branding relates to marketing, not environmental principles.
n.3: Entertainment does not inform material selection.
n.2: Cost avoidance may hinder investment in sustainable materials.

Sustainability.q: An organisation publishes independently verified data on its projects' environmental indicators so that regulators, investors and the public can rely on it. Which term describes this externally published, verified information?
Sustainability.w: Disclosures provide formally verified information on sustainability performance to external stakeholders.

n.4: Scope statements outline project boundaries, not performance data.
n.3: Risk assessments identify potential threats, not disclosed metrics.
n.2: Quality audits assess adherence to standards, not external disclosures.
n.0: Forecasts predict future budgets, not verified environmental data.

Sustainability.q: A project manager is compiling the organisation's first sustainability report for an infrastructure programme and must decide which environmental indicators to include. Which TWO metrics are most commonly included in such reports?
o: Holiday leave balances and payroll data
Daily snack counts and party frequency
Office décor changes and seating plans
Sustainability.w: Carbon and water metrics reflect environmental impacts central to sustainability reporting.

n.2: Snacks and parties are cultural, not sustainability metrics.
n.3: Décor and seating relate to facilities management.
n.4: Social media engagement is marketing data, not sustainability.
n.1: Payroll and leave are HR metrics, not sustainability measures.

Sustainability.q: A project team is agreeing which indicators it will formally capture as part of its sustainability measures on a new facility. Reviewing the proposed list, which of the following is NOT something typically tracked in sustainability measures?
Sustainability.w: Coffee consumption is a cultural habit, not a standard sustainability metric.

n.0: Emissions are key environmental metrics.
n.3: Energy use is central to measuring environmental impact.
n.4: Waste generation reflects resource efficiency.
n.2: Water usage is a core sustainability indicator.

Sustainability.q: At the end of a reporting cycle, a project manager gathers the project's environmental, social and governance data so that stakeholders can review overall performance in one place. This information is typically consolidated into a ____ report.
Sustainability.w: A dedicated sustainability report aggregates environmental, social and governance metrics for stakeholders.

n.0: Risk reports focus on potential threats, not comprehensive sustainability data.
n.2: Quality reports address standards, not broader sustainability impacts.
n.3: Budget reports cover financials, not sustainability metrics.
n.1: Variance reports compare planned vs actual costs, not sustainability indicators.

Sustainability.q: A dam construction project must carefully manage its water use while preserving the surrounding wildlife habitats affected by the works. Which TWO responsibilities best demonstrate sustainable practice in this context?
o: Effluent control measures and biodiversity monitoring
Extended work hours and reduced safety checks
Frequent management parties and new office décor
Eliminating risk reviews and cancelling stakeholder meetings
Unlimited budget allocation and rapid excavation
Sustainability.w: Controlling effluent and monitoring biodiversity directly support environmental protection responsibilities.

n.1: Extended hours and reduced safety increase risks, not sustainability.
n.4: Unlimited budgets may fund unsustainable practices.
n.2: Social events do not ensure sustainable outcomes.
n.3: Risk reviews and stakeholder engagement support responsible practice.

Sustainability.q: A governance board is agreeing why sustainability responsibilities should be written into the project's terms of reference and reporting structure. Considering the reasons put forward, which of the following is NOT a valid reason to embed sustainability responsibilities in project governance?
Sustainability.w: Ignoring regulations opposes the purpose of embedding sustainability in governance.

n.2: Legal compliance is a key driver for sustainability governance.
n.3: Reputation benefits from sustainable practice.
n.1: Innovation often arises from sustainability challenges.
n.4: Resource management is central to sustainability responsibilities.

Sustainability.q: A project team is drawing up the sustainability objectives that will guide decisions throughout a construction programme. Reviewing a draft list of priorities put forward by different members, which of the following is NOT a genuine sustainability priority in project management?
Sustainability.w: Maximising environmental degradation conflicts directly with sustainability goals.

n.4: Reducing waste is a key sustainability priority.
n.2: Supporting communities aligns with the social dimension of sustainability.
n.0: Efficient energy use is central to environmental sustainability.
n.3: Long-term viability is a core objective of sustainable practice.

Sustainability.q: In a manufacturing scenario, sensors record real-time air emissions and energy consumption. Which tool should compile these measures for reporting?
Sustainability.w: Dashboards aggregate live data into visual summaries ideal for sustainability reporting.

n.2: Gantt charts map schedules, not real-time environmental data.
n.4: Org charts show structure, not performance metrics.
n.0: Chat logs record conversations, not quantitative data.
n.1: Calendars track dates, not sustainability metrics.

Sustainability.q: A coastal redevelopment project sets out deliberately to protect local ecosystems and reduce carbon emissions as part of how it will be judged a success. Which sustainability responsibility does this focus best illustrate?
Sustainability.w: Environmental stewardship involves protecting ecosystems and reducing emissions as part of sustainability responsibilities.

n.2: Cost minimisation is a financial goal, not a sustainability responsibility.
n.3: Brand enhancement is a marketing objective, not core to sustainability.
n.1: Scheduling efficiency relates to timeline management, not sustainability.
n.0: Stakeholder entertainment is a cultural activity, not a sustainability duty.

Sustainability.q: During a large mining project, the team decides to reuse excavated spoil for on-site landscaping rather than sending it to landfill and extracting new fill elsewhere. Which sustainability practice does this approach support?
Sustainability.w: Circular economy practices involve reusing materials to reduce waste and resource extraction.

n.0: Risk avoidance is unrelated to material reuse.
n.4: Entertainment is not a sustainability practice.
n.3: Relocation deals with logistics, not resource reuse.
n.1: Budget changes do not define reuse practices.

Sustainability.q: A facilities upgrade project installs solar panels across a distribution centre, and the sponsor asks the team to identify the benefits the organisation will gain. Which TWO impacts best illustrate the sustainability priorities behind this decision?
o: Fewer safety inspections and relaxed quality checks
Lower energy bills and reduced greenhouse gas emissions
Extended work hours and larger budgets
Larger marketing budgets and new branding colors
Increased office parties and higher catering costs
Sustainability.w: Solar panels decrease energy costs and greenhouse gases, reflecting economic and environmental priorities.

n.4: Social events and catering do not reflect sustainability priorities.
n.2: Extended hours and bigger budgets do not guarantee sustainability.
n.0: Relaxing safety undermines responsible practice.
n.3: Marketing focus is separate from sustainability outcomes.

Conflict Resolution.q: During a lessons-learned review, a project manager wants to highlight the benefits that well-managed conflict brought to the team over the life cycle. When considering the potential positive impacts of conflict on a project, which of the following is NOT one of them?
Conflict Resolution.w: Reduced communication is a negative consequence, not a positive impact.

n.0: Enhanced innovation is a positive impact.
n.4: Improved decision making is a positive impact.
n.3: Stronger solutions can result from conflict.
n.2: Greater engagement is a positive impact.

Conflict Resolution.q: In a negotiation where both sides give up something to reach a balanced agreement, which mode and characteristic pair applies?
o: Collaborating: low assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Compromising: moderate assertiveness and moderate cooperativeness
Accommodating: high assertiveness and moderate cooperativeness
Competing: low assertiveness and high cooperativeness
Avoiding: moderate assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Conflict Resolution.w: Compromising uses moderate assertiveness and cooperativeness for balance.

n.4: Avoiding is low assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
n.3: Competing is high assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
n.0: Collaborating is high assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
n.2: Accommodating is low assertiveness and high cooperativeness.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager reflects that conflict within a team is not always harmful and, when handled well, can actually benefit the project. Which of the following is a positive impact of conflict on a project?
Conflict Resolution.w: Conflict can stimulate creative problem solving by challenging assumptions.

n.1: Delays deliverables are a negative impact of conflict.
n.0: Increases cost overruns are negative outcomes.
n.3: Reduced stakeholder engagement is negative.
n.4: Team burnout is a negative impact.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager faces a minor, peripheral disagreement late in a busy delivery week and judges that engaging with it now is not worth the limited time available. Which Thomas-Kilmann mode fits best? The ______ mode is best when the issue is trivial or time is limited.
Conflict Resolution.w: Avoiding is used for trivial issues or limited time.

n.4: Collaborating requires time to address concerns.
n.0: Competing involves confrontation.
n.1: Compromising still requires discussion.
n.2: Accommodating yields to others, not for trivial issues.

Conflict Resolution.q: On a project, tension is mounting because several senior members openly disagree about who actually holds the authority to make certain key decisions. Which source of conflict does this situation involve?
Conflict Resolution.w: Power struggles arise when authority lines are unclear or contested.

n.2: A budget audit is a financial check, not authority conflict.
n.3: Server maintenance is a technical task.
n.4: Routine updates are normal operations.
n.0: Process training is educational, not a conflict driver.

Conflict Resolution.q: Midway through delivery, the project sponsor keeps altering what he wants the project to prioritise and produce, unsettling the team and their plans. This friction most directly stems from which source of conflict?
Conflict Resolution.w: Scope change driven by shifting sponsor priorities is a key conflict source.

n.0: Personality clashes are interpersonal, not priority-driven.
n.4: Vendor issues involve external suppliers, not sponsor changes.
n.1: Cultural differences relate to values and norms.
n.3: Team workload is about capacity, not sponsor demands.

Conflict Resolution.q: A highly skilled engineer is simultaneously assigned to several projects and cannot keep up with the combined workload, creating tension across the teams that all depend on her. This situation exemplifies conflict due to:
Conflict Resolution.w: Resource overload causes conflict when one person is assigned to too many tasks.

n.4: Scope definition relates to what’s included, not workload.
n.1: Positive reinforcement doesn’t create conflict.
n.0: Contract renewal is administrative, not workload-driven.
n.3: Process standardization typically reduces conflict.

Conflict Resolution.q: In a project update, the sponsor avoided further debate to maintain harmony. Which of the following is NOT a negative side effect of this conflict avoidance?
Conflict Resolution.w: Increased innovation is a positive, not a negative side effect of avoidance.

n.0: Unresolved issues are a negative side effect.
n.2: Reduced accountability is negative.
n.4: Communication gaps are negative.
n.3: Hidden risks are negative.

Conflict Resolution.q: During testing, heated debates among the team surfaced several critical flaws that would otherwise have been missed, but the arguments also pushed the delivery timeline back. Which pair of impacts does this represent?
Conflict Resolution.w: Conflict improved quality detection but caused schedule delays.

n.1: Team cohesion and cost reduction aren’t the impacts described.
n.3: Morale and resource gain aren’t both described.
n.0: Governance and approval speed are unrelated.
n.2: Scope reduction and budget increase don’t match the scenario.

Conflict Resolution.q: The deadlines for two critical tasks fall within the same short window, forcing the team to juggle both at once with too little time to do either properly. The conflict the team then experiences arises from:
Conflict Resolution.w: Schedule overlap forces competition for limited time, causing conflict.

n.4: Stable requirements don’t create timing conflicts.
n.3: Standardized tools improve consistency.
n.1: Positive recognition improves morale.
n.2: Clear communication helps prevent conflict.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager wants to illustrate to the sponsor two of the ways in which unmanaged conflict can harm a project and its team. Which of the following pairs illustrates two possible negative impacts of conflict?
o: Faster decision making and stronger relationships
Improved risk management and cost savings
Conflict Resolution.w: Conflict can reduce trust and increase stress as negative impacts.

n.1: Those are positive impacts of conflict.
n.2: Stakeholder alignment and creativity are positive.
n.4: Risk management and cost savings are benefits, not negatives.
n.0: Faster decisions and strong relationships are positive.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager is deciding in which circumstances stepping back and using the avoiding conflict-handling mode would be justified. Which of the following is NOT a scenario where the avoiding mode is appropriate?
Conflict Resolution.w: Avoiding is inappropriate for critical safety decisions.

n.1: Avoiding works for minor tasks.
n.4: It helps when emotions are high.
n.2: It suits trivial issues.
n.3: Delay can help gain perspective.

Conflict Resolution.q: During a heated design discussion, the team's clashing viewpoints ultimately produced an inventive solution to the problem that none of them had considered on their own. Which impact of conflict does this best illustrate?
Conflict Resolution.w: Debating different views stimulates enhanced creativity as a positive conflict impact.

n.2: Scope creep is a negative outcome of uncontrolled changes.
n.3: Resource depletion is a result of poor planning, not conflict-driven creativity.
n.4: Schedule slippage is a negative consequence, not this scenario.
n.0: Stakeholder confusion is not illustrated here.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager is weighing the trade-offs of using the collaborating conflict-handling mode to resolve a significant dispute. Which of the following is NOT a drawback of the collaborating mode?
Conflict Resolution.w: High cooperativeness is a feature, not a drawback of collaborating.

n.4: Collaborating can indeed be time-consuming.
n.1: It requires mutual trust.
n.3: It demands open communication.
n.0: It needs willingness to share.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager is aware that leaving disagreements within the team unaddressed for too long can damage the project. Which of the following describes a negative outcome of unresolved conflict?
Conflict Resolution.w: Unresolved conflict often reduces team cohesion.

n.1: Increased innovation is a positive impact of healthy conflict.
n.4: Enhanced collaboration occurs with constructive conflict.
n.2: Improved decision making is a positive outcome.
n.3: Greater stakeholder buy-in is a benefit, not negative.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project team's prolonged disagreement over the best approach eventually produced a stronger final design, but the extended effort involved pushed the project over its budget. Which pair reflects these two impacts?
o: Faster delivery and lower resource needs
Improved solution quality and increased costs
Greater stakeholder buy-in and time savings
Conflict Resolution.w: Conflict can improve solution quality but also drive costs up.

n.2: Time savings aren't part of the described impacts.
n.3: Reduced innovation is negative and morale increase is positive, but not described.
n.0: Faster delivery and lower resource needs are positive only.
n.4: Budget stability contradicts cost overruns described.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager is coaching a new team leader on the Thomas-Kilmann conflict modes and their defining traits along the assertiveness and cooperativeness dimensions. Which of the following pairs correctly matches a conflict mode to its characteristic?
o: Avoiding: high assertiveness and high cooperativeness
Competing: high assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Accommodating: low assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Compromising: high assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Collaborating: low assertiveness and low cooperativeness
Conflict Resolution.w: Competing is high assertiveness, low cooperativeness.

n.0: Avoiding is low assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
n.2: Accommodating is low assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
n.4: Collaborating is high assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
n.3: Compromising is moderate assertiveness and cooperativeness.

Conflict Resolution.q: A programme manager is reviewing several projects where team friction escalated and outcomes suffered. Reflecting on how conflict can lead to negative project outcomes, which of the following is NOT an example of such a negative effect?
Conflict Resolution.w: Greater stakeholder buy-in is positive, not a negative outcome.

n.4: Resource disputes are a negative outcome.
n.2: Team member attrition is a negative result of conflict.
n.3: Budget overruns are negative.
n.0: Delayed milestones are negative.

Conflict Resolution.q: A project manager firmly pushes their own preferred approach in a heated planning meeting, pressing their position while giving little weight to the other party's concerns. In the Thomas-Kilmann model, which conflict-handling mode is characterised by high assertiveness combined with low cooperativeness?
Conflict Resolution.w: The competing mode is high assertiveness and low cooperativeness.

n.2: Avoiding is low assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
n.3: Collaborating is high assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
n.0: Accommodating is low assertiveness and high cooperativeness.
n.1: Compromising is moderate assertiveness and cooperativeness.

Conflict Resolution.q: On a project where the cost estimates keep being revised, each change ripples out and disrupts other elements of the plan, provoking disagreement among the team. Conflict arising from which of the following does this best describe?
Conflict Resolution.w: Budget volatility—shifting cost estimates—can trigger conflicts elsewhere.

n.2: Clear governance mitigates rather than causes conflict.
n.4: Team alignment prevents conflicts.
n.3: Stable requirements are not a source of conflict.
n.0: Process automation reduces manual errors, not conflict.

Conflict Resolution.q: Two team members resolve a scheduling clash by talking it through and settling it directly between themselves, without calling in any impartial outsider. Which conflict resolution technique is this? In ______, the disputing parties work together without involving a neutral third party.
Conflict Resolution.w: Negotiation involves direct resolution without a neutral third party.

n.4: Arbitration uses a third party for binding decisions.
n.0: Mediation involves a neutral facilitator.
n.1: Escalation involves higher management intervention.
