n.3: The PM may draft change requests, not typically sponsors.
n.1: Sprint backlogs are agile team responsibilities.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project governance board requests assurance reports from an independent reviewer. What is the main purpose of this oversight activity?
o: To take over the project manager's delivery responsibilities
To approve each operational decision made during delivery
To provide confidence that the project is controlled and aligned
To transfer accountability from the sponsor to the reviewer
To remove the need for any further stakeholder consultation
Governance Arrangements.w: Assurance gives governance bodies confidence that delivery, risks and controls remain appropriate.

Governance Arrangements.q: A time-critical project needs decisions made quickly, but it is being delivered within a weak matrix where authority sits largely with the functional departments. The project manager is concerned about how this will affect progress. What is the most likely impact?
o: Delays caused by reliance on functional approval
Faster approvals due to shared authority
Governance Arrangements.w: Weak matrices require functional approvals, slowing decisions.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project is reviewed on schedule at every stage, but even as its risk profile shifts markedly, nothing about the plan or approach is ever changed as a result. What is the main issue?
o: Producing reports containing excessive technical detail
Failure to act on updated business case information
Scheduling far too many formal review points
Lacking the technical expertise to assess risks
Over-communicating minor risks to all stakeholders
Governance Arrangements.w: Review without action undermines the purpose of updating the business case.

Governance Arrangements.q: On a business-change project, the individual who represents the end users has been left out of governance decisions that set the priorities for accepting deliverables. The project manager is concerned about the consequences of this omission. What is the most likely risk that results?
o: The project manager will lose all delivery authority
The governance board will become too large
Decisions may not reflect user needs or acceptance criteria
The escalation process will become unnecessary
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance decisions need appropriate representation so user needs and acceptance priorities are considered.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is establishing how a new project will be controlled and reported within its host organisation. An organisation's governance approach will typically influence which of the following?
o: The project life cycle, controls, and reporting structures
The technical design of the product
The funding source used for a project
Governance Arrangements.w: Governance impacts how the project is structured, controlled, reviewed, and reported.

n.2: Funding is decided more by business case or sponsor.
n.3: External consultants may or may not be influenced by governance.
n.1: Technical design is determined by solution teams.
n.4: Innovation level depends more on project goals and context.

Governance Arrangements.q: Some months after a new system has been handed over to operations, the organisation wants to confirm that the anticipated efficiency savings are actually being achieved. Who is ultimately responsible for the realisation of benefits after the project has been completed?
Governance Arrangements.w: The project sponsor is accountable for ensuring the planned benefits are realised post-project.

n.2: The project manager's role typically ends at project handover.
n.4: The product owner focuses on product delivery, not benefit tracking.
n.0: Users benefit from outcomes but are not accountable for realisation.
n.1: Work package owners are responsible for deliverables, not benefits.

Governance Arrangements.q: An organisation frequently needs to stand up teams quickly and give project managers the authority to deliver at pace. Which organisational structure best supports rapid mobilisation and flexible project delivery?
Governance Arrangements.w: Project-based structures allow fast deployment and high authority for project managers, improving delivery speed.

n.2: Functional structures are not designed for rapid mobilisation.
n.4: Weak matrix offers low authority and fragmented teams.
n.0: Balanced matrix requires alignment, which can slow mobilisation.
n.1: Hierarchical structures often slow decision-making.

Governance Arrangements.q: A newly qualified project manager wants to apply business case reviews well as their project progresses through its stages. Which scenario best demonstrates effective use of business case lifecycle reviews?
o: Continuing the project unchanged regardless of shifting circumstances
Avoiding formal reviews to save time and effort
Delegating all continuation decisions to the delivery team
Focusing reviews only on updated cost information
Updating the business case and reassessing viability at each stage
Governance Arrangements.w: Effective lifecycle management involves updating and reassessing the business case regularly.

Governance Arrangements.q: A project manager is deciding which information the board most needs in order to judge whether a proposed project is genuinely viable. Which TWO components are essential for assessing project viability in a business case?
Governance Arrangements.w: Cost and benefit are fundamental to viability assessment.

Schedule Management.q: Midway through a project, significant changes to scope and resource availability have occurred, yet the project manager continues to report against the original schedule without updating it. What is a potential consequence of failing to re-estimate the schedule after these changes?
o: Lower likelihood of stakeholder escalation and concern
Improved accuracy of the project's reported progress
Better alignment between the plan and reality
Reduced overall project risk exposure over time
Unrealistic deadlines and increased likelihood of project overruns
Schedule Management.w: Ignoring changes leads to deadlines that don’t match reality and increases risk of overrun.

n.1: Success cannot be guaranteed without accurate planning.
n.3: Risks are always present.
n.2: Stakeholders may lose confidence if deadlines slip.
n.0: Transparency may suffer, but overruns are the main risk.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is assessing how ongoing operational work in a busy organisation might affect the delivery timeline of a change project. Which of these is NOT a common impact of business-as-usual activities on a project schedule?
o: Requirement for project activities outside standard hours
Schedule Management.w: Business-as-usual often restricts resources, not guarantees uninterrupted access.

n.1: Staff may be pulled away for BAU, delaying the project.
n.4: Physical space is often shared, creating dependencies.
n.3: IT systems may need to be shared.
n.0: Scheduling project work outside normal hours is a common result.

Schedule Management.q: A large infrastructure programme has many linked activities where a change to one task ripples through to others. As delivery progresses and circumstances change, what is the primary reason for ongoing re-estimation in projects with complex interdependencies?
o: To transfer dependency management onto the project sponsor
To fix the baseline so that dependencies no longer change
To satisfy a mandatory weekly progress reporting requirement
To ensure dependencies and impacts are considered as circumstances evolve
To reduce the total number of dependencies in the plan
Schedule Management.w: Re-estimation ensures the impact of interdependencies is accounted for throughout the project.

n.1: Administrative burden is not the main reason for re-estimation.
n.4: Updates serve planning, not sponsor impression.
n.0: Project management requires ongoing attention.
n.2: The team should remain involved in project planning.

Schedule Management.q: A hospital is running a project to implement a new patient records system. The implementation must not disrupt normal patient care. What does this requirement create?
o: A scheduling dependency on business-as-usual activities
A financial benefit for the hospital
A project risk that cannot be managed
Schedule Management.w: Project work must be scheduled around normal operations, creating a direct dependency.

n.3: Quality assurance is important but not the dependency itself.
n.1: The benefit is not a dependency.
n.4: Risks can often be managed with proper planning.
n.2: Procurement is unrelated in this case.

Schedule Management.q: A project is being implemented in a school during term time. Which is the most likely dependency to impact the schedule?
o: Design of the signage used around the site
The number of teachers attending progress meetings
School holidays and exam periods restricting project work
Choice of contractor for the classroom refurbishment
Availability of the preferred project management software
Schedule Management.w: School events often require project work to be scheduled at less disruptive times.

n.3: Documentation style does not create dependencies with BAU.
n.4: Meeting frequency is an internal project factor.
n.1: Presentation format does not create a dependency.
n.0: Supplier choice is a procurement, not a scheduling dependency.

Schedule Management.q: A project relies on an operational team whose routine work carries its own threats, such as system outages and seasonal workload spikes. How can risks in business-as-usual activities affect the schedule of a project?
o: By guaranteeing extra resources are assigned to the project
By causing delays to project tasks if BAU risks materialise
By transferring all BAU risks onto the project risk register
By automatically extending the project deadline to absorb them
By lowering the project's agreed quality requirements
Schedule Management.w: BAU risks can disrupt project timelines if they materialise.

n.2: Scope changes are managed through formal change control, not BAU risks.
n.3: Contingency is needed precisely because risks exist.
n.4: Risks generally slow down progress, not speed it up.
n.0: Staff availability may decrease if BAU is affected.

Schedule Management.q: While defining the scope of a marketing project, the team is careful to separate the tangible things it will produce from the wider improvements the organisation hopes to gain. In the context of scope definition, what does the term 'output' refer to?
o: A tangible deliverable produced by the project
The summary of project lessons learned
A risk that could impact the project
A financial benefit realised by the organisation
Schedule Management.w: An output is a tangible deliverable, such as a new product or report.

n.4: Benefits are achieved after outputs are realised.
n.2: Risks are managed separately and are not outputs.
n.1: Lessons learned are part of project closure, not outputs.
n.3: Stakeholder numbers do not define outputs.

Schedule Management.q: A project sponsor wants to see how project costs are distributed across deliverables. Which tool should the project manager use to show this information?
Schedule Management.w: The cost breakdown structure (CBS) allocates and visualises costs for each project deliverable.

n.4: PBS shows deliverables, not costs.
n.1: WBS focuses on work, not cost distribution.
n.0: Milestone charts show key events, not costs.
n.3: Network diagrams are used for scheduling, not cost allocation.

Schedule Management.q: While building the schedule for a finance system upgrade, a project manager reviews the organisation's key operational reporting dates before fixing task timings. Why should a project manager assess business-as-usual deadlines when creating the project schedule?
o: To avoid conflicts that could delay project tasks
To set up more project meetings
To improve the company’s public image
To select a new project sponsor
Schedule Management.w: Assessing BAU deadlines helps avoid clashes that can cause project delays.

n.2: More meetings do not solve scheduling conflicts.
n.4: Project sponsorship is unrelated to BAU deadlines.
n.1: Scope reduction is a separate decision.
n.3: Public image is not directly affected by BAU deadlines.

Schedule Management.q: A project team delivering a new visitor centre wants to organise and control its expenditure by grouping costs against the different components of the work. When would a project team typically use a cost breakdown structure (CBS)?
o: To assign quality criteria to deliverables
To allocate and manage project expenses
Schedule Management.w: The CBS is used to allocate costs across project components and manage the budget.

n.1: Quality criteria are addressed separately in the quality plan.
n.0: Stakeholder strategies belong in the stakeholder management plan.
n.2: Communication planning is handled elsewhere.
n.3: Lessons learned are recorded during closure, not in the CBS.

Schedule Management.q: A business’s quarterly reporting cycle will limit staff availability for a key project deliverable. What is the most effective scheduling strategy?
o: Increase the project budget for overtime
Ignore the reporting cycle and proceed as planned
Assign reporting tasks to junior project staff
Plan the deliverable for after the reporting cycle ends
Schedule Management.w: Planning after the reporting cycle ensures necessary staff are available for the project.

n.1: Ignoring the cycle risks project delays and staff overload.
n.3: Quality must be maintained regardless of scheduling challenges.
n.2: Reporting is a BAU responsibility and may require experienced staff.
n.0: Overtime is costly and may not always solve scheduling conflicts.

Schedule Management.q: A project is affected by an increase in business-as-usual demand during the holiday season. What is a likely impact on the project schedule?
o: Project risks transfer automatically to the operations team
Project activities may be delayed due to reduced resource availability
Project scope expands to cover the extra BAU workload
Project costs fall because the staff are already employed
Project quality standards must be raised to match the demand
Schedule Management.w: BAU peaks can reduce resources for the project, resulting in potential schedule delays.

n.4: Increased BAU demand generally causes delays, not acceleration.
n.2: Risks remain and may increase.
n.0: Scope is managed separately and isn't directly affected by BAU demand.
n.3: Quality must still be met despite resource constraints.

Schedule Management.q: A new marketing campaign must not interfere with standard customer support hours. What is the best way to address this dependency?
o: Remove customer support from BAU temporarily
Limit marketing to online channels only
Schedule campaign activities outside core support hours
Schedule Management.w: Running campaign tasks outside support hours avoids conflict—a textbook scheduling dependency solution.

n.0: More budget does not remove the dependency.
n.4: Scope reduction is unnecessary if scheduling can resolve the issue.
n.1: Removing support is impractical and would harm the business.
n.2: Channel limitation does not guarantee no interference with support hours.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager finds that the organisation's annual financial audit, which draws heavily on finance staff, falls during the project's planned testing phase. How could this impact the project?
o: All risks associated with testing are removed
The project will be exempt from documentation requirements
Project testing may be rescheduled to avoid resource clashes
Schedule Management.w: A major BAU event like an audit can limit available resources, requiring the project to adjust its schedule.

n.3: Documentation is still required.
n.2: Audit timing may impact costs if resources are diverted.
n.1: Quality standards should remain consistent.
n.0: Risks may actually increase, not disappear.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager uses schedule optimisation to reassign resources from non-critical to critical path tasks. What is the benefit of this action?
o: It guarantees all deliverables are on time
It increases the risk of missing critical milestones
It reduces the need for project monitoring
It can shorten the overall project duration
Schedule Management.w: Moving resources to the critical path can reduce project length by addressing bottlenecks.

n.1: This action helps meet critical milestones, not miss them.
n.3: Monitoring remains necessary.
n.2: Non-critical work must still be managed, just less urgently.
n.0: No technique can guarantee every deliverable is on time.

Schedule Management.q: A retailer is investing in a project to streamline its warehouse operations, and the project team is defining scope by distinguishing deliverables from the improvements the business expects to gain. In this situation, which of the following best describes a benefit when defining project scope?
o: Enhanced business efficiency resulting from project changes
The creation of a cost baseline
Schedule Management.w: A benefit is a measurable improvement resulting from project outcomes, such as business efficiency.

n.0: A project status report is a deliverable, not a benefit.
n.2: A breakdown of project tasks is part of planning, not a benefit.
n.4: A cost baseline is a planning tool.
n.3: Meetings are a project activity, not a benefit.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager preparing the schedule for a change initiative is mapping out where project tasks and routine operational work will interact. Why is it important to identify dependencies between project and BAU activities when planning the project schedule?
o: To reduce the size of the project team
To increase the number of meetings held
To avoid conflicts that can delay project delivery
To ensure all stakeholders receive status updates
Schedule Management.w: Identifying dependencies helps avoid scheduling conflicts and project delays.

n.1: Meeting frequency is not directly related to schedule dependencies.
n.0: Team size is not determined by BAU dependencies.
n.4: Status updates are important but not the main purpose here.
n.2: Procurement is not simplified by identifying dependencies.

Schedule Management.q: A manufacturing company is launching a new product while maintaining normal production levels. Which factor is most likely to impact the project schedule?
o: Availability of production equipment for both activities
The colour of the final product
Schedule Management.w: If the same equipment is used for project and BAU, its availability creates a dependency and can cause delays.

n.4: Product colour is unrelated to scheduling dependencies.
n.3: Team size may influence progress, but equipment sharing is a direct dependency.
n.0: Marketing is not central to the scheduling dependency described.
n.1: Paperwork volume does not create dependencies.

Schedule Management.q: A project team uses a cost breakdown structure (CBS) to help manage its budget. What does the CBS mainly illustrate?
o: The timeline for each project phase
The risks associated with each work package
The allocation of project costs across deliverables
The hierarchy of the project team
Schedule Management.w: The CBS allocates costs to different project deliverables or components.

n.0: The timeline is shown on a schedule, not a CBS.
n.4: Team hierarchy is represented in an OBS, not CBS.
n.1: Risks are managed in a risk register.
n.2: Stakeholder engagement is not depicted in the CBS.

Schedule Management.q: A project team needs to schedule a major software upgrade. However, the IT department is also supporting month-end business processes at the same time. What should the project manager do?
o: Cancel the upgrade due to resource unavailability
Request more funding to bypass the IT department
Assign the upgrade task to business analysts
Coordinate the upgrade to avoid month-end business-as-usual peaks
Proceed with the upgrade as planned regardless of BAU activities
Schedule Management.w: Project managers must plan around BAU activities to avoid resource conflicts and delays.

n.4: Ignoring BAU activities risks schedule clashes and service disruption.
n.0: Cancellation is unnecessary; better coordination is possible.
n.1: Funding alone does not resolve the resource dependency.
n.2: Business analysts may not have the technical expertise for upgrades.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is reviewing several situations to decide which ones genuinely tie project costs to ongoing operational work when building the schedule. Which is NOT an example of how costs can link business-as-usual activities to a project schedule?
o: Business-as-usual overtime costs delaying project milestones
Temporary staff hired to cover BAU so project staff are released
Increased costs for shared equipment during BAU peaks
Shared costs for joint project and BAU training
Project budget tracking against a separate cost code
Schedule Management.w: Budget tracking with a separate cost code does not create a dependency between project and BAU.

n.0: Overtime costs may divert resources and cause project delays.
n.2: Increased equipment costs during BAU peaks impact project scheduling.
n.1: Hiring temporary staff is a direct response to the resource dependency.
n.3: Joint training links project and BAU cost scheduling.

Schedule Management.q: When defining scope, a project manager distinguishes between a product breakdown structure (PBS) and a work breakdown structure (WBS). What is the key difference?
o: PBS and WBS are identical in purpose
PBS focuses on deliverables; WBS focuses on activities
WBS defines only the project schedule
WBS is only used in agile projects
PBS includes project costs; WBS does not
Schedule Management.w: PBS identifies the deliverables, while WBS breaks down the work needed to produce them.

n.4: Cost allocation is the focus of the CBS, not PBS.
n.3: WBS can be used in any project approach, not just agile.
n.0: PBS and WBS serve different purposes.
n.2: WBS defines work, not the schedule.

Schedule Management.q: A project is approaching the delivery stage. Which document will show the relationship between project deliverables and the required work to produce them?
o: Product breakdown structure and work breakdown structure together
Cost breakdown structure and organisational breakdown structure together
Communication plan aligned with the stakeholder engagement matrix
Organisational breakdown structure mapped against the resource plan
Risk register combined with the project issue log
Schedule Management.w: The PBS lists deliverables, and the WBS maps the work needed for each deliverable.

n.1: The CBS only deals with costs, not deliverables and work.
n.3: OBS shows project team structure, not work or deliverables.
n.4: The risk register identifies risks, not project work or deliverables.
n.2: The communication plan sets out communication activities, not deliverables or work.

Schedule Management.q: A project has to push back several planned tasks after the operations team brings forward its own key reporting deadlines. What does this demonstrate?
o: A weakness in the project's overall procurement strategy
The need to escalate the delay to the project sponsor
The direct impact of BAU dependencies on project scheduling
A failure in the project's quality assurance process
The value of holding an early project closure review
Schedule Management.w: When BAU deadlines change, project tasks often must be rescheduled, demonstrating dependency.

n.1: Quality management relates to standards, not scheduling.
n.0: Project closure is not related to ongoing BAU dependencies.
n.4: Procurement risks are different from scheduling dependencies.
n.3: Communication plans help but are not the main dependency here.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is analysing how expenditure on a delivery project might become tied to the demands of the organisation's ongoing operations. Which scenario best demonstrates a dependency between project and business-as-usual costs?
o: Project manager attends a training course
BAU staff attend a project meeting once
Project requires overtime payments during BAU peak times
Schedule Management.w: Overtime required due to BAU demands links project costs directly to BAU activities.

n.4: Energy efficiency is not a cost dependency.
n.1: A single meeting does not indicate a cost dependency.
n.3: Reporting frequency is not related to cost dependencies.
n.0: Training is a staff development activity, not a cost dependency.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is trying to identify the clearest case where the project's schedule is genuinely tied to the organisation's ongoing operations. Which is the best example of a schedule dependency between project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Project uses shared IT infrastructure needed for daily business tasks
Project sponsor also chairs the operations steering group
Project reuses a report template from an earlier project
Project team is located in the same building as operations
Project adopts the same visual branding as the operations team
Schedule Management.w: Shared infrastructure creates direct dependencies between project and BAU tasks.

n.4: Document templates do not create schedule dependencies.
n.2: Team lunches are unrelated to project scheduling.
n.1: Plan formatting is administrative, not a dependency.
n.3: Sponsor attendance does not affect scheduling directly.

Schedule Management.q: A project team discovers that a supplier will deliver components two weeks later than planned. Why should the schedule be re-estimated?
o: To recover the lost time by removing testing tasks
To pass the schedule impact directly to the sponsor
To reflect the new delivery date and assess project impact
To shift the delay onto the supplier's own schedule
To keep the original baseline dates unchanged for reporting
Schedule Management.w: Re-estimating updates the schedule based on new facts and helps assess the effect on project deadlines.

n.3: Profit margins may be affected, but the main purpose is accurate planning.
n.0: Scope is managed separately and not a reason to re-estimate the schedule.
n.4: Risk management remains essential, not eliminated.
n.1: The goal is accurate scheduling, not cosmetic reporting.

Schedule Management.q: A software upgrade project has listed the following: 1) Updated software installed, 2) Faster system performance, 3) Reduced IT support costs. How should these be classified when defining project scope?
o: 1 is an outcome, 2 is a benefit, 3 is an output
1 is an output, 2 is an outcome, 3 is a benefit
1 is an outcome, 2 is an output, 3 is a benefit
1 is a benefit, 2 is an outcome, 3 is an output
1 is a benefit, 2 is an output, 3 is an outcome
Schedule Management.w: Output: installed software; outcome: faster performance; benefit: reduced IT support costs.

n.2: The updated software is the output, not the outcome.
n.4: The benefit is reduced IT support costs, not software installation.
n.0: Faster performance is an outcome, not a benefit or output.
n.3: Reduced costs are a benefit, not an output.

Schedule Management.q: A project benefits from schedule optimisation by completing tasks in parallel where possible. What is a risk of this approach?
Schedule Management.w: Parallel tasks can save time but require greater coordination and communication.

n.1: Risks cannot be eliminated, only managed.
n.3: Resource savings are possible, but not guaranteed.
n.0: Stakeholder engagement is always important.
n.4: Dependencies must be carefully managed with parallel tasks.

Schedule Management.q: A client has commissioned a project to upgrade its ageing IT infrastructure and replace outdated systems across the business. Distinguishing the value the organisation gains from what is physically delivered, the main benefit expected by the client is:
o: The appointment of a new project team
The network diagram for the project
Improved organisational performance due to enhanced IT systems
Schedule Management.w: Benefits are the measurable improvements gained, such as improved organisational performance.

n.2: Technical specifications are outputs, not benefits.
n.1: Network diagrams are project management tools.
n.0: Team appointments are part of project setup.

Schedule Management.q: While defining the scope of a data centre project, the project manager wants to make sure every element of work identified in the breakdown of activities is properly costed. When defining project scope, why is it important to link the work breakdown structure with the cost breakdown structure?
o: To ensure compliance with procurement law
To assign responsibilities for risk management
To enable accurate budgeting for all project activities
Schedule Management.w: Linking WBS and CBS ensures each work package is budgeted for, supporting accurate cost control.

Schedule Management.q: A company is replacing its manual payroll process with a new automated payroll system, and the project team is careful to distinguish the change the project brings about from what it physically produces. In this context, the outcome they expect is:
o: Payroll processed more quickly and accurately
The business case for the project
Schedule Management.w: An outcome is the change brought about by the output—in this case, improved payroll processing.

n.0: A list of employees is data, not an outcome.
n.4: A Gantt chart is a schedule, not an outcome.
n.2: A business case justifies the project, not its result.
n.3: System testing records are supporting documents.

Schedule Management.q: A project to upgrade a contact centre's systems must be delivered without interrupting the hours during which customers are normally served. What does this requirement illustrate?
o: A benefit to be realised after project handover
A constraint imposed by the project's fixed budget
A risk arising from unclear stakeholder requirements
A quality standard defined within the project scope
A dependency between project activities and BAU operations
Schedule Management.w: Project tasks must be scheduled around BAU to avoid service disruption—a direct dependency.

n.2: Quality should not be reduced.

Schedule Management.q: A sponsor asks a project manager to explain, in a single statement, why so much effort is spent coordinating the project's schedule with the organisation's ongoing operations. Which statement best summarises the need to manage dependencies between project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Project schedules should never influence live BAU operations
Managed dependencies remove the need for a project schedule
BAU activities take priority over project work at all times
Unmanaged dependencies can lead to project delays and operational disruption
Dependencies always shorten the overall project delivery time

Schedule Management.q: At the start of a new product development project, the team is concerned that some required work might be overlooked, and they want a tool that organises all the activities and confirms nothing is missing. Schedule Management.q: A project manager planning a systems rollout is considering the various ways the project could become tied to the organisation's ongoing operations. Which of the following could create a dependency between a project and business-as-usual activities?

n.2: Audits are typically after completion, not concurrent dependencies.

Schedule Management.q: During the refurbishment of a company's head office, the workforce must keep carrying out its normal duties in the same building throughout the works. What is a likely approach to manage this dependency?

Schedule noisy activities outside standard working hours

Schedule Management.q: A project’s quality requirements demand testing to be performed when BAU operations are lowest. What kind of relationship is this?

A procurement constraint linked to supplier delivery timing
A scheduling dependency based on quality and BAU activity levels
A resource conflict caused by competing project funding demands
A scope change arising from revised quality requirements

Schedule Management.q: A project manager preparing to build a new road bridge wants a structured view of the physical parts that make up the finished structure, such as the deck, piers and foundations. Which structure should they use?

Schedule Management.q: Your team has completed the product breakdown structure for a construction project. What is the next logical step to ensure all elements are delivered?

Schedule Management.q: A project manager reviewing a lengthy delivery schedule is looking at schedule optimisation as a way to improve how the project will be delivered. Which of the following is a key benefit of schedule optimisation in project management?
o: It transfers scheduling responsibility away from the project manager
It can reduce unnecessary delays and make better use of resources
It fixes the schedule so that no re-estimation is required
It shortens the project by cutting agreed quality checks
It removes the need to monitor the project's critical path
Schedule Management.w: Schedule optimisation aims to streamline delivery and resource use, reducing delays.

n.4: Risks cannot be completely avoided, only managed.
n.2: Stakeholder communication remains vital.
n.3: Scope changes still need to be considered.
n.0: Not every project can finish early; optimisation just improves efficiency.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager leading a complex office relocation needs a way to divide the entire body of work into smaller, more governable pieces before estimating and assigning it. In project management, the work breakdown structure (WBS) is primarily used to:
o: Assign individual team members to specific project roles
Organise the total scope of work into manageable sections
Sequence the project activities into a logical delivery order
Define the acceptance criteria for each project deliverable
Allocate the project budget across each defined cost centre
Schedule Management.w: The WBS breaks down the total scope of work into smaller, more manageable sections.

n.2: Cost estimation may use the WBS, but it is not its primary purpose.
n.4: Resource scheduling is done separately from WBS creation.
n.0: Stakeholder satisfaction is managed through communication and engagement plans.
n.3: Quality standards are defined elsewhere in the project plan.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager decides to keep refining and adjusting the schedule at regular points across the delivery phase rather than treating the baseline as fixed. Which of the following is a benefit of this continuous schedule optimisation throughout a project?
o: Rigid adherence to the initial plan
Schedule Management.w: Continuous optimisation makes the project flexible and responsive to changes.

n.2: Stakeholders remain crucial throughout the project.
n.1: Lessons learned are valuable and should not be ignored.
n.0: Being rigid can cause problems if circumstances change.
n.3: Quality should never be reduced to optimise schedule.

Schedule Management.q: A newly qualified project manager is reviewing how the work breakdown structure will be used across the planning of a facilities project. Which of the following is NOT a purpose of the work breakdown structure in project management?
o: To identify all tasks required to complete the project
To provide a basis for estimating costs and durations
To allocate work to team members
To define the project’s communication plan
Schedule Management.w: The communication plan is a separate project management document, not a WBS function.

n.0: Identifying tasks is a key use of the WBS.
n.1: The WBS supports estimating by breaking work into smaller tasks.
n.2: The WBS is used for allocating work.
n.4: Managing scope is one of the WBS’s primary purposes.

Schedule Management.q: During a project to upgrade office equipment, deliveries can only be accepted outside of business hours due to ongoing daily operations. What is the best description of this situation?
o: A dependency between project and business-as-usual activities
An issue with the project’s budget
A project risk with no mitigation
Schedule Management.w: This is a direct example of a dependency between project work and normal business operations.

n.2: A risk is potential, but this is a confirmed scheduling dependency.
n.1: Budget is not the issue here.
n.3: Communication may be required but is not the dependency itself.
n.4: Quality is not at fault in this scenario.

Schedule Management.q: A public transport authority is upgrading track infrastructure and has restricted the work to weekends only, when services are far quieter. Why is this scheduling approach often necessary?
o: To allow staff longer rest periods
To reduce the total cost of the project
To ensure sponsors are always present
To minimise disruption to daily business-as-usual operations
Schedule Management.w: Weekend work reduces impact on regular services, managing BAU-project dependencies.

n.1: Weekend work may actually cost more.
n.0: Rest periods are not the primary reason for scheduling choices.
n.2: Risk registers should always be updated regardless of schedule.
n.3: Sponsor presence is not the reason for weekend work.

Schedule Management.q: When assessing how ongoing operational commitments might constrain the timing of a delivery project, a project manager weighs up several possible influences. Which factor is LEAST likely to impact a project's schedule when considering business-as-usual dependencies?
o: Key staff needed for both BAU and project
Schedule Management.w: Décor preferences generally do not affect scheduling dependencies.

n.2: Shared equipment can cause schedule clashes.
n.1: Regulatory inspections may restrict work windows.
n.3: Staff needed for both BAU and project creates dependencies.
n.4: Peak trading periods often limit when project activities can occur.

Schedule Management.q: As a project progresses through its life cycle, the project manager regularly revisits and refines the original estimates in light of new information. Which is NOT a benefit of re-estimating during the project life cycle?
o: Guaranteeing project closure ahead of schedule
Providing a more realistic project timeline
Schedule Management.w: Re-estimation does not guarantee early closure, it just improves schedule accuracy.

n.4: Re-estimation corrects old or wrong assumptions.
n.3: It helps ensure timelines are up-to-date.
n.1: Timely re-estimation allows risks to be identified earlier.
n.0: Stakeholders are more confident when the plan is realistic.

Schedule Management.q: A client wants to ensure all aspects of scope are fully covered. Which combination of structures is most useful for this?
o: Risk management plan and project brief
Product, work, and cost breakdown structures
Change control log and issue register
Schedule Management.w: These three structures together help ensure scope, work, and cost are comprehensively covered.

n.1: These documents do not collectively address all aspects of scope.
n.4: Change and issue logs are important but do not define scope.
n.0: Risk planning and project briefs support but do not fully define scope.
n.2: Stakeholder and time charts are not used for full scope coverage.

Schedule Management.q: When reviewing the links between a delivery project and the organisation's ongoing operations, a project manager considers a range of possible sources of dependency. Which factor is LEAST likely to create a dependency between a project and business-as-usual activities?
o: Need for change approvals from BAU managers
Personal holiday plans of project team members
Schedule Management.w: Personal holidays may create individual availability issues but are not a systemic BAU dependency.

n.2: Shared equipment creates direct dependencies.
n.0: Finance staff demands create resourcing dependencies.
n.3: Approvals from BAU managers are a common dependency.
n.1: BAU reporting deadlines often affect project schedules.

Schedule Management.q: A project is being planned to deliver a new customer management system. The project manager wants to clarify the difference between outputs, outcomes, and benefits when defining the project scope. Which of the following best represents an output in this context?
Schedule Management.w: An output is the immediate deliverable produced by the project, such as the completed software.

n.1: Improved customer satisfaction is an outcome resulting from using the output.
n.0: Increased sales revenue is a benefit achieved after the outcome.
n.4: Reduction in customer complaints is an outcome, not the direct output.
n.3: Higher employee retention is an unrelated benefit.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is reviewing the situations that would justify updating the schedule and re-estimating the remaining work partway through delivery. Which of the following would NOT be a valid reason to re-estimate the project schedule?
o: Personal preference of the project manager
Delivery delays confirmed by a key supplier
A change in the availability of key resources
Unforeseen technical issues delaying the work
Discovery of new risks affecting the plan
Schedule Management.w: Re-estimation should be based on project realities, not personal preference.

n.4: New risks may affect the schedule and require re-estimation.
n.2: Changes in resource availability are a valid reason to re-estimate.
n.3: Unforeseen issues may require updates to the schedule.
n.1: Supplier delays are a classic trigger for schedule review.

Schedule Management.q: Which of the following is most likely to create a risk to the project schedule when there are links with business-as-usual activities?
o: A documented resource-sharing agreement with operations
Early engagement with the operations line managers
Regular joint project and BAU planning meetings
A shared calendar of upcoming BAU milestones
Unexpected staff shortages due to BAU demands
Schedule Management.w: Staff shortages caused by BAU create a risk that can delay project activities.

n.3: A log update is not a risk in itself.
n.2: Reporting does not directly create schedule risks.
n.0: Good morale supports delivery rather than creates risk.
n.1: Escalation processes help manage, not create, risk.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager finds that many of the project's activities cannot proceed without input from teams running the organisation's day-to-day operations. If a project's activities are highly dependent on business-as-usual processes, what is the best action for the project manager?
o: Engage with BAU managers early and regularly to plan around key activities
Reduce the project scope until the dependencies no longer exist
Assume BAU activities will pause while the project is being delivered
Schedule every single project task during normal business operating hours
Delegate all BAU coordination entirely to the project sponsor alone
Schedule Management.w: Effective engagement with BAU managers ensures project activities can be planned around critical BAU events.

n.3: Ignoring BAU will likely result in scheduling conflicts and failure.
n.2: Contingency helps but is not a substitute for planning with BAU.
n.4: Reporting does not resolve schedule dependencies.
n.1: External consultants may not have the required organisational knowledge.

Schedule Management.q: On a software project, a development team completes a major task several days ahead of the planned date, freeing capacity earlier than expected. How should the project manager manage the schedule in response?
o: Ignore the early finish and keep the original dates
Add new unplanned tasks to fill the gap
Reduce quality standards to finish even earlier
Re-estimate and optimise the schedule to reflect early completion
Schedule Management.w: Schedules should be updated to reflect actual progress, improving accuracy.

n.1: Unplanned tasks risk scope creep.
n.0: Schedules should always reflect actual progress.
n.2: Scope should be managed separately.
n.3: Quality standards must always be maintained.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager developing a network diagram is explaining to a junior colleague how the logical links between scheduled activities work. Which of the following BEST describes a dependency in project scheduling?
o: A buffer of spare time added to protect the critical path
A relationship where one activity relies on another to start or finish
A resource assigned to complete a specific scheduled activity
A milestone marking the completion of a major project deliverable
A constraint that fixes the earliest date an activity can begin
Schedule Management.w: Dependencies occur when one activity cannot start or finish until another does.

n.4: Benefits are outcomes, not dependencies.
n.3: Meetings are activities, not dependencies.
n.0: Risk register updates may record dependencies, but are not dependencies themselves.
n.2: Budget changes do not define dependencies.

Schedule Management.q: A project is at the planning stage. The project manager is reviewing the outputs, outcomes, and benefits. Which of the following is NOT an example of an outcome?
o: A new process implemented in the business
Improved response times for customer enquiries
The delivery of a project report
Schedule Management.w: The delivery of a project report is an output, not an outcome.

n.1: Implementation of a new process is an outcome.
n.2: Improved response times result from outcomes.
n.0: Faster processing is a project outcome.
n.3: Customer retention is a benefit, but the improved process is an outcome.

Schedule Management.q: Midway through delivery, the operations team's priorities shift unexpectedly, affecting resources the project was relying on. When business-as-usual priorities change unexpectedly, what should a project manager do to manage dependencies?
o: Transfer the affected tasks straight to the operations team
Raise the quality targets to offset the disruption
Reassess the project schedule and update plans as needed
Escalate immediately to cancel the affected project tasks
Freeze the current schedule and absorb the changes later
Schedule Management.w: Schedules should be updated to reflect new BAU priorities, ensuring realistic planning.

n.3: Abandonment is rarely justified.
n.4: Team changes should be considered carefully and with input.
n.0: Ignoring BAU will cause further conflicts.
n.1: Increasing quality does not resolve dependency issues.

Schedule Management.q: A construction project running through the winter has fallen behind after a prolonged spell of severe weather stopped site work for several days, and the original dates no longer look achievable. As the project manager reviews the plan, what should be done about the schedule?
o: Increase the project’s contingency budget only
Reduce the number of team meetings
Re-estimate remaining activities based on the new circumstances
Continue with the original schedule regardless
Ignore weather impacts on future tasks
Schedule Management.w: Re-estimating ensures plans reflect reality and helps keep the project on track.

n.3: Sticking to the original schedule may result in unrealistic plans.
n.0: Contingency may help, but re-estimation is necessary to adjust plans.
n.1: Meeting frequency is unrelated to schedule accuracy.
n.4: Ignoring impacts can lead to further delays.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager wants to understand when it is appropriate to revisit and improve the schedule during delivery rather than leaving it untouched. What should trigger schedule optimisation during the project life cycle?
o: Any minor variation that stays within agreed tolerances
Sign-off of the project's initial requirements document
Formal closure of the project after final handover
Routine completion of each weekly status report
Discovery of delays, new risks, or opportunities to improve efficiency
Schedule Management.w: Optimisation is prompted by significant events like delays, risks, or new efficiencies.

n.1: The charter comes before detailed planning.
n.3: Budget approval is a milestone but not the sole trigger.
n.0: Lessons learned come after project closure.
n.2: Not every minor issue justifies major schedule changes.

Schedule Management.q: During a project review, the team discovers that certain tasks have taken longer than expected. Why is schedule optimisation valuable in this situation?
o: It removes the need for stakeholder reporting
It helps the team adjust plans to avoid further delays
It guarantees that no tasks will ever run late again
It allows quality standards to be ignored
Schedule Management.w: Schedule optimisation allows the project to adapt and reduce the chance of further delays.

n.2: Delays can be reduced, but not eliminated.
n.0: Reporting is still necessary.
n.4: Risks still need to be managed separately.
n.3: Quality must not be sacrificed.

Schedule Management.q: A sponsor questions why the expected improvements from a new customer portal cannot be reported until some time after the portal itself goes live. Considering the link between what a project produces and the value it enables, which statement is true regarding the relationship between benefits and outputs?
o: Outputs must be delivered before benefits can be realised
Outputs and benefits are the same thing
Outputs are optional in project management
Benefits define the work breakdown structure
Benefits always occur at the same time as outputs
Schedule Management.w: Benefits are realised only after the output has been delivered and used.

n.4: Benefits typically occur after outputs are in use.
n.2: Outputs are required deliverables, not optional.
n.3: The WBS is based on scope, not benefits directly.
n.1: Outputs and benefits are distinct concepts.

Schedule Management.q: Under pressure to bring forward a critical delivery date, a project manager looks at schedule optimisation methods to shorten the overall duration. Which technique might they use?
o: Sequencing all tasks to run one after another
Extending the critical path to reduce daily workload
Fast-tracking tasks that can be completed in parallel
Adding float to every task on the critical path
Levelling resources evenly across the remaining activities
Schedule Management.w: Fast-tracking allows parallel work, reducing overall project duration.

n.4: Delaying non-critical activities does not optimise the schedule.
n.3: Stakeholder updates are important for control and transparency.
n.1: Eliminating all contingency increases project risk.
n.0: Unnecessary deliverables will only add time and complexity.

Schedule Management.q: Partway through a software project, the team adopts a new tool that automates a previously manual part of the workflow. How might schedule optimisation respond to this change?
o: By revising the schedule to reflect potential time savings
By increasing all task durations to be cautious
By locking the original schedule in place
By reducing the quality assurance steps
Schedule Management.w: Optimisation includes updating the schedule when productivity tools improve efficiency.

n.2: Durations should only increase if justified by evidence.
n.3: Schedules should be flexible and reflect reality.
n.0: New tools must be considered for planning.
n.4: Quality must always be maintained.

Schedule Management.q: A project manager is putting in place practices to coordinate the project's schedule with the organisation's routine operational work. Which is NOT a typical action to manage schedule dependencies between project and BAU activities?
o: Holding planning meetings with BAU managers
Proceeding without regard for BAU constraints
Identifying shared resources and planning accordingly
Adjusting project timelines to fit business peaks
Schedule Management.w: Ignoring BAU constraints risks project failure due to unaddressed dependencies.

n.0: Engagement with BAU managers is good practice.
n.2: Shared resource planning is crucial.
n.4: Timeline adjustments can prevent conflicts.
n.3: BAU is dynamic and should be monitored.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager is considering how unconscious bias can shape the way decisions are reached in regular team meetings. Thinking about the consequences of such bias on group discussion, which of the following is a direct effect of unconscious bias in team meetings?
o: All decisions are made by consensus
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Unconscious bias can cause some contributions to be undervalued.

n.0: Consensus does not always occur, especially if bias exists.
n.4: Bias can increase risk, not decrease it.
n.3: Bias is unrelated to documentation needs.
n.2: Team budget is not affected by bias directly.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager is reflecting on how the mix of backgrounds and disciplines within the team adds value across the life cycle. Considering where varied perspectives make the greatest difference to outcomes, in which situation is the benefit of team diversity most clearly visible?
o: When the team faces complex challenges
When the project is fully automated
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Diversity helps most when dealing with complex, multi-faceted challenges.

n.2: Repetitive tasks show less benefit from diversity.
n.0: Communication is always valuable.
n.1: Identical skills reduce diversity benefits.
n.4: Automation does not remove the value of diverse thinking.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A manager believes only certain backgrounds are suited to leadership roles, without realising this belief. This is an example of:
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Unconscious bias often operates without conscious awareness.

n.2: Active listening supports fairer treatment.
n.0: Team building encourages diversity, not bias.
n.4: Scheduling is unrelated.
n.1: Skills assessment should be objective.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: An organisation is building a culture in which differences among colleagues are actively respected and welcomed on its projects. Considering how this shapes the team, complete the statement. A project team that values diversity is most likely to:
o: Allocate project roles through purely random selection
Limit the team's engagement with external customers
Concentrate only on members' technical skills
Create an environment where all team members feel valued
Base every decision solely on members' seniority
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Valuing diversity helps all team members feel respected and included.

n.4: Seniority-based decisions can overlook valuable perspectives.
n.0: Random role assignment may not make best use of skills.
n.2: Diversity includes more than just technical skills.
n.1: Customer engagement is still important.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: During an audit of the team's inclusion practices, a project manager reviews a list of attributes and must identify which one falls outside the scope of equality legislation. Which is NOT a characteristic protected by diversity and inclusion legislation?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Management style is not protected by equality law.

n.0: Religion or belief is protected by law.
n.3: Pregnancy and maternity are protected.
n.1: Sexual orientation is protected.
n.4: Disability is a protected characteristic.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project team includes members from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences. What is a key benefit of this diversity?
o: It guarantees all team members will agree
It increases the potential for innovative solutions
It reduces the need for project management
It ensures every decision is made quickly
Diversity & Inclusion.w: A diverse team brings varied perspectives, leading to greater innovation.

n.1: Agreement is not guaranteed by diversity.
n.4: Diversity may require more time for decision-making.
n.0: Conflict can still occur, even in diverse teams.
n.3: Project management remains essential regardless of diversity.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A capable team member with strong relevant skills is repeatedly passed over when the project manager allocates the more challenging and high-profile tasks. Considering possible reasons for this recurring pattern, this may be due to what?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Bias, whether conscious or not, can affect fair allocation of tasks.

n.1: Budget approval does not affect allocation in this way.
n.0: Scheduling is unrelated to task allocation fairness.
n.4: Regulations are not likely to be the cause here.
n.2: Equipment issues are not a reason for overlooking contributions.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project team consists of members of different ages, religions, and sexual orientations. What is the most important principle for the project manager to follow?
o: Restrict conversation strictly to work topics
Overlook diversity issues to avoid difficulty
Treat all team members equally and with respect
Allocate tasks based on members' ages
Group team members according to their background
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Equal treatment is the foundation of diversity and inclusion.

n.4: Grouping by background can be discriminatory.
n.1: Ignoring issues does not create an inclusive culture.
n.0: Diversity is about the whole person, not just work tasks.
n.3: Assigning tasks by age is discriminatory.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager introduces a policy supporting flexible working for parents and carers. Which protected characteristics is this likely to support?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Sex and pregnancy/maternity are protected characteristics that flexible working can support.

n.3: These are not protected characteristics.
n.0: Job role and salary are not protected by diversity law.
n.1: Personal preferences and physical traits are not protected.
n.4: Lunch and project type are unrelated.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager notices that one particular team member has their contributions frequently interrupted or dismissed during meetings, despite offering sound ideas. Looking for an explanation for this pattern of behaviour, which of the following could be a cause?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Unconscious bias can lead to some voices being undervalued.

n.4: Project goals do not cause this behaviour.
n.1: Progress reporting is unrelated.
n.3: Risk management should not affect fairness in discussion.
n.2: Job title is often a reflection, not a cause, of bias.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager is compiling training material and needs to give the team a set of attributes that are all safeguarded by UK equality legislation. Reviewing the groupings below, which set includes only protected characteristics under UK equality law?
o: Preferred shift, lunch hour, manager’s name, appraisal result
Department, length of service, location, salary
Laptop brand, chair style, office view, car parking space
Project status, performance, team size, hobbies
Diversity & Inclusion.w: All options listed are protected characteristics.

n.2: These are not protected characteristics.
n.4: None of these are protected characteristics.
n.1: None are covered by diversity law.
n.3: Office preferences are not legally protected.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: An organisation's customer base is expanding across different countries and cultures, and the project manager is considering how the delivery team should be composed in response. Why should a project team reflect this diversity?
o: To focus only on technical delivery
To better understand and meet customer needs
To limit the skills within the team
Diversity & Inclusion.w: A diverse team can better relate to and serve a diverse customer base.

n.2: Tradition may not meet diverse needs.
n.0: Good communication is always required.
n.4: Limiting skills is not beneficial.
n.1: Customer needs go beyond technical delivery.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project team member explains that their religious practices require time for observance that clashes with certain scheduled activities, and they feel excluded as a result. The project manager wants to respond appropriately. Which action best supports diversity and inclusion?
o: Adjusting team activities to accommodate religious observances
Discouraging any mention of personal beliefs
Requiring all team members to work the same schedule
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Accommodating religious practices supports inclusion and respects diversity.

n.4: Uniform schedules may disadvantage those with religious commitments.
n.1: Ignoring requests undermines inclusion.
n.0: Limiting discussions can create an unwelcoming environment.
n.3: Discouraging mention of beliefs can reduce openness.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project team includes individuals with a range of working styles, needs and communication preferences. The project manager wants to make sure each person is able to participate on an equal footing. Which of the following is a fair way to support an individual's contribution in a team?
o: Only recognising contributions from senior staff
Adapting communication methods to meet their needs
Expecting everyone to conform to a single style
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Adapting to individual needs facilitates fair participation.

n.2: A single style may exclude some team members.
n.0: Recognition should be inclusive of all.
n.4: Feedback opportunities should be open to everyone.
n.3: Different preferences should be respected.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project team is finding it difficult to crack a complex problem raised by an important customer, having exhausted its usual approaches. The project manager reflects on how a diverse team could break the deadlock. How can diversity help?
o: By providing a range of perspectives and ideas
By reducing the number of options considered
By ensuring only senior managers contribute
By focusing on previous solutions only
By eliminating the need for collaboration
Diversity & Inclusion.w: A range of ideas from diverse members increases the chance of finding innovative solutions.

n.2: Limiting input reduces diversity of thought.
n.1: More options should be considered, not fewer.
n.4: Collaboration remains important.
n.3: Focusing only on the past may miss new ideas.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager is explaining to newer team members the value of welcoming a wide range of perspectives when working through project challenges. Which explanation captures one of the main reasons for embracing diverse thinking within a project team?
o: It leads to more creative problem-solving
It removes the need for a project manager
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Diverse thinking brings creativity and innovation to projects.

n.4: Project managers are still needed.
n.1: Success is never guaranteed.
n.2: Stakeholder input should be encouraged.
n.3: Timelines may not be affected by diversity alone.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager actively encourages team members to bring differing viewpoints and approaches to how work is done. Considering the immediate effect of this on a project, what is a direct result of encouraging diverse thinking?
o: A focus only on existing processes
A greater potential for innovative outcomes
A guarantee of no project delays
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Diverse thinking directly supports innovation in project outcomes.

n.3: Innovation does not guarantee no delays.
n.4: Documentation requirements are not related to team diversity.
n.0: Multiple viewpoints are encouraged, not just one.
n.1: Diverse teams look for new solutions, not just existing ones.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: Wanting to draw on a wider range of viewpoints during a planning workshop, a project manager considers how best to encourage diverse thinking within the team. Which action is most likely to help?
o: Limiting discussions to a small group
Assigning all tasks to one person
Inviting input from all team members
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Encouraging input from everyone fosters diverse thinking.

n.0: Limiting discussion reduces diversity of thought.
n.4: Customer feedback can offer valuable perspectives.
n.1: One person may not represent diverse views.
n.3: Discouraging ideas stifles innovation.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A member of the project team discloses a disability and requests certain changes to help them carry out their work effectively. The project manager considers the right course of action. What should a project manager do?
o: Discuss and agree reasonable adjustments to support their participation
Decline the request without offering any explanation
Recommend the employee moves to another team
Demand medical proof before considering any change
Disregard the request and continue as normal
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Discussing and providing reasonable adjustments is essential for inclusion.

n.1: Denial without explanation is not inclusive.
n.4: Ignoring requests is discriminatory.
n.2: Changing teams is not a solution.
n.3: Proof is not always necessary for reasonable adjustment.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager wants to embed inclusive behaviours in the way the team works day to day, so that everyone contributes regardless of their background. Reviewing the options below, which of these is an example of inclusion in a project environment?
o: Encouraging participation from team members of all backgrounds
Making assumptions about team members’ abilities
Assigning tasks only to those with similar beliefs
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Inclusion involves valuing all team members equally.

n.4: This excludes those with different beliefs.
n.3: Assumptions can perpetuate bias.
n.0: Ignoring adjustments reduces inclusion.
n.2: Discouraging discussion undermines inclusion.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager encourages all team members to share their unique perspectives when developing new products. What is the likely result?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Encouraging unique perspectives boosts innovation and problem-solving.

n.0: Encouragement should increase ideas, not reduce them.
n.1: Speed is not guaranteed by diverse input.
n.3: Budget is not necessarily affected.
n.2: Customer satisfaction is likely to increase, not be limited.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: During a recruitment interview for a project role, a hiring manager asks a candidate about their plans to start a family. A colleague later raises concerns about the question. Which principle is being breached?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Questions about family plans can breach diversity and inclusion policies.

n.3: Team size is unrelated to equality legislation.
n.4: Budget is not relevant here.
n.0: Project scheduling is not related.
n.1: Resource levelling concerns resources, not diversity.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: An employee who recently disclosed their sexual orientation to their manager is then passed over for a promotion they were expected to receive. The employee raises a grievance. Which type of discrimination might this represent?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Direct discrimination is treating someone less favourably due to a protected characteristic.

n.3: Feedback is unrelated here.
n.1: Probation is not relevant.
n.4: Objective assessments should be free of bias.
n.0: Annual leave is not related.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A project manager is reviewing the attributes that equality legislation protects so that no team member is treated unfairly because of their faith or convictions. Which characteristic is protected to help prevent discrimination due to personal beliefs?
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Religion or belief is specifically protected under diversity and inclusion legislation.

n.3: Annual bonuses are not protected.
n.0: Performance ratings are not protected characteristics.
n.4: Work location is not protected.
n.1: Lunch preferences are not protected characteristics.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: An organisation has recognised that unconscious bias may be affecting how work is allocated and how contributions are valued across its project teams. As part of its response, which method would help reduce the impact of unconscious bias in project teams?
o: Only assigning tasks to close friends
Diversity & Inclusion.w: Awareness and training can help identify and reduce unconscious bias.

n.2: Avoidance perpetuates bias.
n.3: Nepotism is a form of bias.
n.0: Discouraging new ideas reduces diversity.
n.1: Feedback should be valued.

Diversity & Inclusion.q: A team member returning from maternity leave requests flexible working hours. As a manager, how should you respond to support diversity and inclusion?
o: Suggest she takes unpaid leave instead
Consider her request and explore reasonable adjustments
Insist all staff have identical hours
Deny the request as it disrupts the team routine
