Scope Management.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager observes that several teams are producing overlapping outputs and effort is being duplicated across different work packages. Examining how the work was originally broken down, what is the most likely cause?
o: The PBS includes too many products
The project schedule is too detailed
The WBS lacks clear structure and decomposition
Scope Management.w: Poor WBS structure can lead to overlapping or duplicated work packages.

Scope Management.q: On a cross-functional project, a project manager reviews how the Organisation Breakdown Structure and Responsibility Assignment Matrix work together. Which TWO outcomes would demonstrate that the OBS and RAM have been effectively integrated?
Scope Management.w: OBS defines roles, RAM assigns them effectively.

Scope Management.q: On a programme delivered across several business units, the Organisation Breakdown Structure has been developed separately from the Work Breakdown Structure, without cross-referencing the two. What risk does developing the OBS independently in this way create?
o: Loss of traceability between costs and deliverables
Misalignment between roles and work packages
Weaker definition of quality acceptance criteria
Scope Management.w: OBS must align with WBS to ensure responsibilities match work.

Scope Management.q: A project scope statement sets out the deliverables in considerable detail, but says nothing about what falls outside the project's boundaries. As delivery proceeds, what risk does this omission most directly create?
o: Scope creep due to undefined boundaries
Scope Management.w: Without defined exclusions, stakeholders may assume additional work is included, leading to scope creep.

Scope Management.q: During planning for a product launch, a project manager deliberately structures the Cost Breakdown Structure so that it mirrors the Work Breakdown Structure. What is the primary benefit of aligning the two structures in this way?
o: Faster execution of the project activities
Clear linkage between costs and deliverables
Reduced overall stakeholder involvement in reporting
Simplified management of the project risks
Improved accuracy of the project schedule
Scope Management.w: Aligning CBS with WBS ensures costs are traceable to deliverables.

Scope Management.q: A project manager has produced a complete Product Breakdown Structure, but the Work Breakdown Structure derived from it does not consistently reflect the products it should deliver. Given the relationship between these two structures, what is the most likely issue?
o: The stakeholders were never properly aligned on the project objectives
The project schedule remained incomplete right through the planning stage
The required resources were all assigned before defining the work
The overall project scope was originally defined far too broadly
The transition from product structure to work structure is poorly managed
Scope Management.w: The WBS must logically derive from the PBS; inconsistency indicates poor translation from products to work.

Scope Management.q: A newly appointed project manager finds that changes are being made to the project frequently, with very little supporting documentation recorded for any of them. Considering how change should be governed, what is the most likely issue?
Scope Management.w: Lack of documentation indicates poor control and governance.

Scope Management.q: A project team begins development based on high-level requirements, but stakeholders later dispute what was agreed. What is the most likely root cause?
o: Stakeholders were not involved in progress reporting
Scope boundaries and deliverables were not clearly defined and agreed
The project manager failed to control changes during execution
The project schedule was unrealistic from the outset
Requirements were too detailed for early stages
Scope Management.w: Unclear scope definition, including boundaries and deliverables, leads to misalignment and disputes.

Scope Management.q: On a multi-team project, members are frequently unsure who is responsible for particular pieces of work, and responsibilities appear to overlap. Looking at how the project has been organised, what is the most likely root cause of this confusion?
o: The milestones have not been scheduled at frequent enough intervals
The OBS is not clearly defined or aligned with the WBS
The project does not have a documented risk management plan
The project schedule has become far too complex to follow
The cost breakdown structure has been defined in excessive detail
Scope Management.w: An unclear OBS leads to ambiguity in roles and responsibilities.

Scope Management.q: On a systems integration project, a project manager reviews how the Product Breakdown Structure and Work Breakdown Structure have been developed together. Which TWO outcomes would demonstrate that the two structures have been effectively integrated?
o: Clear linkage between outputs and work packages
Scope Management.w: Integration ensures completeness and traceability from deliverables to work.

Scope Management.q: On an ongoing project, a project manager finds that expenditure is only being recorded and reported at a high, whole-project level rather than against individual work packages. What limitation does tracking costs at this level create?
o: Inability to establish the total project budget
Poor assurance over the quality of deliverables
Limited visibility of cost performance at work package level
Reduced traceability of scope to stakeholder requirements
Weaker control over the sequencing of activities
Scope Management.w: High-level tracking reduces visibility and control over specific work areas.

Scope Management.q: To keep the plan stable, a project team has decided to reject every change request that arises, regardless of its merit. Considering the purpose of change control, what is the key limitation of adopting this approach?
o: It transfers scope authority away from the sponsor
It reduces the accuracy of progress reporting data
It weakens the reliability of project cost estimates
It prevents necessary changes that could improve outcomes
It removes the requirement for stakeholder sign-off
Scope Management.w: Change control should enable informed decisions, not block beneficial changes.

Scope Management.q: A project manager receives a formal change request but delays analysis due to workload. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Delayed decision-making and potential project disruption
Automatic rejection of the change request
Scope Management.w: Delaying impact analysis postpones decisions and can disrupt planning and execution.

Scope Management.q: A change control board is reviewing a proposed change to a live project and must decide how to judge it. When evaluating a change request, which factor is most critical to consider?
o: The project manager's own preference on it
The number of stakeholders requesting the change
The ease and speed of implementing it
The point in the life cycle it arises
Its impact on scope, time, cost, and quality
Scope Management.w: Comprehensive impact analysis across key constraints is essential.

Scope Management.q: On a large transformation programme, a project manager finds that the Work Breakdown Structure has been organised around the business departments involved rather than around the outputs to be produced. What risk does structuring the WBS in this way create?
o: Misalignment between work packages and project outputs
Improved accountability across the departmental teams
Simplified scheduling across the work packages
Reduced need for ongoing stakeholder engagement
Faster overall delivery of the project outputs
Scope Management.w: WBS should be deliverable-oriented; structuring by departments risks losing alignment with outputs.

Scope Management.q: A stakeholder informally requests a change to a deliverable, and the project team implements it immediately to maintain goodwill. What is the most significant risk of this approach?
o: Uncontrolled scope change without assessing impact
Scope Management.w: Implementing changes without formal control bypasses impact analysis, leading to uncontrolled scope, cost, and schedule risk.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is reviewing how scope was established at the start of a workplace refurbishment project. Reflecting on the definition documentation and how boundaries were communicated, which of the following scenarios best demonstrates poor scope boundary definition?
o: Comprehensive and detailed requirements documentation maintained
Stakeholders assuming additional features are included without agreement
Deliverables defined precisely with agreed acceptance criteria
Explicit statements of what is included and excluded
Regular scope reviews conducted throughout the project
Scope Management.w: Assumptions about inclusions indicate unclear boundaries.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is setting up a formal change control process for a regulated project and wants to ensure the essentials are in place. Which TWO elements are essential in a formal change control process?
Scope Management.w: Formal processes require documentation and impact assessment.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is justifying to a governance board why a Responsibility Assignment Matrix has been introduced on a complex delivery. Which TWO benefits result from using a Responsibility Assignment Matrix?
Scope Management.w: RAM clarifies roles and accountability.

Scope Management.q: While defining the scope of a new project, a project manager finds that two influential stakeholder groups have submitted requirements that directly contradict one another. What is the most appropriate initial action for the project manager to take?
o: Delay scope definition until consensus is reached externally
Select the requirements that align with project constraints
Facilitate clarification to reconcile and prioritise requirements
Escalate the conflict to senior management immediately
Scope Management.w: Reconciling and prioritising requirements ensures clarity and alignment before proceeding.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is defining scope for a new product introduction and wants to strengthen how requirements are captured and agreed with those affected. Which TWO practices would most improve requirement clarity during scope definition?
Scope Management.w: Engagement and clarity of assumptions improve requirement quality.

Scope Management.q: On a software development project, the team repeatedly returns to renegotiate what is in and out of scope, and work is often reopened after it was thought complete. Considering the pattern of behaviour described, what is the primary issue?
o: Poor scope definition and requirement clarity
Excessive and overly detailed project documentation
Inadequate resource allocation across the project
Deliverables that are technically far too complex
Ineffective scheduling of the project activities
Scope Management.w: Unclear requirements lead to repeated revisions and instability in scope.

Scope Management.q: A sponsor asks a project manager to explain what the Cost Breakdown Structure is intended to achieve on a capital project. Which statement best describes the purpose of a Cost Breakdown Structure?
o: Organises project costs in alignment with work packages
Defines the deliverables the project must produce
Sequences project activities according to their dependencies
Records identified project risks and their responses
Assigns responsibilities for delivering each work package
Scope Management.w: CBS structures costs in relation to work packages for control.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is preparing to assign responsibilities across the work packages of an infrastructure project and wants to show accountability is unambiguous. Which scenario best demonstrates effective use of a Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM)?
o: Sequencing the project activities according to their logical dependencies
Tracking the accumulated project costs against each deliverable produced
Clearly linking each work package to a single accountable role
Assigning several people to each task with no clear accountability
Mapping deliverables to stakeholders without clearly defining their roles
Scope Management.w: A RAM ensures clear accountability by linking work to roles.

Scope Management.q: A project team creates a detailed task list but struggles to ensure all deliverables are covered. What is the most likely issue?
o: The schedule was built before resources were assigned to each of the tasks
The team did not identify a defined critical path through the network diagram
The team focused on activities instead of structuring deliverables using a product breakdown
Stakeholders were not consulted when the progress reports were being prepared and issued
The individual tasks in the list were not sequenced in the correct logical order
Scope Management.w: Without a product-based structure (PBS), teams risk missing deliverables because they focus on activities rather than outputs.

Scope Management.q: A deliverable is produced and submitted for review, but the stakeholders reject it on the grounds that it does not meet their expectations of what they were going to receive. What does this rejection most clearly indicate about how the work was set up?
o: The deliverable was produced too early
Requirements were not clearly defined or agreed
Scope Management.w: Rejection indicates a gap between defined requirements and stakeholder expectations.

Scope Management.q: A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is created, but stakeholders still question whether all required outputs are included. What is the most likely cause?
o: The WBS was developed without a preceding Product Breakdown Structure
The project schedule was left incomplete at the planning stage
The WBS was aligned to deliverables rather than to activities
The dependencies between the work packages were not fully identified
The WBS was decomposed into too many detailed lower levels
Scope Management.w: A PBS ensures all products are identified before decomposing into work. Skipping it risks incomplete scope coverage.

Scope Management.q: While reviewing the Work Breakdown Structure for an IT rollout, a project manager finds several tasks that cannot be traced to any of the defined deliverables. Considering how work should relate to outputs, what does the presence of these tasks indicate?
o: Scope has expanded beyond defined deliverables
Scope Management.w: All work in the WBS should link to deliverables; otherwise, scope creep or misalignment exists.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is reviewing a Responsibility Assignment Matrix and notices that one work package has been given more than one accountable role. Considering how accountability should work, which issue is most likely to arise?
Scope Management.w: Multiple accountable roles create ambiguity and reduce ownership clarity.

Scope Management.q: A project manager is explaining to a new sponsor why a Product Breakdown Structure has been prepared before detailed planning begins on a construction project. Which TWO benefits result from using a Product Breakdown Structure?
Scope Management.w: PBS ensures completeness of deliverables and clarifies scope through defined outputs.

Scope Management.q: On a project with several engaged stakeholders, a submitted change request is turned down without any reason being given to those who raised it. What risk does rejecting the request in this way create?
o: Unmanaged expansion of the project scope
Weaker traceability between deliverables and requirements
Reduced accuracy of the cost forecast
Increased duplication of work across teams
Scope Management.w: Lack of transparency undermines stakeholder confidence and trust.

Scope Management.q: A project manager creates a Work Breakdown Structure but struggles to assign clear accountability for each work package. What is the most appropriate tool to resolve this?
Scope Management.w: A RAM links work packages to responsible roles, ensuring accountability.

Scope Management.q: A project manager preparing scope documentation for a facilities upgrade wants to select the technique that captures everything the project must produce. Which scenario best demonstrates appropriate use of a Product Breakdown Structure (PBS)?
o: Assigning the required resources to each individual project task
Sequencing the project activities according to their logical dependencies
Identifying all deliverables and sub-products required to meet objectives
Tracking delivery progress against the agreed project milestones
Listing every project activity in its planned execution order
Scope Management.w: PBS focuses on defining all products and deliverables required by the project.

Scope Management.q: A project manager defines scope in detail but fails to validate it with stakeholders. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Reduced need for any formal change control
Simplified governance with fewer reporting requirements needed
Improved efficiency across the whole delivery phase
Misalignment between delivered outputs and stakeholder expectations
Faster stakeholder agreement on the final deliverables
Scope Management.w: Without validation, scope may not reflect stakeholder needs, leading to misalignment.

Scope Management.q: Under pressure from a sponsor, a project manager approves a significant change request before any assessment of its effect on the budget or timeline has been carried out. What is the most likely outcome of proceeding in this way?
Scope Management.w: Without impact analysis, changes can introduce unanticipated cost and schedule implications.

Scope Management.q: A Cost Breakdown Structure (CBS) shows costs exceeding budget, but the Work Breakdown Structure appears accurate. What is the most likely issue?
o: The product breakdown structure was left partially incomplete
Key dependencies between activities are missing from the network
The stakeholders have not been properly engaged throughout
The project schedule contains errors in its activity durations
Costs are not properly aligned to work packages
Scope Management.w: CBS must align with WBS; misalignment leads to inaccurate cost tracking.

Scope Management.q: A project assurance reviewer is examining how changes are handled on a delivery project and looking for signs that control is weak. Which of the following scenarios indicates ineffective change control?
o: Changes are implemented without formal approval processes
Stakeholders are informed of change impacts
Decisions are aligned with project objectives
All changes are documented and assessed before approval
Impact analysis includes cost, time, and scope
Scope Management.w: Implementing changes without formal approval undermines control and governance.

Change Control.q: A project manager on an agile (iterative) project receives frequent minor change requests. How is change control typically managed differently in iterative projects compared to linear projects?
o: All changes are rejected by default in iterative projects
Plans are never updated after changes in iterative projects
Changes require a formal review board for each request in iterative projects
Changes are expected and managed continuously in iterative life cycles
Change requests are not allowed in iterative projects
Change Control.w: Iterative projects integrate change control continuously, as changes are expected throughout the life cycle.

n.0: Minor changes are not automatically rejected in iterative projects.
n.2: Not every change in iterative projects goes through a formal board.
n.4: Change requests are allowed and expected.
n.1: Plans are updated as necessary in response to changes.

Change Control.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager receives a change request that is urgent and could affect critical project milestones if not addressed promptly. What should the project manager do?
o: Prioritise the evaluation and escalate as needed
Ignore the request until the next scheduled review
Implement the change immediately without review
Change Control.w: Urgent changes require prompt evaluation and escalation to manage risks effectively.

n.3: Ignoring risks delaying responses.
n.4: Implementation without review risks project failure.
n.0: Stakeholders should be informed timely.
n.2: Cancelling without assessment ignores potential benefits.

Change Control.q: During the delivery of a fast-moving project, the project manager reviews a proposed change and prepares to recommend that the change control board rejects it. What is a common justification for rejecting a proposed change?
o: The change is supported by stakeholders
The change negatively impacts critical project milestones
The change aligns well with the business case
Change Control.w: Negative impact on key milestones is a valid reason for rejection.

n.4: Good alignment supports approval.
n.3: Cost reduction favors approval.
n.1: Quality improvement supports approval.
n.0: Stakeholder support helps approval chances.

Change Control.q: A stakeholder disagrees with a change that has already been implemented. What is the BEST action the project manager should take to maintain good change control practice?
o: Update the change register to remove the disputed decision
Review the change control records and communicate the rationale for the decision
Escalate the disagreement to the sponsor for a fresh ruling
Submit a new change request to formally overturn the decision
Reverse the implemented change and restore the previous project baseline
Change Control.w: Good practice includes transparency and clear communication, referencing decision records as needed.

n.4: Reversing changes should only be considered if justified and approved.
n.3: Stakeholder concerns should not be ignored.
n.2: Documentation should always be maintained.
n.0: Responsibility should not be shifted without cause.

Change Control.q: What stage of the change control process involves considering potential impacts, costs, and benefits in depth before making a recommendation?
Change Control.w: A detailed evaluation explores all potential impacts, costs, and benefits before any recommendation.

n.3: Submission is just the initial raising of the change.
n.1: Initial evaluation is a high-level review, not in-depth.
n.4: Plans are only updated once a decision has been made.
n.0: Implementation occurs after evaluation and approval.

Change Control.q: A significant change has been approved that alters aspects of the deliverable being produced on a construction project. Why should the project manager review the quality management plan following such a change?
o: To ensure deliverables continue to meet standards
To speed up delivery regardless of quality
Change Control.w: Quality plans must reflect changes to maintain expected standards.

n.3: Documentation should be adequate.
n.4: Quality should not be sacrificed for speed.
n.0: Stakeholders remain important.
n.1: Closure occurs after delivery.

Change Control.q: While appraising the options for a proposed change to a product's specification, the project manager wants to understand how robust each option remains if the underlying estimates and assumptions turn out to be inaccurate. What is the purpose of carrying out sensitivity analysis in this situation?
o: To allocate the budget across the work packages
To identify and record all new project risks
To define team roles and responsibilities in full
To rank stakeholders by their level of influence
To understand how changes in assumptions affect outcomes
Change Control.w: Sensitivity analysis evaluates how varying inputs influence results, supporting robust decisions.

n.3: It is not intended to cause delays.
n.1: Stakeholder roles are managed separately.
n.0: Risk registers are created independently.
n.2: Budget allocation is separate from sensitivity analysis.

Change Control.q: A project sponsor asks for a cost-benefit analysis before deciding on a change. At which stage in change control is this MOST likely to happen?
Change Control.w: The detailed evaluation includes cost-benefit and impact analyses before recommendation.

n.1: Implementation follows evaluation and decision-making.
n.4: Initial evaluation is high-level, not in-depth.
n.2: Plans are updated only after approval.
n.0: Reviews happen after project completion, not during change control.

Change Control.q: On a linear project, a change authority has considered the recommendation for a proposed change and reached its decision. Which activity typically follows the 'recommendation' stage in the change control process?
Change Control.w: After a recommendation is made, relevant project plans are updated to reflect the decision.

n.4: A new business case is not always required after every recommendation.
n.0: Lessons learned are reviewed after implementation, not after recommendation.
n.3: Procurement cancellation is unrelated to most changes.
n.2: Team-building is not a change control activity.

Change Control.q: A project manager reviews a newly submitted change request but is not yet confident about its full effect on the project's cost, schedule and objectives. Which of the following is an appropriate reason to defer the change?
o: Project is behind schedule and needs speeding up
Lack of sufficient data to assess impact
All required resources are available now
Change Control.w: Deferring allows time to gather more information for a sound decision.

n.1: Consensus suggests proceeding, not deferring.
n.4: Urgency calls for immediate action.
n.0: Speeding up needs prioritizing changes, not deferring.
n.3: Availability of resources supports proceeding.

Change Control.q: A software development project receives multiple change requests each week. What is a key advantage of iterative life cycles when managing change control?
o: They use only annual change control reviews
They accommodate frequent changes without disrupting the project flow
They ignore change requests to maintain stability
They eliminate the need for change logs
They delay all changes until the end of the project
Change Control.w: Iterative life cycles are flexible and can accommodate ongoing change without major disruption.

n.2: Ignoring change requests is not best practice.
n.0: Frequent reviews occur in iterative, not just annual.
n.4: Delaying all changes is not how iterative projects operate.
n.3: Change logs are still required for accountability.

Change Control.q: A change has been approved and the schedule revised, but the project manager does not pass the updated schedule on to the delivery team. What can failing to communicate the schedule updates cause on the project?
o: Conflicts in task execution and delays
Faster progress across the remaining tasks
Lower overall costs for the project
Reduced scope of the project deliverables
Change Control.w: Lack of communication often leads to confusion and schedule conflicts.

n.1: Progress usually slows with confusion.
n.3: Satisfaction declines without clear updates.
n.2: Costs may increase due to inefficiencies.
n.4: Scope is determined by the change, not communication.

Change Control.q: Having evaluated a proposed change, a project manager is deciding how to respond and lists the recognised courses of action open to them. Which of the following is NOT a typical option when assessing ways to address a proposed change?
o: Deferring the change to a later phase
Modifying the change to reduce impact
Change Control.w: Ignoring a change is not a valid or responsible assessment option.

n.0: Accepting, modifying, rejecting, or deferring are valid options.

Change Control.q: During a project, a change request is submitted to alter the design of a key deliverable. What is the immediate next step in the change control process after the request is received?
o: Initial evaluation of the change request
Change Control.w: After a change request is submitted, the first step is to carry out an initial evaluation before any further actions.

n.3: Implementation only occurs after evaluations and approvals.
n.2: A detailed evaluation happens after the initial screening.
n.4: Plans are updated only after approval and decisions are made.
n.1: Stakeholder communication is important but not the immediate next step.

Change Control.q: On a delivery project, a team leader agrees several requested alterations directly with the client, bypassing the agreed change control process and skipping any formal approval. What is the likely impact of allowing changes to be implemented in this way?
o: Loss of control and potential project failure
Improved efficiency from removing approval overhead
More accurate and complete project documentation
Better stakeholder satisfaction with quicker delivery
Lower project risks through faster response
Change Control.w: Skipping change control risks scope creep, confusion, and failure.

n.1: Efficiency often declines without proper control.
n.3: Stakeholder dissatisfaction may increase.
n.4: Risks tend to increase.
n.2: Documentation usually becomes less reliable.

Change Control.q: A project manager is drafting a high-level impact assessment for a proposed change and wants it to show how far the change would push back the project's key delivery points. Which of the following should this assessment include?
Change Control.w: Schedule delays and cost impacts are critical factors in impact assessment.

n.3: Project colors are not relevant.
n.4: Lunch preferences are irrelevant.
n.1: Email counts do not reflect impact.

Change Control.q: A construction project team has completed the detailed evaluation of a change to building materials. What should happen next according to the change control process?
o: A recommendation is made based on the evaluation
A new business case is created
Stakeholders are informed and the change is logged
Change Control.w: Once a detailed evaluation is completed, a recommendation is made regarding whether to proceed with the change.

n.0: Implementation must follow formal decision-making, not immediately after evaluation.
n.4: Informing stakeholders is important but follows the decision process.
n.3: Only relevant plans are updated after a change is approved.
n.2: A new business case is not always required for every change.

Change Control.q: At which stage in the change control process are the potential effects on cost, schedule, and quality most thoroughly examined?
Change Control.w: The detailed evaluation examines all major project factors in depth.

n.3: Submitting a change does not include thorough analysis.
n.4: Initial evaluation is high-level and quick.
n.2: Project close is not the stage for evaluation.
n.0: Benefit reviews come after project delivery.

Change Control.q: A change request has been logged and now requires a thorough analysis of how it would affect cost, schedule and quality before any recommendation is made. Which stage of the change control process involves reviewing the potential impact on cost, schedule, and quality in depth?
Change Control.w: Detailed evaluation assesses all key impacts before making a recommendation.

n.2: Initial evaluation is a high-level review.
n.0: Submission is just the start of the process.
n.3: Implementation happens after evaluation and approval.
n.1: Post-implementation review happens after the change is implemented.

Change Control.q: Several change requests are outstanding on a large programme, and a decision is needed on which to accept, defer or reject. Within a properly governed change control process, who typically has the authority to approve or reject change requests?
o: External suppliers delivering the work packages
End users who requested the change
All project stakeholders by majority vote
Individual project team members acting alone
Change control board or project governance group
Change Control.w: A formal group or board oversees approval to ensure consistency and accountability.

n.3: Team members provide input but do not have final approval.
n.0: Suppliers advise but don't approve changes.
n.1: End users can request but not approve changes.
n.2: Not all stakeholders hold approval authority.

Change Control.q: A proposed change on a fixed-budget project would require additional funding that the project simply does not have available. As the project manager, which of the following justifications supports rejecting the change on budget grounds?
o: The change would shorten the overall project schedule
The cost exceeds available funding and threatens project viability
The change is popular and widely supported by stakeholders
The change would improve deliverable quality significantly
The change carries very low risk to delivery
Change Control.w: Exceeding budget limits without offsetting benefits supports rejection.

n.2: Popularity does not override budget issues.
n.3: Quality improvements are positive but may not offset costs.
n.0: Schedule reduction is beneficial but not guaranteed.
n.4: Low risk alone does not justify budget overspend.

Change Control.q: A change request has been submitted, but the project manager does not yet have enough information about its effects to make a firm recommendation to approve or reject it. Which of the following would support a decision to defer the change to a later point?
o: Insufficient information to fully assess the change
Change Control.w: Lack of information and current resource limits justify deferment.

n.2: Cost savings encourage approval, not deferment.
n.1: Urgent risk mitigation calls for prompt action.
n.4: Stakeholder demand favors approval or prioritization.

Change Control.q: A project manager observes that an iterative delivery team accommodates changes far more readily than a comparable linear project would. In iterative life cycles, why is change control typically more flexible than in linear life cycles?
o: Because changes are expected and integrated continuously
Because changes are only managed at project close
Change Control.w: Iterative life cycles are designed to accommodate frequent, continuous change.

n.0: Changes are not typically rejected outright.
n.4: Documentation remains essential.
n.2: Approvals are still needed.
n.3: Change control is ongoing, not only at project close.

Change Control.q: A project manager is planning when to keep stakeholders informed about changes moving through the control process, from request through evaluation to a final decision. At what stage in the change control process is stakeholder communication most critical?
o: Only if the change is rejected
Throughout the entire change control process
Change Control.w: Effective communication throughout ensures transparency and alignment.

n.2: Communication after implementation only is insufficient.
n.3: Communication is needed beyond submission.
n.0: Project closure is not the only time for communication.
n.1: Stakeholders should be informed regardless of approval.

Change Control.q: During the delivery phase of an IT programme, a change request is raised to add new functionality. Before it goes to the change control board, the project manager wants to appraise how much the change would add to the approved budget. Which of the following high-level impacts is being assessed?
Change Control.w: Cost and schedule are fundamental project constraints affected by change.

n.1: Colors are irrelevant.
n.3: Office layout is unrelated.
n.4: Weather does not affect project change impact.

Change Control.q: A project manager is asked to contrast how change is handled when comparing a linear life cycle with an iterative one. When comparing linear and iterative life cycles, what is a key difference in change control?
o: Iterative projects manage changes more frequently and with greater flexibility
Iterative projects postpone all changes until the final stage
Iterative projects require board sign-off for each individual change
Linear projects incorporate changes continuously throughout delivery
Linear projects manage changes more flexibly than iterative ones do
Change Control.w: Iterative life cycles expect and handle change as part of the process.

n.4: Linear projects do allow changes, but in a more controlled way.
n.2: Documentation is always required.
n.3: Linear projects evaluate before implementing.
n.1: There are important differences in approach.

Change Control.q: Whether a project uses a linear or an iterative life cycle, a consistent activity is applied to determine whether a proposed change should go ahead. Which process is used in both linear and iterative life cycles to decide whether a change should be made?
o: Evaluation of the change's impact and benefits
Unanimous approval by the project team
Change Control.w: All approaches evaluate impact and benefits before making decisions on changes.

n.2: Team input is important but not the only factor.
n.4: Immediate implementation skips proper control.
n.3: Stakeholder input is essential.
n.0: Documentation is vital in change control.

Change Control.q: A project manager maintaining many concurrent change requests needs to see at a glance where each one stands in the process. What is the significance of capturing approval status in a change request?
o: To manage ongoing supplier contract negotiations
To track whether the change is pending, approved, or rejected
To finalise and baseline the overall project schedule
To determine individual team members' salary levels
To archive documents from completed past projects
Change Control.w: Approval status tracks the progress of the change through the control process.

n.2: Schedule finalization is a separate activity.
n.0: Contracts are managed differently.
n.4: Archiving is unrelated to approval status.
n.3: Salaries are outside change requests.

Change Control.q: After a change has been successfully implemented on a project, the project manager wants to make sure the experience improves how future changes are handled. Which action ensures lessons are captured for future change control improvements?
o: Postponing any reflection on the change process
Starting a new project phase immediately
Deleting all documentation related to the change
Change Control.w: Recording outcomes and lessons supports continuous improvement of the change control process.

n.2: Documentation should be retained for accountability.
n.4: Team feedback is valuable and should not be ignored.
n.0: Immediate reflection is important for improvement.
n.1: A new phase can start, but lessons should be captured first.

Change Control.q: A change has been approved and implemented, but was not logged in the change register. What risk does this pose?
o: Overspend against the approved change budget
Duplicate approval by the change board
Automatic reversal of the implemented change
Future confusion and lack of traceability
Change Control.w: Unlogged changes lead to confusion, gaps in records, and reduced accountability.

Transition Management.w: Business-as-usual processes keep core operations stable as new changes are introduced.

n.1: Prototype processes are for testing, not daily operations.
n.0: Emergency processes are for incident response only.
n.3: Ad hoc processes lack standardization needed for BAU.
n.2: Theoretical processes are not applied practice.

Transition Management.q: In a scenario where the operations team resists taking on support for a new system, which activity would best secure their agreement?
o: Reducing communications with the operations stakeholders
Facilitating a risk transfer workshop to clarify responsibilities
Delaying the system cutover date indefinitely
Issuing the finalised transition plan without consulting operations
Outsourcing every support task to a third party
Transition Management.w: A risk transfer workshop helps clarify which risks operations will own, building consensus.

n.3: Unilateral imposition breeds resistance, not agreement.
n.2: Indefinite delays postpone the problem without resolving it.
n.4: Outsourcing avoids stakeholder buy-in for in-house operations.
n.0: Reducing communication increases opposition and confusion.

Transition Management.q: Throughout the transition of a new service, fresh issues and threats continue to surface as go-live approaches. The project manager wants the transition risk register to stay a reliable reflection of the current situation. Complete the statement: transition risk registers should be regularly ________ to capture emerging issues.
Transition Management.w: Regular updates ensure the transition risk register reflects the current risk landscape and supports mitigation actions.

n.3: Deleting the register removes visibility of risks.
n.2: Freezing it prevents new risks from being captured.
n.1: Uploading alone does not guarantee current content.
n.0: Archiving is for closed projects, not active risk management.

Transition Management.q: An organisation wants its store of transition lessons and operational guidance to genuinely feed continuous improvement, so that teams actually reuse past experience on future handovers. A project manager is reviewing what quality the repository most needs to make that possible. Which characteristic is essential for a knowledge repository to support continuous improvement?
Transition Management.w: Accessible repositories ensure teams can easily find and apply past lessons to new transitions.

n.0: Obscure information isn’t useful.
n.3: Excess volume can overwhelm users.
n.2: Complexity hinders quick retrieval.
n.1: Unnecessary redundancy can cause confusion.

Transition Management.q: After a new solution went live, support staff followed the handover documentation but repeatedly applied steps and settings that no longer matched the current system, causing errors. Reviewing why the knowledge transfer failed, the project manager identifies the root cause. Complete the statement: knowledge transfer failure is most likely when documentation is ________.
Transition Management.w: Outdated documentation misleads users and fails to convey current processes or configurations.

n.3: Comprehensive docs aid, not hinder, transfer.
n.1: Accessibility improves knowledge use.
n.0: Good structure enhances clarity.
n.4: Validation ensures accuracy and reliability.

Transition Management.q: Having negotiated a transition plan and agreed how its risks will be allocated among the stakeholders, a project manager now needs a document that formally records their commitment to both. Which document formalises stakeholder agreement to the transition plan and risk allocations?
Transition Management.w: A signed charter captures stakeholder commitments to the plan and assigned risks.

n.0: Floor plans depict facility layouts, not plan approvals.
n.1: Maps show campus geography, not stakeholder commitments.
n.3: Handbooks cover HR policies, not transition agreements.
n.2: Social media policy is unrelated to project transitions.

Transition Management.q: As a new operational system is handed over, the project manager arranges structured knowledge transfer between the project team and the operations staff who will run it. A colleague asks what this activity is fundamentally intended to achieve. What is the primary purpose of knowledge transfer during transition?
o: To reassign the project team to new initiatives
To ensure operational teams can support new processes
To document lessons learned for the closure report
To sign off deliverables against the acceptance criteria
To confirm the business case benefits are realised
Transition Management.w: Knowledge transfer equips operations with the know-how to maintain and support new solutions post-handover.

n.2: Budget finalization is a financial activity, not knowledge transfer.
n.0: Automation is a technical solution, not the transfer of know-how.
n.3: System retirement may follow transition, but KT focuses on people.
n.4: Sponsor recruitment is unrelated to operational readiness.

Transition Management.q: As a project moves into transition, the project manager relies on a particular record to keep track of how involved and supportive each stakeholder is as the handover progresses. Complete the statement: the stakeholder register is used to track stakeholder ________ during transition.
Transition Management.w: Engagement levels indicate each stakeholder’s involvement and buy-in for the transition plan.

n.0: Locations are logged elsewhere (e.g., HR directory).
n.1: Personal hobbies are not relevant to transition management.
n.3: Salary information is confidential and unrelated.
n.2: Holiday schedules are managed separately from stakeholder engagement.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is coaching a junior colleague on the principles that underpin a successful handover of deliverables into operational use. The colleague lists several behaviours they believe support good transition management, but one of them would actually undermine it. Which of the following is NOT a principle of successful transition management?
Transition Management.w: Ignoring stakeholder input undermines buy-in and risks failure during handover.

n.2: Engaging operations early is essential for smooth transition.
n.0: Clear role definitions prevent confusion post-handover.
n.1: Maintaining BAU processes avoids service disruption.
n.3: Planning from the outset ensures transition needs are built in.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is trying to bring a mixed group of technical and non-technical stakeholders to a shared agreement on how transition risks will be transferred. A colleague suggests several approaches, but one would actually block consensus rather than build it. Which technique is NOT recommended for achieving stakeholder consensus on risk transfer?
o: Documenting agreements in a shared model
Mapping risks to owners with clear definitions
Transition Management.w: Unexplained jargon alienates non-technical stakeholders and impedes consensus.

n.1: Clear risk mapping promotes understanding and agreement.
n.3: Negotiation sessions build consensus on contested items.
n.0: Shared documentation ensures transparency of agreements.
n.4: Cross-functional reviews surface diverse concerns and align teams.

Transition Management.q: A project sponsor asks a project manager to explain the value of formally capturing lessons learned as part of transition. The project manager lists several genuine benefits, but wants to correct one claim the sponsor makes that overstates what lessons learned can deliver. Which is NOT a benefit of capturing lessons learned during transition?
o: Informing refinements to future transition processes
Enhancing the knowledge held across the team
Guaranteeing all future transitions are flawless
Reducing the recurrence of past mistakes
Supporting the organisation's continuous improvement efforts
Transition Management.w: Lessons learned cannot guarantee flawless outcomes but do improve future practices.

n.3: They help avoid repeating errors.
n.0: They inform refinements to processes.
n.1: They build collective team expertise.
n.4: They underpin ongoing improvements.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is preparing a cutover plan for switching customers from a legacy system to a new one over a single weekend, and she is determined to keep any downtime to an absolute minimum and recoverable. She wants to include the elements that most directly serve those aims. Which two factors should be included in a cutover plan to minimise downtime?
o: Change request backlog and issue logs
Sequenced task list and rollback procedures
Team performance metrics and scoreboard displays
Transition Management.w: A well-sequenced task list paired with defined rollback steps ensures smooth, reversible cutover execution.

n.3: Holiday schedules and marketing are unrelated to cutover control.
n.0: Backlogs and logs help with tracking but don’t guide execution sequence.
n.2: Performance metrics don’t directly prevent downtime.
n.4: Logistics details like parking do not minimise system downtime.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is explaining to a sponsor why business-as-usual must be protected while the project delivers change. The sponsor asks her to list the legitimate reasons for doing so, but one suggested reason runs contrary to good governance. Which of the following is NOT a reason to maintain business-as-usual during project delivery?
Transition Management.w: Business-as-usual aims for transparency and continuity; hiding issues undermines trust and should be avoided.

n.0: BAU prevents interruption of daily services.
n.2: Compliance often relies on stable BAU processes.
n.1: Customer satisfaction is maintained by uninterrupted service.
n.4: Revenue continuity depends on BAU stability.

Transition Management.q: After completing a significant transition, a project manager schedules a session to record what went well and what did not, so the same problems do not resurface on the next handover. Complete the statement: organisations should capture lessons learned after each major transition to avoid repeating ________.
Transition Management.w: Recording past mistakes helps teams address root causes and refine future transition plans.

n.3: Profits are positive outcomes, not errors to avoid.
n.1: Savings aren’t mistakes.
n.4: Budgets are financial plans, not errors.
n.2: Holidays are scheduled breaks, not transition errors.

Transition Management.q: A project team updates all data sources but forgets to communicate process changes to operations. Which is NOT an effective mitigation in this scenario?
Transition Management.w: Skipping the operations handover would ignore the core issue and lead to further delays.

n.3: A communication plan directly addresses the lack of messaging.
n.0: End-user training ensures operations understand new processes.
n.1: Cutover updates can include handover steps for operations.
n.4: Documenting support processes clarifies how operations should proceed.

Transition Management.q: Which technique is NOT effective for engaging stakeholders in agreeing a transition plan?
Transition Management.w: Imposition without dialogue alienates stakeholders and fails to secure agreement.

n.1: Workshops foster two-way communication and consensus.
n.0: Risk matrices clarify responsibilities and build confidence.
n.2: Impact assessments show stakeholders what's changing and why.
n.3: Training ensures stakeholders understand their roles in transition.

Transition Management.q: After go-live, the team holds a workshop to identify what went well and what didn’t. This is an example of ________.
Transition Management.w: Reviewing successes and failures post-transition drives ongoing enhancements in processes and plans.

n.0: Risk management addresses threats, not experiential learning per se.
n.4: Stakeholder mapping identifies stakeholders, not lessons.
n.3: Budget forecasting is a financial projection.
n.2: Technical design is a development activity.

Transition Management.q: While finalising a transition plan, a project manager needs to agree who will take ownership of the risks being transferred to the receiving organisation as the new service goes live. She wants the right people around the table to reach that agreement. Which two stakeholders should be involved to agree risk transfer in a transition plan?
Transition Management.w: Operations managers and risk owners jointly agree on who will assume specific transition risks.

n.2: Marketing and design roles are unrelated to risk ownership in transition.
n.3: Competitors are not internal decision-makers for risk transfer.
n.1: Facilities staff support logistics but don’t own transition risks.
n.4: Shareholders/customers are recipients of value but not day-to-day risk owners.

Transition Management.q: A project manager wants the stakeholders receiving a new service to reach a shared understanding of who owns which transferred risks. She is selecting activities that will both clarify the allocation and secure collective agreement to it. Which two activities support stakeholder alignment on risk transfer?
o: Finalising the procurement schedule and payment milestone dates
Publishing the marketing plan and the communications calendar
Drafting the closure report and archiving project records
Updating the project schedule and reallocating team resources
Developing a risk ownership matrix and conducting joint review sessions
Transition Management.w: A risk matrix clarifies roles, and joint reviews secure collective alignment on those roles.

n.0: Seating and parking logistics don’t address risk ownership.
n.1: Public announcements don’t replace stakeholder workshops.
n.3: Uniforms are unrelated to risk or transition.
n.2: Celebrations don’t formalize risk agreements.

Transition Management.q: During transition, a critical defect was discovered in the new system. What is the immediate next step according to good transition practices?
Transition Management.w: If a critical defect arises, rollback to the last stable state prevents major service disruption.

n.1: Marketing updates do not address system defects.
n.3: Celebrating success ignores the defect issue.
n.2: Proceeding with a critical defect risks operational failure.
n.0: Deleting the plan removes guidance in a crisis.

Transition Management.q: After a handover, the operations team was unsure who was accountable for various support tasks, and duties were either duplicated or overlooked. Reviewing the transition plan, the project manager realises a key element was not defined clearly enough. Complete the statement: the transition plan lacked clear ________, leading to confusion about role responsibilities.
Transition Management.w: Defining responsibilities clearly prevents overlap, gaps, and confusion during handover.

n.0: Budget clarity is important but not the root cause of role confusion.
n.3: Metrics track performance; they do not assign roles.
n.2: Risk clarity is separate from role definitions.
n.1: Governance structure supports decision making but isn’t the same as individual roles.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is persuading a sceptical sponsor of the value of holding transition readiness reviews before handover. The sponsor lists several outcomes he expects such reviews to deliver, but one of them overstates what a review can realistically achieve. Which is NOT a benefit of conducting transition readiness reviews?
Transition Management.w: Readiness reviews cannot guarantee zero incidents but they do help identify and mitigate risks beforehand.

n.1: They highlight gaps that need addressing.
n.2: Reviews secure buy-in and preparedness from stakeholders.
n.3: They confirm that resources are in place.
n.0: They improve risk awareness and management.

Transition Management.q: After deployment, the service desk reports a surge in incident tickets. Which two transition plan components could have mitigated this?
o: Updating procurement orders and vendor contracts
Holding daily standups and quarterly reviews
Prioritizing marketing activities and social media updates
Transition Management.w: Proper user training and clear support materials equip end users and support teams, reducing incidents.

n.4: Marketing does not address operational incident handling.
n.0: Cutover steps and rollback help with go-live risks but not user support readiness.
n.3: Meetings do not substitute for training and documentation.
n.1: Procurement orders and contracts are administrative and not user-facing support tools.

Transition Management.q: At the very start of transition planning, a project manager decides to bring the affected operational teams and other stakeholders into the conversation early rather than presenting them with a finished plan. A colleague asks what she is mainly hoping to gain from this. What is the key benefit of engaging stakeholders early in transition planning?
o: Eliminating the need for any technical reviews
Avoiding the need for any budget discussions
Removing the need for a formal transition plan
Securing buy-in and commitment to the transition plan
Guaranteeing there will be no post-live issues
Transition Management.w: Early engagement builds stakeholder ownership and commitment to the transition plan.

n.2: You still need a transition plan regardless of engagement timing.
n.0: Technical reviews remain necessary for system readiness.
n.4: Zero issues cannot be guaranteed by engagement alone.
n.1: Budget discussions remain essential to plan viability.

Transition Management.q: A project is about to hand a new IT service over to a live support environment, and the project manager is most concerned that customers experience no break in service during the changeover. She wants to focus on the elements that most directly protect continuity of service. Which two components best ensure continuity of service during transition?
o: Risk closure reports and design prototypes
User training sessions and support documentation
Quality audit schedule and performance appraisals
Marketing campaign launch and press releases
Operations team involvement and detailed SLAs
Transition Management.w: Involving operations and having clear SLAs ensure services continue without interruption during handover.

n.3: Marketing activities do not directly ensure service continuity.
n.1: Training and documentation help, but without ops involvement/SLAs continuity isn’t guaranteed.
n.2: Audits assess quality but don’t manage day-to-day handover operations.
n.0: Closure reports and prototypes do not directly support live service continuity.

Transition Management.q: During a transition, the legal team confirms it will retain ownership of the risk of any data compliance breaches rather than passing it to operations. The project manager wants to make sure this arrangement is properly agreed and cannot later be disputed. Which activity ensures stakeholder agreement?
o: Postponing all legal sign-off until after go-live
Excluding legal from all transition planning discussions
Documenting legal’s risk responsibilities in the transition plan
Reassigning the compliance risk to the marketing team
Disregarding the relevant data protection regulations
Transition Management.w: Documenting responsibilities formalizes agreement and avoids ambiguity about compliance ownership.

n.1: Exclusion leads to misunderstandings and legal exposure.
n.3: Marketing lacks the mandate to manage compliance risk.
n.4: Ignoring regulations exposes the organization to penalties.
n.0: Delays in sign-off stall the entire transition process.

Transition Management.q: Following a handover, a support lead keeps adding new material to the knowledge base but never asks the operations users whether the content is actually helping them do their jobs. A project manager reviewing this identifies a continuous improvement practice that is absent. Which continuous improvement practice is missing?
Transition Management.w: Feedback loops gather user input to refine content and ensure the knowledge base meets operational needs.

n.4: Backups preserve data but don’t improve content quality.
n.1: Avoiding risk is not the same as learning from feedback.
n.3: Cost estimates don’t assess knowledge usefulness.
n.0: Holiday plans are unrelated to knowledge management.

Transition Management.q: Midway through moving a new solution into live service, the operations team finds that one critical business process cannot be supported because the necessary documentation was never produced. The project manager must decide how to respond. What is the priority action?
Transition Management.w: Creating the required documentation enables operations to support the process after handover.

n.3: An auditor may find non-conformities but won’t create the missing docs.
n.0: Reducing support desk capacity worsens the situation.
n.1: Cancellation ignores the core planning need.
n.2: Marketing is unrelated to process support.

Transition Management.q: As a project prepares to move a new solution into day-to-day running, the project manager is deciding who must take part in the transition discussions so that ongoing support is ready. She wants the people accountable for live services and front-line user support at the table. Which two stakeholders are essential to involve in transition discussions?
o: Operations manager and service desk lead
Transition Management.w: The operations manager and service desk lead ensure that support and day-to-day services are prepared for the new delivery.

n.4: Competitors are not stakeholder participants in your transition.
n.3: Finance and marketing have roles but aren’t the core day-to-day operators.
n.2: HR or union reps may be involved but aren’t primary for operational handover.
n.1: ECM admins/designers are technical, not high‐level operational owners.

Transition Management.q: As a project prepares to hand a new service to operations, the project manager is compiling the risks that will pass to the receiving organisation at go-live. A colleague proposes several items for that list, but one of them is not a project risk at all. Which of the following is NOT a risk type typically transferred in a transition plan?
Transition Management.w: Party planning is not a project risk; transition focuses on operational and technical risks.

n.1: Service level breaches are risks transferred to operations.
n.3: Support gaps represent operational risks post-handover.
n.2: Data migration failures are critical technical risks.
n.4: Delays in user acceptance affect go-live risk profiles.

Transition Management.q: A project manager is drafting a thorough transition plan for handing a new service to operations. She has already set out how stakeholders will be engaged and how staff will be trained, and now wants everyone kept informed of timing and responsibilities. Complete the statement: a robust transition plan defines stakeholder engagement, training, and ______.
Transition Management.w: Communication ensures all parties understand timing, responsibilities, and changes during transition.

n.3: Risk mitigation is important but does not complete the core trio of engagement, training, and communication.
n.4: Resource allocation is addressed elsewhere in planning.
n.0: Budgeting is part of cost management, not central to handover messaging.
n.1: Branding is unrelated to operational transition.

Transition Management.q: When a new way of working was rolled out to a business area, staff pushed back because they had not been involved or consulted during planning. Reviewing what went wrong, the project manager identifies the missing element. Complete the statement: without proper stakeholder ________, resistance to new processes increased.
Transition Management.w: Engagement ensures stakeholders understand and buy into changes, reducing resistance.

n.2: Testing does not manage stakeholder buy-in.
n.1: Budget alone doesn’t address resistance.
n.3: Design is a technical activity, not stakeholder management.
n.4: Metrics track performance but don’t directly engage stakeholders.

Transition Management.q: While a project introduces a major new customer system, the operational teams must keep serving existing customers without interruption throughout delivery. The project manager makes a point of accounting for these ongoing operational needs when planning. What is the purpose of considering business-as-usual during a project?
o: Reduces the need for project governance
Transition Management.w: Considering BAU ensures critical services remain stable and uninterrupted while the project runs.

n.1: BAU planning complements, not eliminates, change management.
n.2: Marketing reach is unrelated to operational stability.
n.3: Defect elimination cannot be guaranteed by BAU considerations.
n.4: BAU planning does not replace governance requirements.

Transition Management.q: After agreeing how the risks of a transition will be shared among stakeholders, a project manager wants tangible outputs that evidence exactly who has accepted which risk and confirm their sign-off. Which two outputs help confirm stakeholder agreement on risk transfer?
o: Parking permit forms and ID badges
Press release draft and marketing plan
Risk transfer log and signed responsibility matrix
Transition Management.w: A log and matrix record who assumes which risks and document stakeholder sign-off.

n.1: Menus/calendar are unrelated to risk agreements.
n.0: Logistics forms don’t capture risk responsibilities.
n.3: Marketing documents don’t formalize risk ownership.
n.2: Entertainment schedules are irrelevant to transition risk sign-off.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is justifying to the sponsor why a communication plan should form part of the integrated project management plan rather than be handled informally. Why should communication plans be included in the plan?
o: To hold confidential personal data about each individual project team member
To transfer the project manager's reporting duties onto the wider team
To ensure the right information reaches the right people at the right time
To set out the daily lunch schedule for the project office
To remove the need for any formal stakeholder analysis activities entirely
Integrated Planning.w: A communication plan ensures timely and relevant information flows to all stakeholders.

n.3: Lunch schedules are not part of project communication.
n.4: Stakeholder analysis remains important.
n.0: Confidential data must be managed elsewhere.
n.1: The plan supports, not replaces, management effort.

Integrated Planning.q: During delivery, a project manager is deciding under what circumstances the integrated project management plan should be formally revised and reissued to the team. A project management plan should be updated when which of the following occurs?
o: A competitor releases a rival product onto the market
The office relocates or changes its internet service provider
There are significant changes to scope, schedule, cost, or risk
New stationery is ordered for the project office
A member of the project team takes annual leave
Integrated Planning.w: Plans must reflect significant project changes to remain accurate and effective.

n.4: Annual leave does not require plan updates.
n.0: Stationery is not a plan content.
n.1: Competitor activity may prompt review, but not updates directly.
n.3: Internet providers are not plan content.

Integrated Planning.q: At the start of a new project, the organisation needs to confirm who will lead the preparation of the integrated project management plan and coordinate the necessary contributions. Who is typically responsible for preparing this plan?
o: The finance director acting alone without any wider input
The project manager with input from the team and stakeholders
Individual team members each planning their own work separately
The marketing department working on behalf of the sponsor
External suppliers contracted to deliver the project's outputs
Integrated Planning.w: The project manager leads the process, gathering input from all relevant parties.

n.0: Finance leads budgeting, not planning overall.
n.3: Marketing may contribute, but does not lead planning.
n.4: Suppliers may be consulted, but not responsible.
n.2: Team input is essential, but integration is managed centrally.

Integrated Planning.q: A project team is debating whether to maintain a single coordinated plan or to let each function run its own separate documents. As project manager, you argue for an integrated approach. Why is integration important in a project management plan?
o: It enables each team member to plan and work in isolation
It ensures all elements of the project work together towards common objectives
It provides a guarantee that the project will encounter no risks
It replaces the requirement for a separate project business case
It removes the need to maintain any formal project documentation
Integrated Planning.w: Integration aligns objectives, controls and processes for project success.

n.0: Teamwork is essential.
n.4: Documentation is still required.
n.2: Risk cannot be eliminated.
n.3: Business cases are still needed.

Integrated Planning.q: Before releasing funding for the delivery phase of a major infrastructure project, a sponsor insists on seeing a fully integrated project management plan. Why is it valuable for project sponsors to require an integrated project management plan before authorising delivery?
o: It confirms that the detailed technical design is fully complete before any planning begins
It replaces the need for holding regular stage-gate reviews throughout the delivery phase
It locks the project scope completely so that no further changes can ever occur
It gives assurance that all aspects of the project are coordinated and risks are managed
It transfers full accountability for all delivery outcomes onto the project manager alone
Integrated Planning.w: Sponsors want assurance the project is well planned, controlled and coordinated.

n.4: Progress should still be reviewed regularly.
n.0: Change is a normal part of projects.
n.1: The business case remains important.
n.2: Stakeholder input is vital throughout.

Integrated Planning.q: Within the integrated project management plan for a change initiative, one section is dedicated to how uncertainty affecting the project will be handled. What is the primary function of the risk management approach in this plan?
o: To outline how risks will be identified, assessed, and managed
To set out the profit targets expected from the project
To arrange team-building events and social activities for staff
To describe the marketing activities promoting the project outputs
To record the allocation of staff annual leave entitlements
Integrated Planning.w: The risk section ensures threats and opportunities are managed systematically.

n.1: Profit targets are not a risk management function.
n.2: Team building is managed separately.
n.3: Marketing is not part of risk management.
n.4: Holiday allocation is separate.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager on a large IT transformation programme is consolidating separate team documents into one governing document before delivery begins. When explaining the value of this approach to the sponsor, which is a key benefit of having a single integrated project management plan?
o: It removes the need for a formal change control process
It avoids having to define the project's objectives clearly upfront
It supports a separate management plan for each department involved
It provides a clear reference point for all team members and stakeholders
It makes detailed project budgeting an entirely unnecessary planning activity
Integrated Planning.w: A single plan ensures everyone is working from the same information.

n.0: Change control is still needed.
n.4: Budgets are always necessary.
n.1: Objectives must be defined clearly.
n.2: Integrated planning combines all departments.

Integrated Planning.q: A sponsor questions whether the effort of producing a full integrated project management plan is really worthwhile for the success of an upcoming project. Why is producing such a plan important for project success?
o: It lets team members work independently without any coordination between them
It replaces the requirement to produce a project business case
It aligns objectives, processes and controls across all areas of the project
It provides a guarantee that the project will have no risks
It removes the need for communication between the project team members
Integrated Planning.w: Integration ensures all project elements work together toward common objectives.

n.4: Communication remains essential for project success.
n.3: Risks cannot be fully eliminated.
n.1: A business case is still needed.
n.0: Coordination is required for success.

Integrated Planning.q: An organisation has decided to consolidate its various project documents into one integrated project management plan for a major initiative. What is the main benefit of adopting a single, integrated plan?
o: It removes the need for any formal change management process
It provides a guarantee that the project is delivered on time
It provides a clear and consistent reference for all stakeholders
It lowers the amount of communication the project actually requires
It concentrates attention solely on the project's technical requirements
Integrated Planning.w: An integrated plan gives everyone a unified view of how the project will be managed.

n.3: Communication remains important.
n.1: Plans support delivery but don’t guarantee it.
n.0: Change management is always needed.
n.4: Non-technical areas are also covered.

Integrated Planning.q: Within an integrated project management plan, the project manager is drafting the section that deals with the threats and opportunities the project may face. What would a typical risk management section of this plan include?
o: The marketing strategies used by the external suppliers
Processes for identifying, assessing and responding to project risks
The allocation of staff car parking spaces on site
The catering arrangements provided for the project meetings
The company's profit targets set for its shareholders
Integrated Planning.w: The risk section covers the full approach to managing threats and opportunities.

n.2: Parking is not a plan content.
n.4: Shareholder targets are outside project management.
n.3: Catering is not a plan topic.
n.0: Supplier marketing is unrelated.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is assembling the contents of the integrated project management plan and reviewing which items genuinely belong within it. Which of the following would NOT typically be included in an integrated project management plan?
Integrated Planning.w: Holiday rotas are managed separately from the project management plan.

n.0: Scope is a core part of the plan.
n.2: Risk approach should be included.
n.4: The schedule baseline is key.
n.3: Quality planning is essential.

Integrated Planning.q: A company runs a project through several functional teams that each maintain their own separate plans, with no single overarching document tying the work together. Which outcome is most likely if a project does NOT use an integrated management plan?
o: Clear and consistent direction for the project
Increased confusion, duplication of effort and misalignment
Integrated Planning.w: Without integration, teams may lack alignment and efficiency.

n.4: Communication often breaks down without a single plan.
n.1: Benefits are less likely to be delivered.
n.0: Direction can become unclear.
n.3: Performance monitoring is harder without one plan.

Integrated Planning.q: As the project manager finalises the schedule baseline section of the integrated project management plan, they consider what information this part of the document should capture. What is typically included in the schedule baseline section?
o: Key milestones and timelines for deliverables
A list of social media accounts
Integrated Planning.w: Schedule baseline sets the key dates and delivery times for outputs.

n.0: Personal expenses are not included.
n.2: Office policies may be referenced but not detailed.
n.4: Social media is outside project planning.
n.3: Supplier marketing is not part of the project plan.

Integrated Planning.q: A section of the integrated project management plan sets out how any proposed alterations to scope, schedule and cost will be raised, assessed and approved during delivery. This section is known as which of the following?
Integrated Planning.w: Change control procedures outline how project changes will be approved and tracked.

n.0: Stakeholder analysis reviews project influence.
n.3: Market analysis is outside plan content.
n.4: Reward strategy is a HR function.
n.2: Competitor review is a business analysis task.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is reviewing a draft integrated project management plan and removing any content that does not properly belong in it. Which of the following is LEAST likely to be found in such a plan?
o: The allocation of resources across tasks
The strategy for managing project risks
The definition of the project scope
The procedures for controlling agreed changes
Integrated Planning.w: Personal data like birthdays is not included in the project plan.

n.0: Resource allocation is a core plan section.
n.2: Scope definition is fundamental.
n.3: Change control is required.
n.1: Risk management must be planned.

Integrated Planning.q: A project sponsor asks the project manager to confirm that the integrated project management plan will cover the full range of management areas needed to control delivery. A well-structured plan of this kind will typically include which of the following?
o: The risk register and the project issue log exclusively
The communication plan and the stakeholder register only
Objectives, scope, schedule, resources, risks, and quality management
Procurement contracts and supplier payment schedules on their own
Financial budgets and profit targets set for the shareholders
Integrated Planning.w: A comprehensive plan covers all critical management areas for the project.

n.4: Financials are just one aspect.
n.1: Communication is important but not the only section.
n.3: Holiday schedules are not relevant.
n.0: Risk is just one part.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is briefing the team on how the integrated project management plan will be used to guide and control delivery throughout the project. Which statement about the integrated project management plan is TRUE?
o: It should be withheld from external stakeholders to protect confidentiality
It is produced only after the project has formally closed
It serves as the master document guiding all aspects of project delivery
It removes the need to maintain a separate risk register
It is required exclusively for large information technology delivery projects
Integrated Planning.w: The integrated plan is the main reference for managing and controlling the project.

n.1: Planning happens before work starts.
n.4: All project types require plans.
n.0: Plans should be accessible to stakeholders as appropriate.
n.3: Registers support, not replace, plans.

Integrated Planning.q: A project board wants assurance that the integrated project management plan makes clear who is accountable for what across delivery. Which element is ESSENTIAL to include for the plan to be effective?
o: Confidential personal details of all the project staff
A list of unrelated previously completed company projects
Defined roles and responsibilities for project delivery
The preferred catering options for each project meeting
A record of individual team members' personal hobbies
Integrated Planning.w: Defining roles is essential for accountability and clarity in the project.

n.4: Lunch options are not relevant.
n.1: Unrelated projects are not plan content.
n.0: Private staff details are not included.
n.3: Hobbies are not project content.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is describing to a colleague what the quality management plan contributes when it sits within the wider integrated project management plan. What is the role of the quality management plan within the integrated plan?
o: It manages the marketing campaigns run by the suppliers
It schedules the social events held across the company
It defines standards, processes, and responsibilities for delivering quality outputs
It tracks the holiday bookings of the project team members
It reports the dividends paid to the company's shareholders
Integrated Planning.w: Quality management planning is essential for consistent, accepted project outputs.

n.3: Holiday bookings are managed separately.
n.4: Dividends are outside project scope.
n.0: Supplier marketing is unrelated.
n.1: Social events are not plan content.
