Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is explaining to stakeholders the genuine benefits that an integrated project management plan brings to delivery, and wants to correct a common misunderstanding. Which of the following is NOT a typical benefit of such a plan?
o: Ensuring alignment of all project management processes
Documenting staff birthdays for HR records
Providing a unified source of project information
Integrated Planning.w: Staff birthdays are not relevant for project management planning.

n.4: Unified information supports management.
n.0: Decision support is a main benefit.
n.3: Role clarity is critical.
n.1: Alignment is a key reason for integration.

Integrated Planning.q: During the definition phase of an organisational change project, the project manager is drawing together scope, schedule, cost and quality into one coherent document. In this context, a key reason to produce an integrated project management plan is to:
o: Ensure every team member sets their own objectives
Allow separate teams to develop their own processes in isolation
Align all project activities and objectives to deliver value
Replace the need for quality assurance
Integrated Planning.w: Alignment maximises the project’s ability to deliver planned value.

n.1: Processes should be coordinated, not isolated.
n.3: Quality assurance remains necessary.
n.4: Schedules must be updated as needed.
n.0: Objectives should be agreed for the whole project.

Integrated Planning.q: A newly appointed project manager is asked by the sponsor to produce an integrated project management plan for an upcoming programme of work. Which of the following BEST describes what such a plan is?
o: A set of separate plans each owned by a different function
A detailed schedule listing only the project's start and end dates
A register capturing the lessons learned from previously completed projects
A high-level summary intended mainly for communicating with external stakeholders
A single, coordinated document that combines all key project elements and controls
Integrated Planning.w: An integrated plan brings together all controls, objectives, and management information in one place.

n.1: Schedules are just one component of the plan.
n.0: Personal goals are not project management content.
n.3: Marketing materials are not project plans.
n.2: Lessons learned inform plans but are not the plan itself.

Integrated Planning.q: While drafting the integrated project management plan, a project manager is identifying the sections that establish the time framework and other core controls for delivery. Which of the following is a typical content section of such a plan?
Integrated Planning.w: The schedule baseline sets the time framework for the project.

n.4: Lunch menus are not part of project plans.
n.1: Market analysis may be used, but not as plan content.
n.2: Competitor lists are not standard sections.
n.3: Personal plans are managed separately.

Integrated Planning.q: A project manager is arguing for a dedicated resource management section within the integrated project management plan to support smooth delivery. What is the benefit of including such a section in the plan?
o: It removes the need for regular project progress reporting
It allows personal hobbies and interests to be formally recorded
It provides a full record of staff birthdays and anniversaries
It ensures that people, equipment and materials are allocated effectively
It sets out the company's overall profit and revenue figures
Integrated Planning.w: Resource management planning supports successful, efficient project delivery.

n.2: Birthdays are not relevant.
n.0: Reporting is still required.
n.4: Company profits are not part of project plans.
n.1: Hobbies are not project content.

Integrated Planning.q: A project management plan brings the project's risk, quality and communication strategies together within a single integrated document rather than treating them separately. What is the advantage of this approach?
o: Risk and quality can be ignored
All project aspects are coordinated and aligned
Integrated Planning.w: Integration ensures all management disciplines support each other.

n.1: All areas should still be addressed.
n.4: Stakeholder feedback is always important.
n.3: Both technical and non-technical issues are considered.
n.0: Documentation remains essential.

Integrated Planning.q: On a systems upgrade project, requests to alter scope arrive regularly from different stakeholders, and the project manager has embedded the change process within the wider plan. What is a benefit of integrating change control into the project management plan?
o: Schedule and budget baselines stay fixed once changes are approved
Change requests are logged separately from the management plan
Only the project manager needs to authorise significant changes
Approved changes are applied before their impact has been assessed
All changes are documented and evaluated for impact on the entire project
Integrated Planning.w: Integrated change control maintains project alignment and records impacts.

n.3: Ignoring changes can cause problems.
n.2: Budgets and schedules may still change.
n.1: All changes, not just technical, must be managed.
n.0: Stakeholder approval is usually essential.

Integrated Planning.q: A project affecting several departments has many stakeholders with differing expectations of what will be delivered and when. The project manager relies on the integrated project management plan to keep everyone aligned. How does an integrated project management plan support stakeholder engagement?
o: By providing consistent information and setting clear expectations
By only sharing information with the project manager
By guaranteeing no changes will occur
By removing the need for progress reporting
By focusing only on internal communications
Integrated Planning.w: Consistent information keeps all stakeholders aligned and informed.

n.3: Reporting progress is still needed.
n.2: Change is a normal part of projects.
n.1: Communication should reach all relevant parties.
n.4: Both internal and external communications matter.

Integrated Planning.q: A construction project faces threats spread across design, procurement and delivery, and the project manager wants a coordinated way of handling them rather than treating each in isolation. Integrated project management planning helps to reduce project risks by:
o: Replacing the risk register with a single milestone schedule
Ensuring all risks are identified, assessed and managed in one place
Focusing risk effort only on the project's critical path
Transferring every identified risk to the project sponsor to own
Delegating all risk decisions to a separate risk committee
Integrated Planning.w: A single plan helps spot and manage risks more effectively.

n.3: Risk registers are still needed.
n.4: Documentation, not just verbal updates, is vital.
n.0: Risk management should involve the whole team.
n.2: All significant risks must be assessed.

Planning.q: A project manager is concerned that the current estimates for a project carry a wide margin of uncertainty and wants to improve their reliability before the plan is baselined. Which TWO actions would most effectively reduce the uncertainty in the estimates?
Planning.w: Reducing uncertainty requires better information and validation, not artificial adjustments.

Planning.q: A project team uses analogous estimating based on a previous project, but fails to adjust for scale and complexity differences. What is the most likely outcome?
o: Systematic underestimation or overestimation due to invalid assumptions
Improved stakeholder confidence in the estimate
Faster convergence within the estimating funnel
Accurate estimates due to historical data
Elimination of uncertainty in early stages
Planning.w: Analogous estimates require adjustment for context; failing to do so introduces bias and inaccurate assumptions.

Planning.q: As a construction project progresses from its early feasibility work through to detailed design, the range around its cost and schedule estimates gradually becomes tighter, consistent with the estimating funnel. Which factor most directly drives this narrowing of the estimating funnel over time?
Planning.w: The funnel narrows as uncertainty reduces due to improved information and clarity.

Planning.q: A quality reviewer is examining several examples of project progress reporting in order to identify poor practice. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates ineffective progress reporting?
o: Reporting key milestones achieved and upcoming risks
Using visual indicators for status updates
Providing concise summaries tailored to stakeholders
Including both qualitative and quantitative data
Planning.w: Reporting deviations without impact lacks context and limits decision-making.

Planning.q: On a delivery schedule, an activity that lies on the critical path is finished ahead of its planned finish date, and no other constraints currently limit the work that follows. The project manager is assessing what this means for the timeline. What is the most likely impact?
o: Other dependent activities will be delayed as a result
Float will increase evenly across all of the remaining activities
The critical path through the network will be eliminated
The project will automatically finish ahead of its deadline
The project end date may improve if no other constraints exist
Planning.w: Early completion of critical activities can reduce overall duration if no other constraints limit progress.

Planning.q: At the very start of a novel research and development project, very little detailed information is available and the level of uncertainty is high. The project manager must nonetheless produce an initial cost estimate for the concept phase. Which estimating approach is most appropriate at this early point in the lifecycle?
o: Analogous estimation supported by broad assumptions
Planning.w: Early stages require high-level approaches like analogous estimation due to limited information.

Planning.q: When monitoring progress, a project manager reviews only the activities on the critical path and pays no attention to those carrying small amounts of float. A colleague warns him that this narrow focus is hazardous. What risk does concentrating solely on the critical path create?
o: Non-critical activities may become critical without detection
Planning.w: Ignoring near-critical activities risks them becoming critical due to unmonitored delays.

Planning.q: A project manager identifies that a non-critical activity has been delayed, but the overall project end date remains unchanged. What is the most likely explanation?
o: The activity has available float that absorbs the delay
The project schedule is inaccurate and needs to be rebuilt
The activity is on the critical path but has been incorrectly calculated
The critical path has shifted automatically
The delay has not yet been reflected in the timeline
Planning.w: Non-critical activities have float, allowing delays without impacting the overall project timeline.

Planning.q: A newly appointed project manager is producing the first cost and duration estimates for a project where much of the detail is still unknown, and is relying heavily on a set of assumptions to bridge the gaps. Which statement best reflects the proper role of assumptions in these early estimates?
o: Assumptions should be avoided until estimates are precise
Assumptions underpin estimates and must be documented and validated
Assumptions reduce the need for contingency
Assumptions are only relevant in later project stages
Planning.w: Assumptions are critical drivers of estimates and must be transparent and reviewed.

Planning.q: A project manager is preparing cost estimates and wants to handle contingency in a way that reflects the concept of the estimating funnel as the project moves through successive phases. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates an appropriate use of contingency in this context?
o: Adjusting contingency levels as uncertainty reduces across phases
Applying a fixed percentage contingency regardless of project stage
Adding contingency only after final estimates are agreed
Removing contingency once estimates are reviewed
Planning.w: Contingency should reduce as uncertainty decreases, reflecting increasing estimate confidence.

Planning.q: A project manager is presenting early cost estimates derived from limited scope definition. Stakeholders challenge the wide range and ask for a single definitive figure to approve funding. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refuse to provide any estimate until detailed design is complete
Select the highest estimate to minimise risk of overrun
Provide a single figure based on optimistic assumptions to secure approval
Explain the estimating funnel and present a range with assumptions and confidence levels
Average the high and low estimates and present that as the final cost
Planning.w: Early estimates carry high uncertainty. The estimating funnel justifies a range with explicit assumptions and confidence, enabling informed decision-making without false precision.

Planning.q: In a schedule review, two activities are shown as sequential, but the team argues they could overlap. What should determine whether overlap is appropriate?
o: The duration of the activities involved
The logical dependency type between the activities
The preference of the project manager
Planning.w: Overlap depends on dependency type (e.g., finish-to-start vs start-to-start), not preference or pressure.

Planning.q: A delivery team concentrates almost entirely on hitting each scheduled milestone and pays little attention to the day-to-day progress of the individual tasks that lie between those milestones. What is the key risk of managing progress in this manner?
o: Delays between milestones may go unnoticed
Critical activities will be completed faster
Planning.w: Milestones provide checkpoints, but ignoring detailed progress risks hidden delays.

Planning.q: A sponsor prefers a light-touch view of a project and treats the achievement of scheduled milestones as the primary way of judging whether progress is on track. What risk does relying on milestone achievement in this manner introduce?
o: The critical path will effectively manage itself through milestones
Stakeholder engagement will inevitably improve across the project
Over-reliance on milestones may mask underlying delays between them
Overall project timelines will shorten as a direct result
Milestone forecasts will steadily become more accurate over time
Planning.w: Milestones provide snapshots; relying solely on them can hide issues between control points.

Planning.q: Worried about how the sponsor will react, a project manager chooses to hold back reporting some negative progress in the hope that the situation will recover before it needs to be disclosed. What is the most significant risk arising from this decision?
o: Issues may escalate without timely intervention
Planning.w: Delayed reporting prevents timely corrective action and increases risk of escalation.

Planning.q: An organisation wants milestones in its projects to function genuinely as control points rather than as mere reporting markers. Which of the following situations best demonstrates milestones being used in this way?
o: Monitoring resource usage continuously throughout each stage
Updating the project schedule at the end of each week
Reviewing individual team member performance against targets
Reviewing progress at key decision points before proceeding
Recording task completion percentages on a daily basis
Planning.w: Milestones provide structured points for review and decision-making.

Planning.q: While carrying out a network analysis, a project manager notices that, in addition to the critical path, several other paths through the schedule have durations that are only marginally shorter. What risk does the presence of these paths present to the project?
o: Elimination of float across the schedule
Multiple near-critical paths that could become critical
Planning.w: Near-critical paths can easily become critical if minor delays occur, increasing overall schedule risk.

Planning.q: A project manager is reviewing a schedule and wants to anticipate which type of change would shift the critical path and thereby alter the overall duration. She is weighing several possible adjustments to different activities. Which change is most likely to alter the critical path?
o: Adding resources to a non-critical task
Increasing the duration of a critical activity
Reducing the duration of a non-critical activity with float
Planning.w: Changes to critical activities directly affect the critical path and overall duration.

Planning.q: A project manager produces a status report that carefully lists all the activities completed during the period but makes no mention of new risks that have started to emerge. What is the main consequence of reporting in this way?
o: Delayed identification and response to potential issues
Planning.w: Omitting risks prevents proactive management and can lead to larger issues later.

Planning.q: A stakeholder requests more frequent updates, but the project manager believes current reporting is sufficient. What should guide the decision?
o: Stakeholder information needs and decision requirements
Planning.w: Reporting frequency should align with stakeholder needs and decision-making requirements.

Planning.q: In an effort to keep a close watch on delivery, a project manager builds a schedule in which milestones are packed very tightly together, only short intervals apart. What is the most likely consequence of scheduling the milestones so closely?
o: Improved control over detailed project progress
Reduced visibility of progress for stakeholders
Greatly simplified scheduling of the work
Excessive reporting overhead with limited additional insight
Faster overall completion of the project
Planning.w: Too many milestones create administrative burden without improving meaningful control.

Planning.q: A planned milestone that was intended to act as a control point is missed, but the project manager decides not to raise or escalate the slippage to the sponsor or steering group. What risk does this failure to escalate create for the project?
o: Governance controls will absorb the slippage without any action
The delay remains contained within the current stage only
Contingency reserves will offset the miss without formal reporting
Stakeholders may lose confidence due to lack of transparency
The critical path recalculates automatically to hide the delay
Planning.w: Milestones act as control points; failure to escalate undermines governance and trust.

Planning.q: During a schedule review, the project manager notices that one activity in the network has been calculated with negative float. She needs to interpret correctly what this value is telling her about the project's position. What does negative float on this activity indicate?
o: The activity is ahead of schedule
The critical path has been shortened
The activity is delaying the project completion
The project is ahead of plan
Planning.w: Negative float indicates that the schedule is behind and the activity is impacting completion.

Planning.q: A project plan records that a key milestone has been reached, yet when the project manager checks, several of the deliverables that the milestone was meant to represent are still incomplete. What does reaching the milestone under these circumstances most clearly indicate?
o: Milestones do not need associated deliverables to close
The milestone was incorrectly defined or poorly controlled
The schedule is flexible and inherently accommodates this
The milestone should now be removed from the plan
The project is running comfortably ahead of schedule
Planning.w: Milestones should represent clear completion points; reaching one without deliverables indicates poor definition or control.

Planning.q: A project manager notices that estimates from different teams converge but remain consistently inaccurate. What is the most likely cause?
o: The estimating funnel is incorrectly applied
Teams are using consistent but flawed assumptions
Planning.w: Converging but inaccurate estimates indicate shared incorrect assumptions rather than improved accuracy.

Planning.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager wants to anticipate which developments could cause the critical path to shift to a different sequence of activities. He is considering several things that might happen across the network. Which TWO scenarios could cause a change in the critical path?
Planning.w: Changes to critical or near-critical activities can shift the critical path.

Planning.q: During an infrastructure project, successive estimates are narrowing but still diverge significantly between engineering and procurement teams. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: Procurement has insufficient authority to influence cost estimates
Differences in estimating techniques are creating inconsistent assumptions
Engineering estimates are always more reliable than procurement estimates
The estimating funnel requires all estimates to converge at the same rate
The project has moved beyond the estimating phase
Planning.w: Divergence often reflects inconsistent assumptions or methods rather than process failure. Alignment of assumptions is critical as estimates mature.

Planning.q: A project manager sets a milestone in the plan to mark the completion of a significant piece of work but does not define any acceptance criteria against which it will be judged complete. What is the most likely outcome of defining the milestone in this way?
o: More consistent reporting across the project stages
Reduced effort needed to validate the milestone output
Stronger stakeholder confidence in the milestone status
Faster agreement on when the milestone is complete
Ambiguity in determining whether the milestone is achieved
Planning.w: Without criteria, milestone completion becomes subjective and difficult to validate.

Planning.q: A sponsor has asked the project manager to bring the planned completion date forward and is pressing for the most effective scheduling response. The manager is deciding where to direct compression effort within the network. Which action would most effectively reduce the overall project duration?
o: Adding extra float into the schedule
Extending the durations of critical activities
Reducing the duration of critical activities
Shortening the duration of non-critical activities
Planning.w: Only reducing critical path durations directly shortens the overall project timeline.

Planning.q: In a project with evolving requirements, a project manager continues to refine estimates without revisiting initial assumptions. What risk does this create?
o: The project will automatically reduce its overall uncertainty
The estimating funnel will cease to apply to the project
Estimates will converge far faster than the funnel predicts
Underlying assumptions may no longer reflect reality, reducing estimate credibility
Stakeholders will automatically gain greater confidence in the estimates
Planning.w: If assumptions are not updated, estimates may appear precise but are based on outdated context, undermining reliability.

Planning.q: A project manager reports that the project is ‘on track’ based on overall percentage completion, despite several critical activities being delayed. What is the key issue with this approach?
o: Percentage completion provides too much detail for stakeholders
Stakeholders prefer qualitative updates over quantitative data
Critical activities are less important than overall progress
Progress reporting should focus only on completed tasks
Aggregated progress can mask issues affecting critical activities
Planning.w: High-level metrics like percentage completion can hide critical delays, leading to misleading status reporting.

Planning.q: Under pressure from senior stakeholders, a project manager considers presenting tightly specified cost and schedule figures very early in the lifecycle, even though the underlying information is still limited. Which TWO outcomes are the most likely risks of presenting such overly precise estimates at this stage?
Planning.w: False precision leads to unrealistic expectations and poor decisions.

Planning.q: A stakeholder insists that narrowing estimate ranges indicate improved team performance rather than reduced uncertainty. What is the correct interpretation?
o: Narrowing ranges typically reflect reduced uncertainty as information improves
Narrowing ranges have no real bearing on uncertainty
Narrowing ranges always demonstrate genuinely improved team performance
Narrowing ranges usually indicate poor or manipulated estimating
Narrowing ranges should generally be avoided during planning
Planning.w: The estimating funnel narrows as uncertainty reduces with better information, not necessarily due to team performance.

Planning.q: A steering group receives a project report in which every activity is shown as 'green', despite the fact that several delays are already well known to the delivery team. What does this discrepancy most clearly indicate?
o: The project manager is reducing unnecessary detail
The project is performing well overall
The reporting system is highly efficient
Status reporting is not accurately reflecting project reality
Planning.w: Misleading status indicators undermine transparency and decision-making.

Planning.q: A project manager identifies that several activities appear independent but later discovers delays due to hidden dependencies. What is the most likely cause?
o: The timeline was too aggressive for the project scope
The critical path was incorrectly calculated
Activities were incorrectly sequenced due to incomplete dependency identification
Resources were not allocated efficiently across tasks
Planning.w: Hidden dependencies typically arise from incomplete identification during planning, leading to sequencing issues and delays.

Planning.q: While building a network diagram, a project manager is defining the logical relationship between two activities, A and B. Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates a finish-to-start dependency between them?
o: Activity B can start once Activity A has finished
Activity B must finish before Activity A starts
Activity B can start once Activity A has started
Activity B overlaps fully with Activity A
Activity B runs independently of Activity A
Planning.w: Finish-to-start means the successor begins only after the predecessor finishes.

Planning.q: A project manager reviews a schedule that clearly shows many dependencies between activities, yet delivery is repeatedly hampered by delays that were not anticipated. On closer inspection the logical order of the work does not match how the tasks can realistically be carried out. What is the most likely underlying issue?
o: Stakeholders are not sufficiently engaged in delivery
Individual activities have been estimated too short
Sequencing does not reflect actual execution constraints
Dependencies have been documented in excessive detail
The timeline contains too much granular detail
Planning.w: If sequencing does not reflect real-world constraints, dependencies may exist but not be accurate, causing delays.

Planning.q: A project manager is pressured to reduce the estimate range to satisfy stakeholders without additional information. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reduce the range arbitrarily to preserve stakeholder confidence now
Delay communication until the estimates naturally converge later
Increase the contingency reserve to compensate for the pressure
Explain that reducing range requires reducing uncertainty through additional information
Present the range midpoint as the single final estimate
Planning.w: Estimate ranges reflect uncertainty; reducing them without new information misrepresents reality.

Planning.q: A sponsor challenges a project timeline that shows several activities running in parallel, arguing that the plan is overly optimistic. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Recalculate the schedule using only sequential activities
Demonstrate the logical dependencies that allow parallel sequencing
Remove parallel activities to reduce perceived risk
Delay the project start until sequencing is simplified
Extend all activity durations to create buffer
Planning.w: Parallel activities are valid where dependencies allow. The key is to justify sequencing based on logical relationships rather than perception.

Planning.q: A project manager defines multiple milestones but notices they are not being used in reporting or decision-making. What is the most likely issue?
o: Milestones should only be used at the end of the project
Milestones are not aligned to meaningful control points in the project
Milestones are only relevant for large projects
Stakeholders are not interested in milestone tracking
Milestones are too detailed and should be removed
Planning.w: Milestones must represent meaningful control points to support decision-making and progress tracking.

Planning.q: A project has formally moved from the concept phase into the design phase, yet the cost and schedule estimates the project manager presents remain almost as wide as they were at the outset. Given the expectations of the estimating funnel, what is the most likely explanation for this?
o: Stakeholders are actively resisting the required changes
Uncertainty has not been sufficiently reduced through analysis
The estimating process has already been fully completed
The project has been significantly overestimated throughout
The estimating funnel does not apply to this project
Planning.w: If estimates remain wide, uncertainty has not been adequately addressed despite phase progression.

Planning.q: A sponsor requests cost certainty before approving the next phase, despite the project being in early concept stages. Which approach best balances governance and uncertainty?
o: Provide a detailed bottom-up estimate regardless of available information
Commit to a fixed cost and manage deviations later
Present staged estimates linked to decision gates with defined tolerances
Delay approval until cost certainty is achievable
Escalate the request as unrealistic and refuse to proceed
Planning.w: Linking estimates to decision gates aligns with the estimating funnel and governance, enabling progressive refinement rather than premature certainty.

Planning.q: A project manager issues thorough written progress reports to stakeholders every week, yet those same stakeholders continue to complain that they feel poorly informed about the project. What is the most likely reason for this disconnect?
o: The stakeholders have chosen to disengage from the project
The weekly reporting cycle occurs far too frequently now
The project manager is communicating far too much overall
The reports simply do not contain enough underlying detail
The reports are not aligned with stakeholder information needs
Planning.w: Effective reporting must be tailored to stakeholder needs, not just frequency or detail.

Planning.q: A project manager is arranging the order in which the activities in a work package will be carried out and wants the sequence to be both logically sound and achievable in practice. Which TWO factors are most critical when determining the sequencing of these activities?
Planning.w: Sequencing depends on logical relationships and resource constraints, both of which influence execution order.

Planning.q: To save time, a project manager adopts a single fixed report format and issues an identical report to every stakeholder, from the executive board through to the delivery team. What risk does using one standard format for all stakeholders create?
o: Reduced ability to standardise future project reporting
Increased time spent producing each individual report
Failure to meet different stakeholder information needs
Greater difficulty in archiving the completed reports
Loss of consistency across the reports issued
Planning.w: Different stakeholders require different levels and types of information for effective decision-making.

Planning.q: As a project moves from its early concept work through detailed planning and into delivery, the project manager observes that the estimates become steadily more dependable. Which TWO factors most strongly influence this improvement in estimate accuracy as the project progresses?
Planning.w: Accuracy improves with better data and clearer scope.

Planning.q: A delay occurs on a critical activity, but the project completion date does not change. What is the most plausible explanation?
o: The activity was incorrectly identified as critical
Float was available on the critical path
Additional resources were added to compensate
Planning.w: Critical activities have zero float; if a delay does not affect completion, it was not truly critical.

Planning.q: A project manager has been building a schedule while taking no account of the float on various activities as he plans and sequences the work. An assurance reviewer cautions that this oversight carries consequences. Which TWO risks are associated with ignoring float in scheduling decisions?
o: Unexpected delays affecting the critical path
Planning.w: Ignoring float can lead to resource misallocation and delays impacting critical activities.

Planning.q: When constructing the schedule network for a project, a project manager is aware that the logical relationships between activities must be defined correctly. If some of these dependencies are set up incorrectly, which TWO consequences are the most likely to result?
Planning.w: Incorrect dependencies distort sequencing and critical path, leading to delays and rework.

Planning.q: A project manager is examining a network diagram and needs to work out which activities lie on the critical path by applying the correct defining test. She wants to reason from the underlying rule rather than a general impression. Which situation most accurately indicates that an activity is on the critical path?
o: It is the most complex task
It is the first activity in the schedule
It has the longest duration in the project
It has zero float and directly impacts project completion
Planning.w: Critical path activities have zero float and directly affect project duration.

Resource Management.q: When staffing a project with several distinct work packages, the project manager assesses both how many people and which specific competencies will be needed. Why is it important to determine both the number and the skills of people needed for a project?
o: To reduce the amount of documentation the team produces
To ensure all required tasks are completed to the right standard
To ensure every team member carries an identical workload
To allow the project deadline to be brought forward
To keep the overall staffing cost as low as possible
Resource Management.w: Right skills and headcount ensure activities are completed properly and on time.

n.4: Cost control is important, but not the primary reason.
n.2: Communication is always essential.
n.3: Efficient resource planning should support timely delivery.
n.0: Team motivation should be supported, not minimised.

Resource Management.q: A project team is finalising its schedule and finds that resource demand repeatedly exceeds what is available. The sponsor has confirmed that the completion date is not fixed and can flex if needed. In this situation, why might the team choose resource levelling instead of smoothing?
o: When the fixed end date must be protected above all
When deadlines are flexible and avoiding resource overload is critical
When only the financial budget needs rebalancing across tasks
When resource availability constraints can be safely disregarded entirely
When accelerating delivery outweighs any resource overload concerns
Resource Management.w: Levelling is chosen if resource limits require relaxing deadlines.

n.0: Smoothing is better for fixed deadlines.
n.3: Ignoring constraints risks failure.
n.2: All types of resources must be managed.
n.4: Levelling often slows the project down.

Resource Management.q: A project’s OBS is incomplete and missing key roles. What is a potential risk if the RACI is created from this incomplete structure?
o: The risk register will be unnecessary
There will be no need for quality assurance
All team members will have too many tasks
The project will always finish ahead of schedule
Important responsibilities may not be assigned
Resource Management.w: If key roles are missing, important tasks may be unassigned or overlooked in the RACI.

n.3: Schedules are not directly controlled by the RACI.
n.2: Under-assignment is just as likely as over-assignment.
n.0: Risk management is always required.
n.1: Quality must always be checked regardless of structure.

Resource Management.q: A project manager wants both a clear picture of the team structure and a precise breakdown of who is responsible for each activity. Why might a project manager use both an organisational breakdown structure and a RACI matrix?
o: To double the number of project meetings
To ensure roles are defined and responsibilities are clearly allocated
To track the use of office stationery
To eliminate the need for project reports
To reduce the size of the project team
Resource Management.w: Using both tools provides a full picture of who is in the project and what they are responsible for.

n.0: Meetings are unrelated to OBS and RACI.
n.2: Office stationery is not a project management concern.
n.4: Team size is determined by project needs.
n.3: Reporting remains essential.

Resource Management.q: A software development project has a fixed release date, and the network shows that some non-critical tasks have available float. The project manager applies resource smoothing to deal with periods where developers are over-allocated. Which result is expected from this approach?
o: Additional resources are hired to keep every task on time
Resource availability limits are raised so no tasks need shifting
The project end date slips later to resolve the conflicts
Non-critical tasks are shifted within their float to avoid resource overloads
Critical path tasks are delayed to relieve the resource overloads
Resource Management.w: Smoothing keeps the project on time by using float on non-critical tasks.

n.4: Delays are avoided in smoothing.
n.2: Budget may not change.
n.1: Critical activities remain unchanged.
n.0: Quality should be maintained.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is planning a project delivered through a sequence of distinct, non-overlapping phases and needs to decide how resources will be committed to the work. Which of the following best describes resource allocation in a linear (waterfall) life cycle?
o: Resources are assigned at random all throughout the whole project
Resource allocation is decided only once the whole project closes
Resources are allocated in advance to each phase, following a sequential plan
Resources can never be adjusted after they are first assigned
All resources are shared across every phase at the same time
Resource Management.w: In linear life cycles, resources are assigned to each sequential phase as per the plan.

n.4: Simultaneous resource sharing is more typical of iterative cycles.
n.1: Allocation must occur before closure to deliver the work.
n.3: Resource needs may be reviewed at stage gates.
n.0: Allocation is structured, not random.

Resource Management.q: A software development project using an iterative approach needs test resources for every cycle. What does this illustrate about resource allocation?
o: Certain resources must be available repeatedly, not just once
Material resources are not used in software projects
Financial resources are always more important
Resource allocation is not required in iterative projects
Resources are only needed at the end
Resource Management.w: Iterative cycles require certain resources to be scheduled for multiple rounds.

n.4: Some resources are needed throughout, not just at the end.
n.2: Financial and non-financial resources may be equally critical.
n.1: Material resources (like hardware) can be necessary.
n.3: Resource allocation is required in every life cycle.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is deciding between resource smoothing and resource levelling for a plan where the demand on specialist staff is uncertain and the sponsor has agreed the completion date can move if necessary. Which scenario would require resource levelling instead of smoothing?
o: No resource conflicts exist anywhere across the project schedule
The critical path must stay unchanged throughout the delivery
The project end date is flexible and resource availability is unpredictable
Resource usage already remains comfortably within the agreed limits
All project deadlines are fixed and the end date is immovable
Resource Management.w: Levelling is used when deadlines can move to resolve resource shortages.

n.4: Smoothing is used for fixed deadlines.
n.3: If there are no conflicts, neither method is needed.
n.0: Levelling may alter the critical path.
n.1: Critical path changes may occur with levelling.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is comparing how resources are committed in a linear, sequential approach with how they are committed in an iterative, cyclical one. How does resource allocation differ between linear and iterative life cycles?
o: Iterative cycles require more flexible resource allocation as priorities may shift each iteration
Linear life cycles will rely only on financial resources all throughout
Linear cycles require resources to be allocated at random each phase
Both approaches will always follow exactly the same fixed resource plan
Iterative cycles never make any use of the available material resources
Resource Management.w: Iterative cycles demand flexibility to adjust resources as work is reprioritised in each cycle.

n.2: Linear allocation is structured, not random.
n.3: Plans are tailored to the life cycle.
n.4: Material resources may be needed in all cycles.
n.1: Financial, human, and material resources are all important.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is worried that the current plan will push several team members beyond their available hours, yet the contractual delivery date cannot be moved under any circumstances. Which technique is the most suitable for the project manager to apply in this situation?
Resource Management.w: Smoothing is appropriate when deadlines must be maintained, and resource usage needs to be controlled.

n.4: Levelling may cause delays.
n.0: Risk transfer is about managing threats.
n.3: Quality should not be compromised.
n.1: Random allocation is not a valid technique.

Resource Management.q: In a product launch project, the marketing manager is marked as 'A' for a task in the RACI. What does this mean?
o: They must perform the task directly
They are only consulted if issues arise
They only provide information, not decisions
The marketing manager is Accountable for the task’s completion
They have no involvement with the task
Resource Management.w: 'A' means Accountable, the person who must answer for task completion, not always the doer.

n.0: Responsibility is 'R'; accountability is about oversight.
n.2: Consulted ('C') provide input, not just information.
n.4: No involvement would mean no entry in the matrix.
n.1: Consulted are included, but accountability is a separate role.

Resource Management.q: A project manager expects priorities to shift often and people and equipment to be moved between tasks repeatedly as the work evolves. In which life cycle is it most common to reassign resources between tasks as priorities change frequently?
Resource Management.w: Frequent reassignment is a hallmark of iterative cycles, supporting adaptability.

n.3: Linear cycles tend to keep allocations fixed per phase.
n.1: All phases may require resource reassignment in iterative cycles.
n.4: Resource allocation is not restricted to procurement or testing.
n.0: Adaptation happens in all project stages if needed.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is preparing the organisational breakdown structure (OBS) for a new IT system implementation. Why is the OBS important before creating a RACI matrix?
o: It provides the overall strategy for mitigating the project risks
It sets the sequence and dates of project activities
It finalises the list of materials the project needs
It identifies all roles and reporting lines needed for assigning responsibilities
It establishes the total budget for the whole project
Resource Management.w: The OBS defines project roles, which is the foundation for building a responsibility matrix like RACI.

n.4: Budgeting is managed separately from OBS.
n.1: The schedule is not defined by the OBS.
n.2: Materials are detailed in other documents.
n.0: Risk mitigation is handled through other processes.

Resource Management.q: On a project that has been reorganised, the RACI matrix still reflects the old team layout and no longer matches how the project is actually staffed. What can happen as a result of this mismatch?
o: The immediate closure of the whole project
A reduced need for communication between members
Faster and easier decision making across the team
The automatic identification of every project risk
Confusion and missed responsibilities due to misaligned assignments
Resource Management.w: A RACI that does not match the real team structure leads to confusion and possible errors.

n.2: Decisions may actually be delayed if roles are unclear.
n.0: Projects will continue until closed properly.
n.1: Communication is even more important if RACI is unclear.
n.3: Risks must still be actively identified and managed.

Resource Management.q: A project manager needs a structured document that sets out the types and quantities of people, equipment and materials required across the project's activities. Which document typically details the types and quantities of resources required for project activities?
Resource Management.w: A resource breakdown structure (RBS) lists all resources needed for the project.

n.4: Communication plans do not list resource requirements.
n.1: The risk register records risks, not resources.
n.3: The issue log records project issues.
n.2: Marketing strategy is not a project resource tool.

Resource Management.q: A construction project uses a linear life cycle. Which of the following resources is most likely categorised and allocated at the start of the build phase?
Resource Management.w: Tangible resources for the build phase are identified and allocated before work starts.

n.4: Sponsors provide governance, not build resources.
n.3: Marketing consultants are more relevant post-build.
n.1: Support staff and testers are needed in later stages.
n.2: Testing comes after the build phase.

Resource Management.q: On a sequentially phased project, resources for a later phase have not been secured in time for when that phase is due to start. What is a typical risk of this poor resource allocation in a linear life cycle?
o: All of the project risks will be completely eliminated altogether
Additional project resources will simply be created by default here
The whole project will turn iterative instead of staying linear
Project phases may be delayed if resources are not available as scheduled
Stakeholder engagement will automatically rise right across the whole project
Resource Management.w: If resources are not available when needed, sequential phases will be delayed.

n.4: Engagement is a separate management area.
n.2: The life cycle model does not change automatically.
n.0: Poor allocation increases risks.
n.1: Resource creation requires planning and investment.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is filling in a RACI matrix for a series of engineering tasks and wants to make sure each of the four role letters is applied correctly against every activity. In the RACI matrix, what does the 'C' stand for?
Resource Management.w: 'C' in RACI stands for Consulted, indicating those who provide input before a decision or action.

n.3: Controlled is not part of RACI.
n.1: Completed refers to tasks, not RACI roles.
n.2: Certified is unrelated to responsibility assignment.
n.0: Calculated is not a RACI role.

Resource Management.q: A software development project needs access to a secure testing environment. What should be checked before scheduling the test phase?
o: The visual layout and décor of the testing room
The availability of the testing environment and required personnel
The seating capacity of the main project office
The catering arrangements booked for the testing team
The number of followers on the project channel
Resource Management.w: Access to the right environment and staff is crucial for test phase success.

n.2: Kitchen size does not affect testing.
n.4: Social media is irrelevant to testing resources.
n.0: Room colour does not impact test capability.
n.3: Catering is not essential for testing environment availability.

Resource Management.q: A project team delivers work through successive iterations, adjusting who works on what at the start of each cycle. Which statement best summarises resource allocation in an iterative project?
o: External supplier resources are excluded from every iteration's allocation
Resources are reassigned as work priorities and tasks evolve each cycle
Only the financial budget is treated as an allocatable project resource
Resources are categorised only once, during the initiation phase alone
Resources are committed in full at project start and never reassigned
Resource Management.w: Resources are regularly adjusted to suit current iteration needs.

n.4: This is a feature of linear cycles.
n.3: Categorisation is essential for both cycle types.
n.2: Human, material, and equipment resources also matter.
n.0: Suppliers may be used in any project.

Resource Management.q: A project team has produced an organisational breakdown structure showing who sits in which team, but has not yet developed a RACI matrix. What is a potential disadvantage of this?
o: The complete removal of every single project risk involved
The immediate failure of the entire project delivery effort
Lack of clarity on exactly who does what for each activity
The automatic approval of all of the project documents
No further requirement to carry out any stakeholder analysis
Resource Management.w: OBS gives structure, but only RACI specifies precise responsibility for each task.

n.0: Risks remain regardless of documentation.
n.1: Lack of RACI does not guarantee failure, but increases confusion.
n.4: Stakeholder analysis is still needed.
n.3: Document approval follows other processes.

Resource Management.q: A newly appointed project manager is compiling a list of the resources needed to deliver an office relocation and wants to be sure each item genuinely counts as a project resource. Which of the following is NOT typically considered a project resource?
o: Specialist equipment required for the tasks
Members of the assigned project team
Raw materials consumed during project tasks
Resource Management.w: An annual report is a document, not a resource used to deliver project activities.

n.3: Team members are human resources.
n.1: Equipment is a tangible resource.
n.4: Materials are resources needed to carry out tasks.
n.2: Budget is a financial resource.

Resource Management.q: A project manager wants to group and commit all the resources needed for each phase up front, before any of the work in that phase starts. Which type of project life cycle is most likely to categorise resources for each distinct phase before work begins?
Resource Management.w: Linear cycles categorise and allocate resources in advance, phase by phase.

n.0: Iterative cycles assign resources for each iteration.
n.2: Hybrid approaches may use either method.
n.4: Procurement is a component, not a cycle type.
n.3: Risk-driven allocation is part of risk management, not a life cycle.

Resource Management.q: A project’s timeline is tight and relies on a key supplier’s materials. What should the project manager confirm before starting work?
o: The supplier can deliver materials when needed
The project team’s favourite lunch options
Resource Management.w: Resource planning includes confirming external suppliers will deliver as scheduled.

n.4: Lunch preferences are irrelevant to delivery timelines.
n.0: Annual reports don’t confirm material delivery.
n.1: Logos are not relevant to material scheduling.
n.3: Unrelated meeting schedules do not affect the supplier’s timing.

Resource Management.q: Before assigning roles across a RACI matrix, a project manager first maps out the project's teams and reporting lines. When developing a RACI matrix, why is it important to have an accurate organisational breakdown structure?
o: It takes the place of formal stakeholder analysis work
It guarantees the project will be delivered on time
It ensures all necessary roles are identified for assignment of responsibilities
It sets the format used for the communication plan
It removes the need for any project risk management
Resource Management.w: An accurate OBS is essential to ensure all roles are covered and responsibilities can be allocated effectively.

n.1: Finishing on time depends on many factors beyond the OBS and RACI.
n.4: Risk management is still required.
n.0: Stakeholder analysis remains a separate activity.
n.3: The OBS does not dictate communication formats.

Resource Management.q: A construction project is delivered by separate design, build and test teams, and the project manager needs to allocate responsibilities clearly across them. How can the organisational breakdown structure help with responsibility allocation?
o: It maps teams and individuals, providing clarity for the RACI matrix
It determines the construction materials that the project will require
It documents the local building codes that will apply here
It calculates the overtime payments that are owed to staff
It sets the calendar dates for each of the project milestones
Resource Management.w: The OBS shows who is in each team, making it possible to assign RACI roles clearly.

n.1: Materials are managed elsewhere.
n.4: Milestone dates come from the project plan, not the OBS.
n.3: OBS does not deal with payroll.
n.2: Regulations are a compliance issue, not for the OBS.

Resource Management.q: A construction project faces a shortage of specialist equipment. The project manager moves several activities to later dates, extending the project timeline. What is this an example of?
Resource Management.w: Levelling delays activities to ensure resources are available, even if the project runs longer.

n.0: Smoothing would avoid changing end dates.
n.2: Fast tracking involves parallel activities, not delay.
n.1: Exploitation is about using opportunities, not rescheduling.
n.3: Scope expansion is not relevant here.

Resource Management.q: A project uses a linear life cycle to build a bridge. What is a typical resource categorisation for this project?
o: Only financial resources considered right across the whole project
All resources assigned only during the initial design phase
Resources categorised only after the whole project has finished
Resources grouped by phase, such as design, build, and test teams
No resources needed at all for the build phase
Resource Management.w: In linear cycles, resources are assigned according to sequential project phases.

n.1: Each phase needs its own allocation.
n.4: The build phase is resource-intensive.
n.2: Resource planning happens before execution.
n.0: Many resource types are involved.

Resource Management.q: A project manager finds that several team members are scheduled to work on multiple activities at the same time, exceeding their available capacity. To resolve these conflicts, the manager decides to apply resource levelling across the plan. What might happen to the project schedule as a result?
o: Resource limits are ignored to preserve the original end date
The end date may be delayed to resolve resource conflicts
The critical path remains unchanged despite the resource conflicts
Activities are compressed so the project finishes earlier than planned
Overall project costs are always reduced when levelling is applied
Resource Management.w: Levelling resolves resource clashes by allowing schedule adjustments, potentially causing delays.

n.3: Levelling can require more time, not less.
n.0: Allocation is central to both levelling and smoothing.
n.4: Costs may rise or fall depending on adjustments.
n.2: Risks must always be managed.

Resource Management.q: Why should the OBS be regularly updated throughout a project?
o: Because it finalises the total budget for the project
Because it locks the RACI matrix at project start
Because it removes every risk the project might face
Because it sets the quality standards for the deliverables
Because roles or team members can change, affecting RACI assignments
Resource Management.w: Updates to the OBS ensure new roles or staff changes are reflected in responsibility assignment.

n.3: Quality standards are managed separately.
n.0: Budgeting is a separate process.
n.1: The RACI should be flexible as the project evolves.
n.2: Risks must always be managed, not avoided through documentation.

Resource Management.q: In a scenario where multiple people are marked 'R' for a single task in the RACI, what risk can arise?
o: Automatic success across the whole project
Duplication of effort or confusion over responsibility
The complete elimination of all project risks
Clearer and stronger lines of individual accountability
A reduced need for team communication overall
Resource Management.w: Multiple people as 'Responsible' can cause overlap, confusion, or missed steps.

n.4: Communication needs may increase to resolve confusion.
n.2: Risks are always present.
n.0: Success depends on clarity and execution, not just the RACI.
n.3: Accountability may actually become less clear.

Resource Management.q: A project requires delivery vans for a marketing campaign, but another department is using them for a separate project. What should the project manager do?
o: Deliver the whole campaign using office-based staff only
Postpone every project activity until the vans are free
Proceed with the campaign without any transport arranged
Cancel the other department’s booking to take the vans
Negotiate a schedule to share the vans or seek alternatives
Resource Management.w: Negotiation or finding alternatives ensures that required resources are available when needed.

n.2: Transport is essential for a delivery campaign.
n.3: Budget increases must be justified.
n.1: Delays should be a last resort.
n.0: Office-based staff may not meet delivery requirements.

Resource Management.q: A project is operating with very limited specialist resources and a tightly packed schedule that contains little float. The project manager intends to rely on resource smoothing alone to manage periods of over-allocation. What is a potential risk of taking only this approach on such a resource-constrained project?
o: The project budget can never be exceeded under smoothing
Every scheduling risk is eliminated once smoothing is applied
Resource limits may still be breached if float is insufficient
All resource conflicts are guaranteed to be fully resolved
The project will always finish ahead of its planned schedule
Resource Management.w: If there isn’t enough float, smoothing alone may not resolve overallocation.

n.4: Finishing early is not guaranteed.
n.3: Some conflicts may persist.
n.0: Budget can still be at risk.
n.1: Risks must always be managed.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is working through a RACI matrix and assigning one of the four role letters to each stakeholder against every activity. In a RACI matrix, what does the 'I' stand for?
Resource Management.w: 'I' is for Informed, meaning the person who must be kept up to date on progress.

n.3: Instructed is not used in RACI.
n.1: Initiated is not a RACI role.
n.2: Invested does not relate to RACI.
n.0: Integrated is unrelated to responsibility assignment.

Resource Management.q: While planning a project that relies on a small pool of specialist engineers shared across the organisation, the project manager reviews when those engineers can be released to the work. During project planning, why is it important to check the availability of specialist staff?
o: To reduce the need for quality assurance
To avoid scheduling conflicts and potential delays
To increase the number of project meetings
Resource Management.w: Specialist staff may have other commitments—checking their availability helps avoid bottlenecks.

n.2: Quality assurance is always needed.
n.0: Risks must be managed, not ignored.
n.4: Meetings should be purposeful.
n.1: Scope change is not related to resource checks.

Resource Management.q: Between iterations on an agile-style project, the team pauses to reassess how people and equipment are deployed before starting the next cycle. What is a key benefit of these resource allocation reviews in iterative life cycles?
o: Guarantees the resource budget remains fixed across all iterations
Removes the need for any planning meetings between iterations
Confirms that upfront planning at project start is unnecessary
Ability to adapt resource allocation to changing project needs
Sets a final allocation that later reviews cannot alter
Resource Management.w: Reviewing allocation lets the team respond to new priorities and information each cycle.

n.0: Budgets may change if priorities shift.
n.1: Meetings are still required for communication.
n.2: Initial planning is always necessary.
n.4: Risks must still be managed.

Resource Management.q: A project needs specialist analytics work that the organisation's own staff are not trained for and cannot cover within the timeframe. Why might a project require external resources rather than just using internal staff?
o: To access specialist skills or additional capacity not available in-house
To remove the need to manage any project risks
To transfer full accountability for delivery onto the supplier
To guarantee the work will always cost less overall
To avoid having to plan the project schedule internally
Resource Management.w: External resources are often needed when internal staff lack the required skills or availability.

n.2: The aim is efficiency, not unnecessary complexity.
n.4: Quality should always be maintained or improved.
n.3: Good resource planning supports scheduling, not ignores it.
n.1: Risks can never be fully eliminated.

Resource Management.q: A project team must use a shared meeting space that is often booked for other purposes. What’s the best approach to ensuring this resource is available when needed?
o: Replace all project meetings with email updates instead
Reduce the number of project meetings held each week
Book the meeting space well in advance and confirm reservations
Reserve the space exclusively for senior management use
Hold meetings only when the space is unexpectedly free
Resource Management.w: Advance booking and confirmation is the best way to secure a shared resource.

n.1: Meeting frequency should meet project needs.
n.0: Not all issues can be resolved via email.
n.4: Meetings may be necessary for project progress.
n.3: Resource allocation should be based on project need, not status.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is assessing which factors could affect whether key resources will be available when the schedule requires them. Which of the following would NOT be considered when assessing the availability of resources?
o: A team member’s annual leave during the project
Resource Management.w: Lunch preferences do not affect resource availability.

n.3: Annual leave affects when staff are available.
n.2: Other commitments can create resource conflicts.
n.1: Equipment maintenance can limit availability.
n.0: Location can impact material accessibility.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is drawing up the list of resources that will be required to deliver the project's activities. Which of the following is NOT a resource that may be required for project delivery?
Resource Management.w: Lunch preferences are unrelated to project resource planning.

n.1: Software is a resource required for many projects.
n.2: Funding is essential for resource acquisition.
n.3: Equipment hire may be necessary for specific tasks.
n.4: Raw materials are often critical for project work.

Resource Management.q: A project manager ensures that every entry in the RACI matrix maps back to the real teams and reporting lines set out in the organisational breakdown structure. Which is a direct benefit of aligning the RACI matrix with the organisational breakdown structure?
o: Allows a single person to fill every project role
Guarantees the project will finish under its budget
Removes the requirement to keep any project documentation
Ensures responsibility assignments match actual team roles and reporting lines
Removes the need for any regular progress reporting altogether
Resource Management.w: Alignment with the OBS ensures the RACI reflects how the project team actually functions.

n.2: Documentation remains important.
n.1: Cost depends on many factors.
n.4: Progress reporting is always required.
n.0: Roles should be distributed based on capability.

Resource Management.q: A new project manager is learning about scheduling techniques and is comparing resource smoothing and resource levelling before applying one to a plan with over-committed staff. Setting aside their differences in how they treat the end date, what do both techniques have in common?
o: They both aim to resolve resource over-allocation
They ignore the project’s resource constraints
Resource Management.w: Both techniques deal with matching resources to the needs of the schedule.

n.4: Constraints are considered in both.
n.2: Durations may stay the same or increase.
n.1: Stakeholder communication remains important.
n.0: Budget impacts depend on changes made.

Resource Management.q: An iterative project is running two development cycles that overlap in time, and each cycle draws on the same small pool of specialist testers and equipment during the same period. What is a potential resource allocation challenge in this situation?
o: All resources are automatically available when needed
Resources can only be allocated to one task per project
Competing demand for the same resources in different cycles
Resource Management.w: Overlaps can cause conflicts when different cycles require the same people or equipment.

n.1: Availability must be managed, not assumed.
n.3: Resources may be multitasked in iterative projects.
n.0: Regular review is needed in all cycles.
n.2: Sequential phases are a feature of linear, not iterative, cycles.

Resource Management.q: In an iterative cycle, a project manager adjusts resource allocation after each sprint review. What is the main benefit of this approach?
o: It removes the need to manage a project budget
It allows resources to be aligned with changing priorities and feedback
It avoids any need at all to involve project stakeholders
It fixes the team structure from start to finish
It ensures the project will never encounter any risk
Resource Management.w: Iterative approaches benefit from flexible resource allocation in response to new information.

n.4: Risks must always be managed, regardless of allocation.
n.0: Budgeting is still necessary.
n.3: Teams may change between sprints or iterations.
n.2: Stakeholder input is important in all cycles.

Resource Management.q: A project manager wants a graphical view showing how demand for particular resources rises and falls across the project timeline. Which tool can help visualise when specific resources will be needed during a project?
Resource Management.w: A resource histogram graphically shows resource requirements over time.

n.1: Risk logs track risks, not resources.
n.3: PBS details deliverables, not resource needs by time.
n.4: The PID describes the project but doesn’t visualise resource needs.
n.2: Lessons learned are collected at project end.

Resource Management.q: During planning, a project manager reviews a resource histogram that shows uneven peaks and troughs in team utilisation, but the agreed delivery date cannot move. The manager decides to apply resource smoothing to the schedule. Which of the following best describes the main goal of this technique?
o: Allocate resources while disregarding all availability constraints entirely
Keep resource usage within limits without extending the project’s critical path
Delay non-critical tasks beyond their available float deliberately
Fully load every resource up to their maximum daily capacity
Resolve overallocation by extending the project’s critical path
Resource Management.w: Smoothing prevents overallocation while maintaining delivery dates.

n.3: Overtime should be avoided if possible.
n.0: Smoothing is about respecting resource constraints.
n.4: Scope is not increased by smoothing.
n.2: Communication is always important.

Resource Management.q: A project manager adjusts the timing of non-critical tasks to keep resource usage below a set threshold, without affecting the end date. What technique is being used?
Resource Management.w: Smoothing shifts activities within float to balance resources but keeps the project on schedule.

n.2: Levelling might impact the schedule.
n.4: Risk avoidance is a separate activity.
n.0: Scope creep refers to uncontrolled scope change.
n.1: Procurement is unrelated.

Resource Management.q: A project manager is preparing for a new office relocation. Which step is most important in determining the resources needed for moving IT equipment?
o: Identify all items to be moved and required technical expertise
Agree the relocation date with the building landlord
Book the removal vehicles needed for the move day
Send a progress update to all project stakeholders
Confirm the desk layout plan for the new office
Resource Management.w: Knowing what needs moved and what skills are required ensures the right resources are secured.

n.4: Colour scheme does not affect resource planning.
n.3: Updates are useful, but not part of resource determination.
n.1: Lunch is not a primary resource for the activity.
n.2: Marketing budget is unrelated to the move.

Resource Management.q: A refurbishment project depends on a small number of qualified electricians who are in high demand across other jobs. When building the schedule for the electrical work, what should the project manager consider?
o: The colour scheme of the electrical fittings
Electrician availability and timing of electrical tasks
The advertising budget set for the campaign
The dates of upcoming team social events
The arrangement of plants around the office
Resource Management.w: Matching skilled resource availability to task timing avoids project delays.

n.2: Advertising does not impact electricians.
n.0: Poster design is not a resource concern.
n.3: Social events are not relevant to scheduling technical work.
n.4: Office plants do not affect resource scheduling.

Resource Management.q: A project manager wants to organise the project's resources into standard groupings that apply regardless of the life cycle being used. What is a common method of categorising resources in any project life cycle?
o: Using the order in which suppliers are paid
By type: human, material, equipment, and financial
By colour coding the project schedule
Resource Management.w: Standard categories are human, material, equipment, and financial.

n.3: Sponsor preference is not a method of categorisation.
n.2: Alphabetical order is unrelated to resource management.
n.4: Colour coding is a scheduling, not a resourcing tool.
n.0: Payment order is an administrative concern.

Resource Management.q: A project manager introduces a matrix to make clear who does the work, who is answerable for it, who gives input and who is kept informed for each activity. What is the primary function of a responsibility assignment matrix (RACI)?
